#3526. GTA 6 Is Apparently Everything Rockstar Promised And Then Some

At long last, Grand Theft Auto 6 launch day has come. With Rockstar's latest project steadily unlocking as the clock strikes midnight worldwide, GTA 6 reviews have gone live, and the praise has been overwhelmingly positive so far. In fact, GTA 6 is reviewing so well that it's currently tied with the 1998 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game of all time on GameSpot's sister site Metacritic, a feat that has taken 28 years to equal.

So what are the reviewers saying? Amongst the flurry of perfect scores, a lot of the consensus is geared toward the world that Rockstar Games has created for its co-protagonists to inhabit, a sandbox that reacts to you in a variety of unique and interesting ways. It's a genre-defining experience for open-world games, as Rockstar has raised the bar to a tremendously high level for any other open-world game that'll follow in its footsteps.

Here's what some reviewers have to say, and for more on the game, check out GameSpot's GTA 6 guides hub for an evolving collection of walkthroughs, tips, and tricks.

Grand Theft Auto 6

  • Platforms: PS5 and Xbox Series X|S
  • Price $80 for the Standard Edition, $100 for the Ultimate Edition
  • Release date: November 19

GameSpot -- 10/10

Only Rockstar commands the time and money necessary to make a game as dedicated to small details. And only Rockstar can execute on the realizing such a granular vision unimpeachably. The obsession with the minutia both explains and justifies the 13-year wait. This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7.  -- Tamoor Hussain [Full review]

IGN -- 100

Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played. -- Luke Reilly [Full review]

The Guardian -- 5/5

With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, over the top chaos--as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its center -- Keza MacDonald [Full review]

Destructoid -- 10/10

Grand Theft Auto 6 is part criminal come-up tale, part love story, and part life sim all wrapped up in an impossibly deep and detailed Rockstar Games open world that may never run out of things to do. For the last three-plus weeks, I have been gleefully vacationing in Vice City: robbing banks, fighting drug dealers, stealing cars, and enjoying the view while not coming close to finishing everything it has to offer. GTA 6 is finally here now, and it was well worth the wait. -- Scott Duwe [Full review]

Eurogamer -- 5/5

A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that. -- Chris Tapsell [Full review]

Bloomberg -- 5/5

It turns out that the secret ingredients to a great game are a lot of money, time and talented people. -- Jason Schreier [Full review]

Game Informer -- 10/10

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love. -- Matt Miller [Full review]

SiliconEra -- 90/100

Rockstar made strides in incorporating all the systems and the open world into the campaign in a satisfying way. But Jason and Lucia are the glue that keeps everything together. It’s their chemistry and complicity that made me want to experience everything, and it’s them that will keep me coming back. -- Daniel Bueno [Full review]

Screenhub -- 4/5

At its core, GTA 6 is a pretty good game. There are large sections where it is an absolutely epic game, and large sections that are boring and too limited. However, after I pushed through the boring parts and it opened up enough to become a proper GTA title, it became worth it. Regardless of whether the game was good, it was always going to be an inescapable cultural moment. Luckily, it’s one largely worth participating in. -- Alice Clarke [Full review]

Kotaku -- No score

GTA 6 is a truly remarkable game. A masterpiece of open-world design that brings forward the best parts of all of Rockstar’s past games into one billion-dollar adventure that is unlike anything I’ve played before. It’s a game I’ll be playing for years, and I can’t wait to talk about it with others. -- Zack Zwiezen [Full review]

The Verge -- No score

It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA 6is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it. -- Andrew Webster [Full review]

#3525. Christina Ricci Claims Her 'Mermaids' Costar Cher 'Holds a Grudge' Against Her

Christina Ricci has opened up about the alleged breakdown of her friendship with Mermaids costar Cher.

“I’m not [still in touch]. Unfortunately, she’s still mad at me, she holds a grudge,” Ricci, 46, said on the Tuesday, November 17, episode of Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen when asked by the host about their friendship after bonding on the set of the 1990 film.

When Cohen, 58, expressed shock over Ricci’s response, the Yellowjackets star broke down her perspective on what went wrong with the pop icon, 80. Ricci said that during a joint magazine interview conducted when Ricci was 19 years old, Cher had said “all these things that were not that amazing about me.”

Her story continued, “Then she left me a voicemail about how journalists are always trying to get the worst things and blah, blah, blah, and she was so sorry, and I was 19, and so I didn’t return that message.”

Cohen, who pointed out that Ricci had spoken highly of her former costar previously on his show, then concluded, “She was mad at you for not returning the message,” to which Ricci agreed before further claimed that she’s reached out to the singer since and “gotten radio silence.”

Despite the claimed friction, Ricci said that she remains fond of Cher. “I adore her, she’s the best and I absolutely, 100 percent, can imagine being Cher and being like, ‘Oh my god, they misquoted me and I’m going to call this young person and explain to her that they misquoted me,’ and then the gall of that young person to not return the call,” she explained. “I would be so pissed, I get it. Do you know what I’m saying?”

She then offered a direct message to Cher, turning to the camera and saying, “Love you, Cher, I love you so much.”

While it’s unclear which magazine had published Cher’s quotes about Ricci, Ricci did tell Rolling Stone in 1999 — when she was 19 years old — that Cher’s early support saw her land the role of Kate Flax, the daughter of Rachel Flax, played by Cher, after six auditions. She added that she avoided doing her school work while on set by hiding “in Cher’s trailer, because my tutor was too intimidated to knock on her door.”

Ricci also sung the praises of Cher in a 2024 interview with Entertainment Weekly, detailing how close they became while filming Mermaids, which also starred Winona Ryder as Kate’s older sister, Charlotte Flax. “Cher took me under her wing, and she recognized that sometimes you could be on a set, and you don’t know exactly what is going on behind the scenes — power struggles, or different issues,” Ricci told the outlet at the time. “And if you don’t know any better, and have no experience, you can think it was your fault.

She added that Cher served as a mentor at the time, concluding, “She never wanted me to feel insecure.”

#3524. Atlas Atelier Is Making Makeup for People Who Want to Be Remembered

You know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is happening vibe. The Paris-based brand makes just lipstick, blush, and a black liquid eyeliner, all engineered to be best shown off at night, maybe under the light of candles, or as you sip a cocktail or wear a jacket with strong shoulders. It’s makeup that is supposed to look like makeup. Severe is not too strong a word to use.

The brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier. “I am a New Yorker, and I’ve been living in Paris primarily for the last four or five years. When I arrived in Paris, everyone was so well-heeled that you would never see somebody wearing a gym look to go to dinner. This resonated with me about this idea of dressing up to go out no matter what you were doing, even if it’s going to a café. That was a huge inspiration for me,” she says.

Duncan knew the industry she was getting into. She’s a veteran of brands owned by Estée Lauder, including both MAC and Tom Ford Beauty, and she also worked for Cartier. Atlas Atelier—the “atlas” is in homage to Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged—just came out this fall in the US (now available at Violet Grey and Bergdorf Goodman). Vanity Fair spoke to Duncan about Paris expat life, rejecting celebrity brands, and what happens to makeup in unstable times.

The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: You know the challenges of the beauty industry. You’re not an influencer; you didn’t pick a celebrity to be the face of the brand or to partner with. Why not make it easier on yourself?

Michelle Duncan: Friends will ask, “Didn’t you want to do this with a celeb?” I wouldn’t want to. Culture and society is so focused on a quick buck right this second, which I’m totally into. I love making money very fast. This is so much about the world of Atlas, with the packaging and with the storytelling. The brand ethos of Atlas is about the night, about this seductive environment that, to me, will actually cut through the clutter in a long-term way. When a high-profile person launches a brand, the bet that they’re taking is on who they are as a person. For me, the bet is, do you buy into Atlas’s story?

Makeup has gotten very big and plastic and in some ways looks like toys. That was sort of my first remit on it. The whole brief was: We want to create something that looks like an object that you want to be able to keep. My inspirations really are the 1930s, the Art Deco, Paris moment, and how do we make it leap into the ’80s in some ways because that’s obviously also just a second extension of the ’30s?

The 1980s version of Art Deco is so good. All that lacquer and glass blocks and chrome lamps.

It felt like something that was radically different from what’s going on in the world right now, at least in beauty land. We’re exiting this no-makeup era, or hopefully exiting this quiet-luxury era. Those things were very pared back. Maybe focusing more internally about wellness and things like that. I understood that this was missing and that it was going to come back.

The idea of self-expression in a sort of glamorous way. In the 1930s, it was not a great time in the world. And if we remember, the 1980s in New York City was decadent and over the top and seemed very fun, but as a reaction to what was going on. I would argue that we are kind of in that place right now. We don’t really need to go into politics, but it is chaos right now. And so the answer to that is always this other form of self-expression.

The name of the brand is a reference to Atlas Shrugged. Are you a big fan of Ayn Rand?

I’ve always admired and been inspired by Dagny Taggart, one of the most iconic characters in 20th-century literature. She’s written as a fiercely independent entrepreneur in a male-dominated world, who is in control of her own life and embracing its complexity. When creating my business, I was trying to channel that vision of what a woman can be: intellectually formidable, professionally ambitious, and comfortable with her sensuality. I was especially struck by one moment in the novel, when Dagny draws on a statue using her lipstick, reminding us that makeup isn’t just to change our appearance—it can be a tool for women to own their own power. I wanted to create a makeup line that gave women that same feeling of confidence, ambition, and sensuality through tools like lipstick, blush, and eyeliner.

Yes. I have been wearing this winged-eyeliner situation for a very long time. Actually, since I was a teenager. If I don’t have my eyeliner on, I feel naked and I don’t feel like I have everything with me.

So you’re wearing eyeliner at home. What about the people who are reading this who may be thinking, I never go out, or I have kids, or I’m tired, or I work a lot, or all of those things? Do you want people to go out a lot? Do you go out a lot? Is it more just the mindset of going out at nighttime?

The idea of my brand is it should be a pleasure to put on makeup, and I want people to experience pleasure again and just forget about all of the things that are happening, like picking up the kids, or going to the grocery store, or getting the dry cleaning, or whatever it is. Just remembering what it means to have a nice time and be inspired by the night. I, on purpose and by design, did not launch foundations or these technical components of makeup, because that’s just not really what it’s about.

How is expat life? I know so many people who have moved to France, or they would love to move to France. What do you think that’s about?

In my social circle, it tends to consist of either people somehow in the fashion industry, the music industry, or the arts communities. A lot of those industries have just become quite commercial in America, as an example. And I haven’t lived in a lot of other countries, so I don’t really know expat life so well. But the amount of Italians that are here, the Spanish, the Germans, the Americans, and everyone just has this chaotic, frenetic energy of being around each other and doing things together. It’s pretty remarkable.

I know you’re not doing celebrity spokespeople, but who would you want if you didn’t have to think about money or access or if they already had a beauty contract?

Somebody like [the artist] Nadia Lee Cohen. She’s super glamorous. She’s quite creative. She’s a genius in a lot of ways, and she actually uses makeup as art. And then somebody like Dakota Johnson. I think she’s so chic now. Dua Lipa. I love her. She’s got the perfect energy for this. She’s there, she’s having a good time, and she’s powerful.

Do you want to expand into other products ? It feels like you could do a fragrance. Or maybe a very chic makeup remover?

I can’t wait for the day that we are able to launch a fragrance because that is one of those things you remember, along with lip color. You remember what they smell like, and when they leave the room, and so that’s the impression that Atlas is supposed to be giving—you’re remembered when you left the room.

#3523. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

#3522. GTA 6 Isn’t Worth Buying A Fancy Controller For

In all the excitement surrounding Grand Theft Auto VI (check out our 10/10 review), it might be tempting to upgrade your setup. For a game 13 years in the making, is now the time to upgrade my TV? Maybe a PS5 Pro is in order? It's a coincidence I finally upgraded my speaker system after 18 years, I swear.

One cheaper upgrade than those above you might be considering is a better controller, like a DualSense Edge or Xbox Elite controller. For all of their myriad upgrades, the most essential reason to ever buy one of these, in my opinion, is for the back paddles. Although they are not technically extra buttons, the ability to map an inconveniently placed button to one of them can make an experience far smoother. 

Some games make an exceptionally strong case for only playing with paddles. You do a lot of sprinting and picking things up in Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, and having to take my thumb off the right stick (thus temporarily locking the camera in place) is something I find to be a constant annoyance. It's such an improvement to be able to do those things while keeping my thumbs where they belong.

Grand Theft Auto VI, on the other hand, is not such an example. Rockstar has finally made a change to the default control scheme it uses in its games, mapping sprint to a click of the left stick, rather than the traditional usage of the X (PlayStation) and A (Xbox) buttons. That alone alleviates a potential argument for needing back paddles (at least as much as one can need such a thing).

That's not to say there's literally zero use for one of these pro-style controllers in GTA 6. In our experience, tapping a paddle is arguably still an improvement to clicking the left stick to sprint or holding L1/LB to bring up the weapon wheel. Enabling Focus Mode is done by clicking both sticks, which you might find awkward; accomplishing that with paddles might be comfortable for you.

GTA 6 doesn't allow its controls to be freely remapped, though there are some options available (such as reverting to that previous style of sprinting). So while there are some reasons you may want to set up the paddles of your pro controller before diving into GTA, it's safe to say that buying one just for this game ain't worth it.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the Live Shows' Y2K Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 16. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

The Voice Live Shows are in full swing on the 2026 TV schedule, and have been narrowing down Season 30’s incredible talent to the Top 10. In the latest episode of NBC’s long-running singing competition, they continued to pay tribute to the hits of the late ‘90s and early 2000s with Part 2 of Y2K Week with Team Riley and Team Kelly. From the Goo Goo Dolls hit “Iris” to The Chicks’ tune “Cowboy Take Me Away” to Keane’s indie rock track “Somewhere Only We Know,” there was a blend of musical genres that traveled all over the map and gave a glimpse into how challenging it will be to continue to cut singers, moving ever closer to the winning coach and star. I need to talk about the country music.

While veteran coach Kelly Clarkson knows firsthand what it takes to win, having taken the title four times in nine seasons, including during her first season as a coach, The Voice newbie Riley Green should not be deterred, as Season 30 is proving to be anyone’s game. Take it from this rock music fan, who’s quickly being won over by one of Team Riley’s country singers. Sure, Kelly has 14-year-old and 16-year-old powerhouse singers on her team – Brianna Cameron, who sang “Reflection” by Christina Aguilera, and Koumba Diallo, who sang the Alicia Key’s hit “Fallin’” – but it’s the teenager on Team Riley that is making the best case for crooning his way to the finals.

Country singer Joe Henley (not to be confused with Joe Hendry) is only 19 and had never played a gig before auditioning for The Voice, which only makes his journey on the show more impressive. After grabbing the attention of Kelly Clarkson and Riley Green during the Blind Auditions, making it through the Battle Rounds, and hands-down reclaiming his spot on Team Riley for Cut Week, he took on Lee Ann Womack’s “I Hope You Dance.”

It's one of those country tracks that has crossed over into the mainstream, with deeply emotional lyrics that I’ve personally connected with and that always pull on my heartstrings when I hear it. It was an unexpected choice to hear the #1 hit covered by a male, but Joe crushed it, reinforcing the possibility that he really could win it all in Season 30.

For a rock girlie to be saying that is a big deal! Just saying!

Sure, Team Adam and Team Kelly have the numbers advantage, with three singers still left on each of their teams while the other coaches only have two. I can’t believe I’m still on the country train, but I actually think that Team has a very good chance of winning in his first season, whether that’s with Joe Henley or the duo Ferryn & Brinkley. He’s proven to have an excellent ear for talent and has given great advice and guidance to his team as their performances have only gotten stronger.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who will take it all in Season 30, and if that could be country singer Joe Henley, until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

#3520. GTA 6 Finally Changed The Default Rockstar-Game Controls

If you've played Rockstar series like Grand Theft Auto or Read Dead Redemption over the past few decades, then you're familiar with their default control scheme, which maps sprinting to a face button instead of the left analog stick. But Grand Theft Auto VI isn't being hailed as a revolutionary game for nothing--at long last, the default scheme has changed.

As we learned while playing Grand Theft Auto VI, instead of the default setup mapping sprint to a button (A on Xbox and X on PS5), the game maps it to the left analog stick. However, you're free to switch it back to the style used in games like Red Dead Redemption 2, if you prefer.

This is a very handy change, because mapping sprinting to a face button effectively stops you from being able to easily do some of your other actions, unless you have no dignity like me and will use your own face to press a button when your hands are full.

The new default control scheme is far from the most impressive thing in Grand Theft Auto 6, of course. The game earned a rare 10/10 in our GTA 6 review, with Tamoor Hussain calling it "the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach."

For more on the game, check out our ever-expanding GTA 6 guides hub and learn what you should do first. That shouldn't include buying a whole new pro controller, however.

(Pumpkin shares four children with ex-husband Josh Efird.) “You’ve stood beside me and for that I’m so thankful I get to do life with you,” she added. “I’m so excited for this next chapter, for our future, for our family, and for all the memories we still have ahead of us. 🥹❤️.”

Days of Our Lives star AnnaLynne McCord revealed to People on April 11, 2026, that English rugby player Danny Cipriani popped the question on Christmas Day 2025. “I cried for 10 minutes straight," AnnaLynne recalled. "At some point, I realized I had to answer. I said, 'Yes, but I can't even speak,' and he replied, 'That's okay, it's actually a good sign that you are quiet for once.' Then, we're all laughing." Cipriani proposed with a 15-carat, emerald-cut diamond with seven round accent diamonds set in front of McCord’s friends and family, some of whom were watching virtually via Zoom. Us Weekly broke the news that the two were back together in 2024 after originally dating on and off from 2016 to 2020. “We’re together and it’s new, but we are both showing up for ourselves in life,” she told Us at the time. “And because we can show up for ourselves, we’re matching each other on every level and we’re having painful conversations of where we were, because they’re honest and they’re real and I wouldn’t want anything else.”

Former Bachelor Jake Pavelka announced his engagement to his girlfriend of two years, Aimee, on Saturday, February 14. “We went and had a great dinner and laughed and had champagne,” Pavelka told People of his November 22, 2025, proposal to Aimee at their home in Dallas, Texas. “Then we took an Uber back to our apartment. I had rose petals on the ground and a table set up with candles. We walked in the apartment and she was like, ‘What’s going on here? Did somebody break into our apartment?’ She was looking at a table trying to figure out how a candle got lit.” “When she turned around, I was down on one knee with a really pretty ring, and I asked her to marry me,” Pavelka added. “She kind of gasped and then muttered yes. It was sweet and intimate. I definitely made the right choice keeping it private. It was a really special moment.”

#3517. McDonald’s Knows You Won’t Want To Pause GTA 6 To Make Dinner

Contrary to popular belief, you'll need some nutrients to sustain your Grand Theft Auto 6 sessions this week. That means losing valuable time whipping up a meal or driving to your nearest Cluckin' Bell, but McDonald's in the US is aiming to make refueling easier by teaming up with the instant messaging app Discord.

While the fast-food chain already offers a delivery service via its McDelivery app, you won't need to reach for your smartphone to access it. Instead, you can open the McDonald's activity in Discord--which is available on console--place a McDelivery order on Uber Eats, and go back to GTA 6 while you wait for your order to arrive. Alternatively, you can also play Fast Lane Feast, a Discord-exclusive minigame where you collect burgers and chips while racing for a spot on the leaderboards.

Wait for that knock at the door, grab your grub, stuff your food-hole, and get back to your GTA 6 session after you've washed your hands. Repeat as necessary until either the game or the fast food fills the void inside you.

As the GTA 6 week kicks off across the globe — starting in Middle-earth AKA New Zealand — it looks like multiple brands are looking to get involved in what is shaping up to be a major cultural moment for interactive entertainment. KFC is holding a fake funeral in case you want to use up some of your compassionate leave to attend it and take the day off; The Weather Channel has shared a preview of Leonida's weather system, and Xbox is doing its own thing while not explicitly mentioning GTA 6 due to the marketing deal that PlayStation has with the game.

Another big promotion tonight is with the NBA's Miami Heat, as the team will represent the game with GTA 6-inspired gear and a Vice City-themed court for their match against the Milwaukee Bucks.

#3516. Vanity Fair Announces New Hires and Promotions Across Departments

Vanity Fair Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci today announced 11 new hires and appointments to the magazine’s masthead, deepening the magazine’s coverage across technology and politics, while adding talent to its operations and creative teams.

Vanity Fair’s new hires bring fresh perspectives to the magazine’s reporting on power and influence, alongside new creative voices to help shape its visual storytelling.

Maggie Coughlan is promoted to global managing editor. Since joining the team in 2021, she has held several positions at Vanity Fair, most recently as executive editor. She previously held editorial roles at the New York Post and People.com. She holds a master’s degree in digital publishing from NYU.

Emily Shugerman joins Vanity Fair as a senior staff writer reporting on wealth and politics on the West Coast. Emily comes from The San Francisco Standard, where she covered the shifting political allegiances of Silicon Valley’s richest, the fight over California’s proposed billionaire tax, and the growing power of AI lab workers. Before that, she was a reporter at The Daily Beast, where her investigations spurred leadership changes at national nonprofits and policy shifts at major corporations. Her work has also appeared in The Cut and The Guardian. She lives in San Francisco.

Jack Holmes joins as a senior editor for Vanity Fair, where he’s been editing features and political coverage since January. He will continue that work and expand into society and technology. Previously he was a senior staff writer and political editor for Esquire. He’s also the founder and publisher of The Football Weekend, a publication covering world soccer. Jack graduated from Vanderbilt University with a degree in philosophy and political science.

Nina Joyce is vice president of communications, based in New York, leading Vanity Fair’s communications globally. With 17 years of experience, she previously oversaw media relations for Condé Nast’s UK business and portfolio of brands, managing corporate reputation, brand strategy and major cultural events. Prior to joining Condé Nast, Nina spent a decade at Vice Media Group, holding senior roles across VICE, Refinery29, and i-D, and ultimately leading corporate PR across EMEA.

Roxanne Doucet joins as global visuals director. She has worked across New York and Paris, and collaborated with renowned artists and luxury houses including Dior, Loewe, and Balenciaga, building a practice rooted in fine art, documentary photography, and editorial storytelling. She was previously visual director at Vogue US and has consulted for Vogue France.

Dondre Stuetley joins Vanity Fair as senior visuals editor. Previously he was the photo editor at WSJ Magazine, commissioning stories on art, fashion, entertainment, design, food, and architecture.

Sameet Sharma joins as senior visuals editor. He was most recently the visuals director at V Magazine, and prior to V, he oversaw visual production at G-III, working on brands such as DKNY and Karl Lagerfeld. He also brings experience from Hearst magazines, where he worked on the photo teams at ELLE, Marie Claire, and Esquire.

Christian Zelaya joins as a senior designer. He brings more than five years of experience shaping editorial reporting into creative and clever visual stories for digital and social platforms and attracting readers for global brands like NBC, Forbes, and Scholastic.

Michael Kanyongolo joins Vanity Fair as audience development manager. He was most recently the news producer for Quanta Magazine, where he carried out web development, visual design, and production. He previously worked on web production at the New York Post and has a background in media and psychology.

Nazanin Hakim joins Vanity Fair as a creative producer on the video team. She brings a background in documentary filmmaking, having worked on a range of projects exploring politics, culture, and technology, including the Emmy-nominated series Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror and What’s Next? The Future With Bill Gates.

Chris Black joins Vanity Fair as a contributing editor. He is a writer, photographer, and cohost of How Long Gone. He lives in New York and Los Angeles.

What does the future hold for DC Studios?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To say that DC Studios is in the midst of a big change would be a major understatement. It was announced a little over a week ago that in the aftermath of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, James Gunn and Peter Safran would step down as co-CEOs of the studio. As a result, film producer (and Marvel Studios alum) Jeremy Latcham will lead the brand moving forward. There may, however, now be reason to believe that DC may be leaving WB and by extension, parent company Skydance. This is all due to some recent rumors.

A common claim that’s been reported in the aftermath of the Gunn/Safran news is that Skydance has acquired a lot of Warner Bros.-amassed debt following the merger. It’s been said that a number of DC Studios’ projects were particularly pricey for the company. In a wide-ranging piece, Page Six mentioned sources who alleged that Supergirl, which flopped at the box office earlier this year, lost WB $135 million. With that, X user @entylawyer alleges that Skydance wants to unload the superhero brand for monetary purposes:

The comic studio heads were fired. They didn't quit. Their boss wants to sell off the entire comic book universe to help get rid of some of that $100B debt.

Of course, all of this should be taken with a massive grain of salt, as Skydance’s David Ellison has not indicated that the company plans to sell DC Studios. If that were to actually happen, though, it would result in the availability of a major asset. If Ellison and co. were to sell it, it could theoretically draw some significant interest on the open market.

I’m honestly just not sure who would seek to acquire DC Studios if Skydance were to theoretically choose to sell it. There’s also the matter of which entertainment company would actually have the money to do it. One of the first brands that comes to mind is obviously The Walt Disney Company, which acquired Marvel Entertainment back in 2009 for $4 billion. However, another brand that should be considered as a hypothetical buyer is Netflix,the company that was set to acquire WB before Paramount made a higher bid.

All of that is just speculation but, of course, James Gunn’s DC exit is real, with him and Peter Safran officially stepping down on December 1. News of Gunn’s departure has generated disappointment from those who were all in on his DC plans, and some have expressed concerns about the future of his DCU continuity. As for the actual decision to part ways with Safran and Gunn, a source for Page Six alleged that their bosses had been in talks with Latcham for weeks ahead of the announcement despite publicly saying otherwise:

It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing.

Naturally, there are a lot of unknown variables here, and it’s currently unclear as to it or when Skydance might confirm or deny the rumor that DC Studios will be sold. In the meantime, there are still film projects from the brand that are in different stages of development as James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow is set to hit theaters on July 9 amid the 2027 movie schedule. Matt Reeves’ The Batman: Part II is also filming right now and will hit theaters on February 18, 2028.

On weekdays, he also writes TV and movie-related news and helps out with editing and social media as needed. He graduated from the University of Maryland, where he received a degree in Broadcast Journalism. After shifting into multi-platform journalism, he started working as a freelance writer and editor before joining CB. Covers superheroes, sci-fi, comedy, and almost anything else in film and TV. #3513. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang May Just Survive His Scandal

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Exactly three years ago today, the tech world found itself in an all-too-familiar crisis. On an otherwise ordinary Friday afternoon, the board of OpenAI abruptly fired Sam Altman, following a secretive deliberation about what was believed to be a pattern of deceptive behavior by the CEO. A shock wave of panic rippled through the industry: Employees rallied around Altman, who set up a makeshift war room in his Russian Hill home; investors made furious calls to the board to demand a reversal; and Satya Nadella offered to create the conditions within Microsoft for Altman and his loyalists to rebuild OpenAI from the ground up.

As the members of OpenAI’s board racked their brains for who might make a worthy replacement, the extent of their miscalculation quickly dawned on them. OpenAI could not survive without Altman, and the tech industry might not survive without OpenAI. Within four days of Altman’s firing (an event so fleeting that it came to be known as “the blip”), he was reinstated as CEO, and the board coup that failed to kill him only made him stronger.

Three years later, the foibles of a different man at a different AI company—Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post as CEO of Nvidia last week after the revelation of several compromising affairs—have thrown the industry and the stock market into tumult.

Not one to go down without a fight, Huang has reportedly hunkered down with his inner circle to plot his own comeback. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate him, pending an independent investigation not unlike the one that exonerated Altman, has garnered nearly 200,000 signatures, including from the likes of Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick, and Garry Tan. Even President Trump has weighed in, noting that he “would certainly not mind” if Huang were reinstated. The news from today’s earnings report that the company had brought in a record-breaking $100 billion+ in sales last quarter under Huang’s leadership will only help their cause.

While an inside source told CNBC yesterday that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang, the former executive is continuing to court public opinion independently. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a public statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It would be difficult to overstate Huang’s influence on the AI industry and US tech policy at large.

This entire mess has felt uncannily validating of the thesis behind Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list this fall, for which I wrote, “Never in the list’s history have the scale and the stakes of individual influence felt so high,” noting the “Ouroboros of investments and insular networks that make you realize how small and self-serving circles of power can be—and how quickly they could come tumbling down.”

We’ve officially entered the age of the too-big-to-fail CEO, in which our economy increasingly hinges on—and endlessly forgives—the moods and misdeeds of a handful of powerful men with few accountability structures. It’s not just the companies they founded that have become entwined with these founders. “The whole economy has basically been financed by Nvidia and in turn by Jensen’s ability to raise money,” says Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures.

Huang deserves a great deal of credit for having built his company from the ground up. But his trespasses—namely, becoming romantically involved with someone the State Department has linked to Chinese intelligence, and who has undeniably helped get America’s high-performance chips into the hands of our adversaries—are more than worthy of the scrutiny they’ve received.

Like a person who’s sick with a life-threatening illness but refuses to make a will, Huang demonstrated a staggeringly hubristic leadership. He had no real succession plan, installed a board and executive staff of yes-men and women, and created a “culture of omertà,” as his biographer, Stephen Witt, put it, that allowed his affairs to become an open secret within the company. Nvidia didn’t even protect itself with basic D&O insurance, which would have shielded it from the kinds of shareholder lawsuits it could now face. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq have all continued their precipitous decline since the news of his departure was announced last week.

As a result, how many of us have found ourselves asking, Why should the fate of my 401(k) have anything to do with one man’s sex life?

If you need another example, consider Musk, who has gained almost single-handed control over our space and satellite infrastructure. At SpaceX, he’s also become a master of the newly popular dual-class voting structures that have allowed founders like himself and Mark Zuckerberg to consolidate control of their companies. On more than one occasion, his erratic whims have left our geopolitical fate hanging in the balance.

Perhaps start-ups do need these larger-than-life characters to get off the ground. As Rechtman puts it to me, “Great businesses don’t get built by committee. They get built by small groups of people and singular leaders. And necessarily, in the pursuit of some huge and lofty project, a person becomes elevated to the status of ‘great.’”

But as companies mature—and especially as they go public—they owe it to themselves and to investors to outgrow their founders. Plenty of the companies keeping our economy afloat, like Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix, have indeed survived the parting of their founders.

Unfortunately, public markets are now falling victim to the same hype frenzy as VCs. AI-linked stocks now account for nearly half of the S&P 500, and 47 of those stocks made up three quarters of the index’s gains in the first half of this year. Nvidia, in one way or another, is connected to just about all of those companies through an intricate web of loans, partnerships, and investments.

So how do we deal with tech’s “great man” problem? This extreme concentration of power has helped foster a startling lack of resilience in our geopolitical and economic systems. But ask any antitrust expert, and they’ll remind you that it can also erode product quality, endanger consumer protections, and raise prices.

The answer cannot simply be for these men to improve their moral character, and it cannot be for us to become more forgiving. After all, any one of them could drop dead of a heart attack and leave us in the same predicament.

Walter Isaacson, the Silicon Valley biographer who is now interviewing many of the field’s “great men” on his new podcast, The Builders, believes the only possible answer “is to have more entrepreneurs who can build competing products, who can shoot off rockets and get them into orbit and create satellites and create chips and build fabrication plants.”

Rumors are already circulating that if he does not return to Nvidia, Huang may start his own competitive chip manufacturer, which helps explain why VCs are lining up to demonstrate their goodwill.

In the meantime, as we prepare for more mega IPOs, we would be wise to examine the structure of these deals to see what checks on power exist within these companies, from strong succession plans to empowered boards. Unfortunately, Anthropic is preparing super-voting shares for founders, which will give them decisive control over the company following its $1.4 trillion IPO. But hey, at least there are seven of them.

Amidst all the tributes and wonderful stories about Patrick Stewart that hit the internet after his passing, one other viral video stood out. Stewart's fight with actor and comedian James Corden onstage at the 2011 Glamour Awards was a rare public outburst by the legendary Star Trek actor, and one that he deeply regretted as the years passed.

For those unfamiliar, the video went viral back then when Stewart took the stage and criticized Corden, the host, for looking disinterested between awards. Corden told Stewart to "get on with presenting," which then escalated to Stewart telling the audience he could see Corden's belly sticking out from the back row. Corden jabbed back that he could see Stewart "dying" onstage due to his age, and after one odd joke involving the Jonas Brothers, the moment ended. People have seen that, but fewer might know how Stewart felt afterward.

Stewart later expressed deep regret about the incident while speaking about it to Classic FM (via Glamour). The Star Trek actor admitted he'd been drinking, and it all went off the rails once he took the stage:

My part of the evening came late and it was alcohol (that prompted the remark), I'm afraid. I went too far, I was somewhat out of control. I have nothing but admiration for Mr Corden. I still blush in remembrance of it.

Buzzfeed also reported that Stewart said elsewhere he was upset by a comment Corden made toward another actress earlier in the evening. He began to drink and, unfortunately, made comments that he regretted. Fortunately, he also confirmed that he'd spoken to the Corden since then, and they agreed to bury the hatchet.

The resurfaced viral video was the most I've seen of James Corden since he retired from late-night, and based on how he spoke about the event, I'm sure he wasn't thrilled to see it back in the news either. The comedian later said he had zero problem with Sir Patrick Stewart, and said that despite how it looked at the moment, he was not mad:

I couldn't have less of a problem with him. He just went for it, he was unscripted, and I've no idea where it was going... And I wish I hadn't looked like I was so angry. Because I was just bemused. I'm not entirely sure what he wanted to happen, but I'm sure what happened wasn't what he wanted. But you know, he's Sir Patrick Stewart and he's great. Everyone's allowed a mistake. My hunch is he's a nice guy.

It's important to know the context of how both sides felt after the fact, because unfortunately, I think people unfairly pushed a narrative about the interaction that wasn't true. The implication was that Patrick Stewart hated James Corden, who has been a polarizing figure since stepping into the limelight.

In reality, the moment went down as one of Stewart's biggest embarrassments, and went against many of the other pleasant interactions that the world knew him for. I'm glad that he found the time to reconcile with Corden after what happened all those years ago, but it's sad to see it resurface again after his death.

CinemaBlend continues to pay respects to Patrick Stewart and offers condolences to his friends and family as they mourn his death. I'm sure more stories about the actor will surface ahead of his appearance in Avengers: Doomsday, which is out in theaters on December 18th.

#3511. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

"iOS 27.3 adds three new features I've used almost every day", "Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving". What's with these terrible clickbait titles lately? Did we go back to 2014?

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

Which new iOS 27.3 features have you been enjoying in the beta? Let us know in the comments.

#3510. Apple, Chase, United Outages: What’s Going On?

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”

It feels like I could write a parody verse a day at the rate our infrastructure is faltering. A few weeks ago I wrote about the spate of cybersecurity incidents that led the industry to label last month “Black October.” Now my phone is blowing up, with everyone from colleagues to high school friends asking, what the hell is going on out there?

Are we under attack by a rogue nation? Are outdated software systems suddenly all throwing in the towel? Is this all just cyber-business as usual, with an unusually on-edge public?

I’m inclined to believe it’s some combination of all of the above. The FBI issued an urgent warning today that bad actors have been using ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration testing platform, to attempt widespread attacks. A source at a financial services company tells me, “It’s been a miserable month…. Just constant probing and hacking attempts.” Companies—and especially government agencies—with outdated software systems are scrambling to patch these vulnerabilities, and are often unable to do so securely without taking their systems entirely offline.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours,” says Snehal Antani, cofounder and CEO of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3. In other words: With AI, bad actors can pretty easily jiggle every doorknob around the globe to see who’s left their doors unlocked.

Meanwhile, the total lack of clarity from the Trump administration hasn’t exactly been reassuring. Even one administration-aligned VC partner I spoke with this morning called the joint presser between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a “clown show.”

For now, I’d urge you to heed the same advice I gave last time I wrote about this: Make sure those passwords are airtight and that multifactor authentication is activated. And maybe, just maybe, stock up on some light supplies you’d like to have around if 21st-century services stop working the way they’re supposed to.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional,” Antani tells me. “We should expect persistent disruption of digital services—travel, banking, commerce, etc.—in the coming months as these organizations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

$7 billion: That’s how much Sound Ventures, the firm founded by actor turned VC Ashton Kutcher and former music manager Guy Oseary, stands to profit from its 0.5% stake in Anthropic after the IPO this week.

#3509. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

There are few things I love more than a reality show, and after years of devouring The Traitors with my Peacock subscription, I was thrilled to hear that the folks behind that Emmy-winning series were creating another. Enter The Mob, another campy competition show that's available in its entirety with a Hulu subscription. The show once again proved that RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top-tier TV personality, but it turns out that not even the cast knew the rules when cameras went up.

The Mob's jobs feel more urgent than The Traitors' missions, but it took some adjusting to its format. Even the cast had a hard time with this, mostly because they didn't actually know all of the rules of the show they were competing on. During a recent clip from Gayety's Instagram, Willam spoke about her experience shooting the series, saying:

I asked for the rules every episode and I didn't get them until Episode 4, a printed copy. We did not know what was going on and we really wanted to. But information is power, and I understand that you don't want a reality show contestant to have power. So keeping them in dark leads to better stakes for the game and I understand that now.

Well, my mind is blown. It was hard enough to nail down the rules and format of The Mob as a viewer, but the fact that the cast was similarly clueless is truly wild to me. It didn't make the show's first four episodes any less entertaining, even though many of my favorite contestants got whacked way too early. Still, I'd think that the powers that be on production would want the reality TV personalities to at least know everything about the game they were expected to play.

As much as I enjoyed the first season of The Mob, I have to assume that the gameplay might have been even more dynamic if the cast knew the show's rules from the jump. Indeed, the first few eliminations were a little sleepy, such as Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli pledging allegiance to Joe Gorga and then immediately getting whacked.

You can see Willam Belli's comments about The Mob and feeling a bit clueless at the start of filming below:

Willam might be the only contestant from RuPaul's Drag Race to get disqualified, but that doesn't mean she went against the rules in every situation. After all, The Mob cast were starting a brand new competition series, and didn't have any previous episodes to use as a reference. The folks who caught on seemed to make it the farthest, but it was curtains for other favorites like Willam, Bruno, and Debi Mazar.

The Mob is streaming in its entirety on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if it gets renewed for a second season, and how the gameplay changes with contestants who know what to expect.

#3507. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.
