#3489. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3488. Constantine Sequel With Keanu Reeves Gets Update After James Gunn's DC Universe Exit

The entertainment world is still reeling from the recent shake-up at DC Studios. James Gunn and Peter Safran have departed their posts as heads of the studio, meaning the DC Universe is in for some big changes. In fact, Gunn's DCU is reportedly being dismantled as DC Studios prepares for another reset. Whether that's good or bad remains to be seen and will be a matter of personal opinion. However, it could be good for the long-awaited sequel "Constantine 2."

In an interview with Collider, director Francis Lawrence addressed the status of the proposed follow-up to his 2005 DC Comics adaptation starring Keanu Reeves. The "Constantine" sequel was said to be officially happening with Lawrence returning back in 2022, but updates have been few and far between ever since. And while Lawrence clarified that he doesn't "want anybody to lose their jobs," he said the latest happenings at DC Studios are ultimately beneficial to his "Constantine" follow-up. As he put it:

"We have an idea, and we have a script, and we've been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it. So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday's news that maybe now there will be another opportunity. But again, we've been trying to make this for 20-something years, and there's always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it's not me, it's not Keanu, it's not [producer] Akiva [Goldsman]. J.J. [Abrams] is on it as well. We all want to do it.

"It's really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever's running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, 'Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of 'Constantine,?" Lawrence added.

Setting aside one's personal feelings about James Gunn and Peter Safran no longer being at DC Studios, this is a movie that all involved have wanted to make for a long time. Keanu Reeves kept pestering Warner Bros. about "Constantine 2" until it said yes, but that happened before Gunn and Safran were installed to launch their DC Universe. That complicated matters. Now, the situation is complicated once again, only this time in a way that could benefit Francis Lawrence and Reeves.

We only just got word that DC Studios is developing a new John Constantine movie, but that was also before the announcement about Gunn and Safran leaving broke. Even so, Lawrence addressed that as well, suggesting that both projects could co-exist:

"Personally, I don't even care if somebody has a plan for some sort of shared universe, and they want to do another version of Constantine. If they just let us do the sequel to our version, they can coexist. So, I have renewed hope as of yesterday that there might be some possibility for forward movement there."

2005's "Constantine" wasn't an out-and-out hit at the time of its release, but it's become something of a fan favorite over time. I previously noted that a "Constantine" legacy sequel would have mixed box office prospects, yet it might just work at the right price. It's simply a matter of whether or not the regime at Skydance, Warner Bros.' new parent company, sees this as a prudent investment. Reeves is currently a bigger star than he's ever been, while Lawrence, who has shepherded the "Hunger Games" movies for years, knows how to make a hit. We'll see how things shake out.

"Constantine 2" doesn't have a release date yet, but stay tuned.

#3487. The GTA 6 Review

Rockstar’s magnum opus searches for love and catharsis in desperate times — and finds them

Who gets to break the rules in America? A cryptobro living off of financial scams. A girlboss CEO who turns feminine vulnerability into a pyramid scheme. A cop who shoots a civilian in the face and walks away scot-free. It’s an exclusive club of societally acceptable grifters and killers, and Lucia Caminos’ name isn’t on the VIP list.

When we first meet the co-star of Grand Theft Auto 6, she’s scraping the bottom of the cultural barrel. She’s a lowly street rat. The only person who seems to give a damn about her is Jason Duval, another small-time crook who connects with her during a star-crossed carjacking turned meet-cute. It doesn’t take long for the law to interrupt her rom-com dreams, landing her in prison with other low-tier riffraff crammed together like sheep in a pen.

When Lucia is finally set free, it’s not because society has decided that this financially desperate Latina has earned a second chance. It’s because of an overcrowding crisis at the jail.

In a sprawling satirical sandbox filled with loudmouth radio DJs and over-the-top conservative cartoons, it’s the sharpest stab GTA 6 lands on American culture. Justice is big business in the Florida-inspired state of Leonida, and people like Lucia are products to be cycled in and out of a flawed system. All the while, the real criminal masterminds of Leonida trash their penthouses into the wee morning hours.

Lucia’s unjust origin story is the key to understanding and embracing GTA 6’s tantalizing power fantasy, panicked parents and politicians be damned. Rockstar Games’ astonishing open-world adventure, the most impossibly grand and expensive video game that may ever exist, doesn’t just generate its morbid pleasure from cop-killing sprees and armed robberies; that comes from living in a reactive place governed by intricate rules that beg to be bent and busted. If you can learn to outmaneuver police helicopters and escape with duffel bags full of unmarked bills, you’ll be rewarded with a small taste of the law-breaking freedom that’s only offered to a certain class of crook in America.

It’s no wonder that, after decades of moral panic, GTA once again earns its title as public enemy #1 — only this time, Rockstar accomplishes that less through bloodshed and more with an empathetic love story built for an era of stark economic uncertainty. It’s a bold choice, considering the series’ cold-blooded reputation, but it’s also what makes GTA 6 one of Rockstar’s finest games to date.

Following an opening prologue that ends with Lucia behind bars, the story really kicks off as her sentence is winding down. Jason, now living in a dilapidated shack in the Keys, has found a modest living doing odd jobs for Brian, an old-timer who has mastered the art of laying low far outside of Vice City. When Jason receives word that Lucia is getting an early release, it lights a fire under him to get his house in order so that the lovers can have a chance at a normal life. Key word: normal.

The opening chapter, filled with low-level crimes and mundane roof-patching missions, makes for a strong introduction to a story about a couple scraping by. Whereas some GTA games explicitly focus on the myth of the American Dream, following wannabe kingpins who can’t get enough money and power, Jason and Lucia’s motivations are more down to Earth. The duo’s ultimate goal is to earn enough cash to skip town and support one another. While you can spend your riches on guns and designer clothing, your big-picture aim is to fill up a savings account via the in-game BuckMe cash app. That’s the real dream.

It’s a more human GTA story that’s sold by Jason and Lucia. Both characters get equal screen time during the campaign, and both are compelling leads in their own way. Jason is a veteran, a detail that’s never deeply explored, but one that subtly establishes him as a person who has been left behind. Why is he living in a leaking shack and reduced to working shady gigs while patriotic right-wing media dominates Leonida’s radio waves and TV stations? There’s a lingering sense that he’s been used and tossed aside on the literal outskirts of America.

Jason is also a true himbo: a monotone musclehead who reveals his heart of gold early on when quietly obsessing over home renovation tasks once he learns Lucia is getting out. He has the energy of a young Channing Tatum, with charm and sincerity always poking through his tough guy persona. Jason also works as the perfect straight man for the oddball rat race that is Leonida. He’s just as confused as you are when a stranger escapes a car crash and decides to hop back into the burning vehicle to ensure he gets a bigger insurance payout. The shit people will do for money in this town.

But Lucia is the real star of the power couple. She’s unapologetically brash, and has no reservations about getting back to a life of crime after getting out of prison. That can make her seem one-dimensional at first, but it’s grounded in a real anxiety that crops up between her snarkiest one-liners. A key flashback shows her struggling to make ends meet as a ride-share driver, weathering racist abuse from passengers who in turn tank her rating. There’s a sense that she’s hit a dead end in a world that hates her; even an app is rigged against her. She sees little choice but to accept risky jobs in hope that she can put even $500 into her bank account. The shit this town makes us do for money.

Leonida is full of natural predators that circle its swamps like hungry alligators.

The central story, which has the rhythm of a five-season prestige TV series, sees the couple graduating to bigger crimes and even bigger apartments as they move throughout the state. Small gigs in the Keys soon give way to harmless carjackings upstate, and then to tense bank robberies in Vice City’s urban core. While there are some thrilling heists along the way that require meticulous planning across multiple missions, the story can sag when it’s inventing elaborate excuses to tutorialize features, reposition Jason and Lucia around the map, and introduce last-minute villains in time for its rushed final stretch. Instead, its most effective moments come in all the quiet conversations that happen between bank jobs, where Jason and Lucia trade insecurities about the viability of their shared future in a place like Leonida.

That feeling does not exist in a cultural vacuum. In true South Park fashion, Rockstar takes as many potshots as it can at the current state of American culture. It plays out like a damning, if sometimes dated, retrospective of the past decade — you could subtitle it “I Hate the 2020s.” Jason finds himself tangled up in a crypto scam. Lucia stumbles into a multi-level marketing scheme disguised as a noble women’s wellness business. Flip on a radio, and you might catch the all-too familiar sounds of a conservative whining about trans athletes in school sports, only to reveal that he’s a little too eager to "protect" young girls, if you catch my drift. Leonida is full of natural predators that circle its swamps like hungry alligators.

That’s the environment that our antiheroes find themselves sinking in while the bastards swim. Petty theft will earn someone like Lucia an immediate trip to jail, but everyone else appears to be getting away with much worse. Through its satirical mirror, GTA 6 questions why some people need to play by the rules while others don’t. (You can even see that reflected in the game’s own comedic targets: Rockstar goes out of its way to avoid lampooning powerful political figures like Donald Trump, but it’s not shy about dunking on rural rednecks and people living in the slums, struggling with substance use disorders.)

It doesn’t always feel like there’s much an individual can do to topple structural inequities in real life. But in a safe digital playground like this? You can start to understand the inherent appeal of blowing off steam in GTA 6’s punching-bag world.

While there’s a lot to unpack in this downright enormous game, the basic catharsis of GTA remains unchanged here. When you’re not working through story missions filled with third-person shootouts and car chases pulled straight from a Hollywood movie, you’re free to cause as much chaos as you want in Leonida. Jack a car, mug a pedestrian at gunpoint, rob a gas station — live your criminal fantasies as long as you can before the police rain on your parade. Decades after it first stirred moral panic, GTA’s appeal remains its unmatched ability to let players see just how much they can get away with as you test your relationship to authority.

Video games are a perfect avenue for that because they’re built on rules. You can only jump this high. You can’t access this area until you’ve found the right key. Killing this character will result in this consequence. Every time you enter a new world, your immediate task is to learn the law of the land. Your second, and more fun, task becomes figuring out how and when to break those laws. GTA 6’s greatest strength is that it offers an entire nation of laws. They spill out from countless criss-crossing systems that require you to keep your head on a swivel at all times.

Steal a car without scanning it first with a phone app that reveals its security system, and you might find yourself panicking when an unseen tracker starts beeping. Fail to find someone hiding in a back room during an attempted bank heist? They’ll have enough time to get free and trigger an alarm. Robberies are an especially strong addition to GTA 6 in that respect — not just because they let you explore interior spaces, but because they require you to get every detail right. You need to act quickly to compel guards to drop their guns, threaten cashiers to hand over safe codes, or destroy any security camera footage hiding in a server room. There are so many ways you can screw up unexpectedly, but that makes it all the more satisfying when you pull off a clean getaway just before the cops pull up to the scene of the crime.

Even GTA’s signature wanted system requires much more of your attention now, as police are now able to track your car, face, and outfit if someone sees you. Listen to the cops on your scanner, and you’ll hear them sharing the vehicle and outfit you were spotted in, or even your build. You’re not even fully out of the woods when you outrun the fuzz, as you’ll leave a temporary heat level in the area you committed a crime as cops continue to look for you. My first three-star chase was a 30-minute cat-and-mouse game that had me abandoning vehicles and scrambling over fences to get away. Just when I thought I was safe after having thrown on a hat and glasses, the chase began again once a passing cop car got a look at me for a moment too long.

All of this is different for a GTA game that is chasing a certain level of hyperrealism. Here, Rockstar very much builds on the groundwork it laid in 2018’s laborious Red Dead Redemption 2. For instance, you can build muscle by following a strict workout routine that requires you to do a certain number of reps within a set time period, and even build rests into your training regiment. If you want to steal a locked car without smashing the window and setting off an alarm, you’ll need to use a slim jim to carefully pick the lock. While that attention to detail could often feel tiresome in the slow-paced world of Red Dead, everything moves mercifully faster here, which makes sense considering that you’re barreling around town in sports cars instead of plodding down dusty roads on horseback.

Still, it takes some adjusting to. In my first sessions, I found myself almost scared to do anything I wouldn’t do in real life. Something about the photorealistic visuals has changed my usual GTA brain chemistry; I was suddenly stopping at traffic lights and refusing to cut in front of cars. But that would end up being a functional anxiety. Every session offered another opportunity to see what rules I could bend. Broken traffic laws led to quiet stick-ups in isolated pawn shops led to full-scale assaults on Leonida’s most well-guarded banks. Progression like this is baked into a story of escalating crimes, but it’s also built into the very psychology of GTA 6.

It’s easy to get reductive when discussing the broad appeal of GTA. Many would have you believe that its popularity is a symptom of a sick society that glorifies crime and violence. Maybe there’s some truth to that, but it doesn’t get to the heart of the series. Its joy has more in common with a kid screwing around in class as much as they can without landing in detention. When you possess little power in the world, there’s a pleasure in getting to push what buttons you can. (Even calling out sick from work to play GTA 6 on launch day can be seen as workers exercising the tiniest bit of institutional rebellion.) That’s made all the more powerful in this story, with these characters, within this laundry list of intricate laws.

None of this would matter much if the world wasn’t worth living in, but Leonida makes for the perfect setting. An enormous map that has been in the works since 2015, as Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson told Polygon in an interview last week, GTA 6’s take on Florida packs an entire state’s worth of scenic landscapes and local eccentrics into one coherent place. While returning players might be most excited to spend time in the glitzy Vice City, that’s arguably the least interesting location in the game.

In the south, you have the Leonida Keys. Almost designed with the same tutorial zone philosophy underpinning Breath of the Wild’s Great Plateau, it perfectly captures the compact, distant nature of the real Florida Keys. It feels like you’re in a world physically detached from the state, where you don’t have a lot of avenues for escape if you go on a murder spree. It’s the perfect place to learn the rules of the road before things open up the further north you get. That stands in contrast to the very top of the state, a wide open rural landscape that’s built for hunters and hikers (and, unlike IRL Florida, actually features topography of differing elevations). Some of my favorite moments of the game so far have simply come from biking around mountains and stumbling into off-road racetracks and crumbling ruins.

It’s the rare open-world game that feels a mile wide and a mile deep.

There’s a lot to take in, especially considering how much work Rockstar puts into locking down the right aesthetics. The world itself is astoundingly detailed, with everything from a crowded strip club to a stray island off in the water feeling like it was hand designed and placed with purpose. That comes at the expense of peak performance, as GTA 6 runs at 30 frames per second with some dips when police chases hit the five-star mark. But that’s a negligible impact on the overall experience, given how smoothly it runs most of the time. (I played GTA 6 on a PS5 Pro.) And it’s a fair trade for a world that deserves its own line of postcards.

Driving around it is an auditory delight too, as GTA 6 features a soundtrack so large and diverse that you have to wonder if half of the budget went to music licensing. Metallica and Slayer are there for the metalheads, Charli XCX and Chappell Roan for the modern pop aficionados, and a whole lot of Trick Daddy and Juvenile for those who want to pay respects to the greats of the Dirty South rap scene. All of is spread between satirical commercials and radio shows that clue you into Leonida’s political climate as you drive. (Though be prepared to hear a lot of low-hanging dick jokes; GTA 6’s writers lean hard on cocks as a comedic crutch.) Every little artistic touch helps bring Leonida to life beyond its landmarks.

While there’s plenty to see and hear, I’m more impressed with how much of the world doesn’t feel constructed for players to explore. I occasionally drive by the kind of roadside construction areas that you pass by while on the highway. I don’t think much of them in real life; that’s not an area that I need to pull over and see! GTA 6 mirrors that experience, loading the world with so many mundane sights that ground the world in realism. You can go to them, of course. You might even find a collectible trading card or a wad of cash there. But there’s always a sense that life is happening in Leonida, even when you’re not there.

The best example is in how Jason and Lucia stumble into happenings in Leonida. While the map is filled with markers indicating main story quests, robbery locations, and other activities of note, many other things can just happen out of nowhere. Entire side quests can be discovered by noticing a guy drunkenly barreling down the highway on a tractor, or following the voice of a man looking for his lost cow. Those missable moments often hide the best quests in GTA 6 and imbue the world with more personality than you can imagine.

Other world events aren’t there to kick off missions at all. In one session, I heard the sound of police sirens and followed them downside road to find the cops surrounding a garage. A woman emerged and revealed that she was making kitty litter in there, not drugs. That wasn’t tied to a quest, nor did it have any story implications or rewards tied to it. It’s just a thing that I happened to catch. I’ve similarly seen plane crashes in the distance, watched the cops get into a standoff with a furry, and passed under a bridge as a group of troublemakers above threw tires down on the cars below. Sometimes I insert myself into those situations. (I sure gave those rabble-rousers a talking-to.) Other times, I decide it’s just not my business. The fact that I can make that choice adds a remarkable level of depth to Leonida, a place where you’re always reminded that Jason and Lucia aren’t the only two people who are up to some shit. Everyone is off on their own hustle.

That barely begins to cover what you can experience in Leonida. There are shooting ranges, golf courses, basketball hoops, meditation spots, diving expeditions, stunt jumps, drone-flying challenges, scannable landmarks, and more collectibles than you can imagine. Hell, there are multiple street racing leagues that will make you feel like you’re playing Forza Horizon 6 as streets get repurposed into natural circuits. There’s even an extensive vehicle modification system to allow you to fine-tune cars to your liking. It’s the rare open-world game that feels a mile wide and a mile deep.

What’s surprising about all of that is that it somehow avoids feeling totally overwhelming. Maybe it’s just because there’s so much to do that it’s easy to accept from the jump that you will likely never see it all, but I haven’t felt a compulsion to do anything in GTA 6. Everything is just another potential avenue to make money in a world where stable employment isn’t an option for Jason and Lucia. Want to earn a living fencing cars? You could just do that. Feel like busting up meth labs and selling the goods instead? You’ll have plenty of opportunities. The ultimate power of GTA 6 is that you have the freedom to pick your poison and carve out your own life in Leonida. Why shouldn’t Lucia have that privilege that’s afforded to everyone around her?

So, you can break all the rules in GTA 6. You can do more crimes than ever before. You can kill seabirds and throw them at people. You can amass a fortune on mounds of stolen cocaine and unmarked bills. So what?

That’s an important question not just for finding value in a video game that you could probably play for a decade, but in real life too. One of my deepest daily anxieties comes when I think too hard about existing in an employment battle royale. I know that I need a job to get the money to live, but what’s the point? Aren’t I just busting my ass for the privilege of waking up another day and busting my ass again? I spiral over it constantly; the eat-work-sleep cycle becomes claustrophobic the more I focus so tightly on it that I can no longer see its endpoint. (I imagine that Rockstar’s own staff may be grappling with similar feelings right now, as they are currently fighting to unionize.) It’s easy to lose your hope, motivation, or sense of self when you don’t have something to fight for.

GTA 6’s secret weapon for addressing that malaise comes back to Jason and Lucia. A video game starring a couple has a lot of upsides on a pure design level, and Rockstar takes full advantage of that dynamic. You can freely swap between characters outside of some early story stretches, allowing you to dress up and manage two heroes with distinct personalities. Some missions even have you flipping between them during dramatic set pieces, letting you cover yourself when you wind up pinned down during a tense shootout. When you’re about to do a bank robbery, you can invite your partner to the spot and go in together to ensure you can carry more bags and cover your vulnerabilities. When you leave, you can even command one character to head off and fence the spoils instead of lugging it back to a buyer manually. All of these scenarios allow you to think more strategically about how you pull off crimes, and how you spend your time.

But what’s more effective is how the two can interact when they’re not on the job. GTA 6’s real hero feature is an optional relationship system that allows you to create a romantic bond between Jason and Lucia. When I’m playing as one character, for instance, I can pull out my phone and call or text my partner. (You can text and drive, but be prepared to learn why you should never do that in real life.) That can be just to check in and see how they’re doing, or to invite them to come hang out on a whim. They’ll arrive either in their own car or a ride-share a few moments later, and you’ll find yourself on an impromptu date.

The benefits of GTA 6’s activity-filled world and systems-heavy design reveal themselves in those tender moments. One time, I took Lucia out for a round of mini-golf. Another time, I invited her out to the club and spent hundreds of dollars on champagne for us as we danced together. At any point, you can pull up a menu that allows you to strike up a conversation, flirt, or even hold hands. The two can also fall into natural conversations while hanging out. One time while driving, a country song came on the radio. Lucia started talking about how she thought country music was a big joke growing up, prompting a sweet little exchange between the couple as they chatted about the genre. It felt like a real conversation that would come up with your partner during a road trip.

I already know the wild story moments that GTA 6 will be widely remembered for — there are some fantastic ones involving a pulse-pounding airport caper and an accidental porn set misadventure. But I don’t think I’ll remember many of the repetitive drive-and-shoot chases that clog up a long story that recycles the same ideas a few too many times. Instead, it’s the intimate interactions that stick with me now. One of my favorite moments in the entire game didn’t happen during a mission or cutscene at all. It was when I woke up one morning to find Lucia standing on the balcony of our apartment. I walked up behind her, gave her a kiss, and held her in silence as we looked out across the beach below. I let it play out as long as I could before heading out for another day of blood and bullets.

That’s the so what. Through Jason and Lucia’s genuine chemistry, GTA 6 gives you a better reason to work through Leonida’s daily grind. Yes, there’s always another bank to rob or car to steal, but that’s not the reason you wake up in the morning. It’s to prove that love can survive in a cruel culture that tries so hard to beat it out of people. So be it if you have to play dirty to keep pace with the cold-hearted crooks who make their fortune from someone else’s pain. It shouldn’t be this hard to settle down with your lover and enjoy a sunset together in the rotten social climate that Rockstar has been eager to lampoon for decades at this point.

People will hem and haw about Grand Theft Auto’s purported glamorization of lawlessness. They always have; they always will. But it will be different this time. GTA 6’s empathy is bound to be the most controversial thing about it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. The game was reviewed on PlayStation 5 Pro using a prerelease download code provided by Rockstar Games. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

#3486. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3485. Christian Bale Pushed To Play Batman Before Christopher Nolan's Reboot Was Announced

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The Tim Burton "Batman" films introduced the wider public to a more gothic Batman, but they only scratch the surface of Batman's (Michael Keaton) own character. Conversely, the Joel Schumacher movies drowned in their attempts to recreate the campy 1960s "Batman" show, but both "Batman Forever" and "Batman and Robin" at least try to understand Bruce Wayne (Val Kilmer then George Clooney).

Christopher Nolan's still-beloved "Batman Begins" finally struck the balance, putting Batman (Christian Bale) in a darker movie and also creating a believable and compelling lead out of Bruce Wayne. In effect, "Batman Begins" perfects what "Batman Forever" tried. Since he starred in the most consistently good "Batman" movies, it's also little surprise Christian Bale is still considered one of the best Batman actors.

In 2005, during the "Batman Begins" press cycle, in an interview with Blackfilm, Bale said he had wanted to play Batman for a while. He'd claimed he even asked his agent to "keep [their] eyes out" for a Batman movie before it was announced Nolan was doing "Batman Begins." Bale continued:

"By the time I actually came to be cast I [had] kind of gotten so obsessed about it that, I kind of viewed it as it being mine already. It would've been more like...if they had told me like 'No, it's not yours,' I would've been like 'No way that's not working out, that's not going to happen.'"

Indeed, Bale wasn't Nolan's only choice for the role. Josh Hartnett turned it down, while Cillian Murphy's screen test got him cast as the Scarecrow instead. But considering Bale's determination, and talent (he'd recently cast off his child actor image with "American Psycho"), it's little surprise he got the part. What quality is more like Batman than refusing to accept defeat?

In the aforementioned Blackfilm interview, Bale claims he wasn't a Batman fan from childhood, but reading some comics won him over. He specifically listed Grant Morrison and Dave McKean's "Arkham Asylum," Frank Miller and David Mazzucchelli's "Batman: Year One," and Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale's "The Long Halloween" and "Dark Victory." He named those same four in a 2005 interview with Wizard Magazine, as well as Alex Ross' "War on Crime."

"I realized that [Batman] was a really great character, a dark severe character unlike anything that I had realized he [could] be before," Bale said to Blackfilm. Now, keep in mind, every actor who appears in a superhero movie says during the press cycle they read the comics and fell in love with the character. And, every time, I'm skeptical that it's more than just PR talking points (unless the actor's name is "Nicolas Cage" or "Iman Vellani").

The comics Bale named are all from the late 1980s through the 1990s, when "dark Batman" was becoming the norm and comic writers/artists were now considering the character a prestige assignment. To this day, those books remain some of the essential Batman stories recommended to new readers, in part because they can make you take Batman seriously.

Part of the sales pitch for "Batman Begins" was, coming off of the disastrous "Batman and Robin," that this Batman would be different. Naming comics the fans love as influences is a great way to get them on your side. Bale claiming he wasn't a Batman fan until reading those comics showed him the darker side of Batman, with the implicit promise "Batman Begins" would do the same for the moviegoing public, is even a compelling fan-friendly meta-narrative.

Where Christian Bale's claims about his comic reading have some substance is that those books do influence "Batman Begins." As an origin story, the movie takes the most from "Year One." Like in that comic, "Batman Begins" features Bruce learning to be Batman through trial and error, as well as forming an alliance with Detective Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman). "Begins" also includes mob boss Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson), who was introduced in "Year One."

"Batman Begins" isn't outright horror like "Arkham Asylum" is, but many scenes do have a genuinely scary and intense atmosphere because of the League of Shadows' fear toxin. In turn, "The Dark Knight" takes after "The Long Halloween," having Batman, Gordon, and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) form a triumvirate to take down the Gotham mob.

Christopher Nolan, for his part, cited 1989 comic "The Man Who Falls" by Dennis O'Neil and Dick Giordano, which tells Bruce Wayne's life from childhood to crime fighting. "Batman Begins" has a similar scope of time. During the 1970s, O'Neil (who wrote novelizations of both "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight") had pushed Batman in a darker direction alongside artist Neal Adams. The pair notably created the villain Ra's al Ghul, who appears in "Batman Begins" (played by Liam Neeson) as Bruce's mentor and the twist villain. A scene of Bruce and Ra's sword-fighting mirrors their duel in O'Neil and Adams' "Batman" #244.

The O'Neil/Adams Batman stories were also a stylistic influence on "Batman: The Animated Series." In turn, "Batman Begins" lifted one of its plot points from that show's episode "Dreams in Darkness," where the Scarecrow tries to poison Gotham's water supply. The people who made "Batman Begins" respected the character and that respect shows onscreen.

The Last of Us is a TV show that has meant a lot to a lot of people, as it has successfully translated the emotional core of the hugely popular video game and built on the complexity of the character relationships. The final season, anticipated to debut in 2027, is sure to be emotional for fans, too. So it’s not at all surprising to hear that the cast is emotional as they get to the end of filming and will have to say goodbye to each other.

An HBO show that got the world talking from the moment it debuted, the post-apocalyptic drama started by following Joel (Pedro Pascal) as he escorted the teenage Ellie (Bella Ramsey) across a devastated United States ravaged by a fungal infection that had turned people into violent creatures. With Season 3 delving deeper into the journey of Joel’s brother, Tommy Miller, actor Gabriel Luna not only has to say goodbye to a character he’ll know much better, but he’ll also be leaving the cast and crew behind after bidding them an emotional farewell. Here’s what he told Entertainment Weekly about the emotions that are already starting to swirl:

Oh man, a lot of emotions are going around. But right now I think we’re all too tired to feel them. [Laughs.] Because it’s just massive. Obviously I can’t give anything away, but people who’ve played the game know the level of the scope of what we’re dealing with here towards the end of the story. I’m so proud of Bella [Ramsey], Kaitlyn [Dever], and Kyriana [Kratter], who’s joined the cast, for being the tip of the spear and shouldering the weight of this production and what it requires from them.

If you played The Last of Us games, you knew that Abby would be seen on the show as a villain after killing Pedro Pascal's Joel. No matter her motivation or the extent of her own trauma, it would be challenging for viewers to understand the actions of someone taking out such a beloved character. And then, the Season 2 finale ended with the focus shifting to Kaitlyn Dever's Abby, who will take center stage in The Last of Us Season 3.

In a world like the one portrayed in The Last of Us, where everything is heightened as you just try to survive and not get killed or infected, emotions understandably run high for the cast helping bring that world to life. And even though Tommy comes in and out of the story, The Terminal List actor can’t help but be impressed by how the Ellie, Abby, and Lev actors are handling everything required of them, as they head closer to the finish line. He went on to say:

The bulk of my work was back in the summer, and then I’d go back and forth and come in for two, three weeks of time, but they’re here every day and doing the lion’s share of the work.

Since the Naughty Dog video game-turned-TV series is a massive production, it sounds like there’s going to be a prolonged series of goodbyes taking place as storylines are wrapped up and actors depart. Gabriel Luna not only has to process the emotion of saying goodbye to his own character and wrapping up a story that he likely feels very connected to after three seasons, but he also has to handle the departure of each of his co-stars. That’s a lot of emotions for the Dexter: Resurrection star, who will probably be exhausted by the time it’s all said and done. He pretty much said just that:

We’re getting to the end of it, and people are starting to wrap, and we’re giving them their flowers, and then they’re heading off, and one by one, the family is dwindling down to just the final few. We’re about to get a welcomed break and respite from what we’ve been doing, and then we have to come back and finish strong after the holiday. We’re so excited for this thing to come out.

I can only imagine the tears that will be flowing and the emotions that will be felt as the final days of the HBO series come to an end, and everyone says their final goodbyes. Fans anxiously anticipating the third season will have to pack their patience pants while waiting for details on when it will officially premiere. In the meantime, the first two seasons of The Last of Us are streaming with an HBO Max subscription.

Prince Harry, Meghan Markle and their two kids, Archie and Lilibet, have been adapting to a completely new life in the U.K. these past few months. However, some recent reports claim the family may already be getting ready to head back to Southern California to spend Christmas this year. The Royal Family famously spends their Christmas holiday at the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk. However, while Prince Harry may have grown up doing Christmas at the countryside property, he and Meghan only spent two holidays there – a month after they got engaged in 2017 and their first Christmas as a married couple in 2018. New claims by InStyle speculate that since they broke the tradition eight years ago, they aren't expecting this year to be any different despite the geographical convenience.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle spent their first two Christmas holidays with the Royal Family at Sandringham Estate. When that time of year rolled around in 2019, they had already formally separated from the Royal Family and appeared in a candid documentary interview where Harry said he and Prince Williams were "on different paths." So in 2019, they decided to spend the holidays privately in Canada with a nine-month-old Archie. And, in March 2020, they stepped away from being senior royals.

It’s expected that Harry and Meghan will share a more intimate holiday season with Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland, as they usually do. While it’s been suggested they’d likely end the year in the U.S. (via People), a source with the Daily Mail reports Doria may be the one to head to the U.K. instead. They know it would be too awkward and too difficult [to spend Christmas with the royal family]. They also know they’re not going to be invited, and they’re not waiting for an invitation.

It's also worth taking into account that Meghan Markle and her mother have been reportedly leaning on each other following Markle’s father facing allegations of possessing child sexual abuse material. Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested by federal agents on November 6 and could serve prison time.

Over in the U.K., the couple reportedly haven’t found their forever home yet since relocating in August. They are currently living at a friend’s private estate in the Cotswolds. Perhaps they are searching for familiarity this holiday season after the big move?

#3480. Ted Lasso Star Jason Sudeikis Starred In A Gritty Crime Thriller With Marvel Actors

Plenty of comedic actors have played dramatic roles that didn't work out too well. The same can't quite be said of "Ted Lasso" star Jason Sudeikis, who proved he could handle a dramatic role in "South of Heaven," a crime thriller that should have been much better than it was. Oddly enough, the film also happens to be a surreptitious comic book team-up event movie, with a cast full of Marvel Cinematic Universe alumni.

We don't often talk about the "Saturday Night Live" to noirish crime thriller pipeline. But a fair few "SNL" stars have made the transition, from Adam Sandler in "Uncut Gems" to Jim Belushi in "Gang Related." Sudeikis, who appeared on the legendary sketch comedy series from 2003 to 2013, found his biggest post-"SNL" success by playing the lead role in Apple TV's "Ted Lasso." The actor's inherent charm has served him well as the endearingly optimistic college football coach tasked with leading a British soccer team to greatness. But with "South of Heaven," the "SNL" alum clearly wanted to branch out and try something new. He was close to succeeding, too.

The film sees Sudeikis play a convicted felon who's released from a prison sentence early to spend a year with his terminally-ill girlfriend. Unfortunately, things don't quite go to plan, and Sudeikis' ex-con finds himself in a fight for his and the life of his beloved. It's a sort of okay crime thriller that starts out great before taking a major turn part-way through. Luckily, it also has a solid cast to help carry the melodrama, a surprising amount of whom have played MCU characters.

"South of Heaven" — not to be confused with the Western flop Vince Vaughn and Billy Bob Thornton would probably like you to forget about, "South of Heaven, West of Hell" — is directed by Israeli filmmaker Aharon Keshales, who also co-wrote the script with Navot Papushado, and Kai Mark. Keshales similarly co-wrote and co-directed his first feature, "Rabies" in 2010, and his second, "Big Bad Wolves," in 2013, earning him and his co-director, Papushado, praise from Quentin Tarantino who called it the "best film of the year." "South of Heaven" represents Keshales' first solo feature and sees him team up with Jason Sudeikis for a gritty thriller that sadly devolves into a fairly rote genre exercise. Hey, at least the director brought together some MCU vets to support his leading man.

Sudeikis plays convicted felon Jimmy Ray, who's serving a 15-year sentence for his role in a robbery, but convinces the parole board to set him free after 12 to spend a year with his dying girlfriend, Annie Ray (Evangeline Lilly). For the first half of the movie, Keshales presents a noir-infused love story with an indie drama spirit that sees Sudeikis and Lilly demonstrate some surprisingly good chemistry. Jimmy is trying to go straight as best he can, turning down offers to meet up with his prison buddy Frank (Jeremy Bobb) and generally trying to do right by Annie. Then, things go off the rails.

When Jimmy reluctantly accepts a "side job" from his crooked parole officer Schmidt (Shea Whigham), he winds up stoking the ire of crime boss Whit Price (Mike Colter), who kidnaps Annie. Jimmy then takes Whit's son, Tommy Price (Thaddeus J. Mixon) captive and the whole thing devolves into violence.

You might have noticed that almost everyone in "South of Heaven" has been involved in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The most obvious is, of course, Evangeline Lilly, who portrayed Hope van Dyne/Wasp in the "Ant-Man" movies and "Avengers: Endgame." Mike Colter, meanwhile, played the title role in Netflix's "Luke Cage" series from 2016 to 2018, and appeared in the team-up miniseries "The Defenders" in 2017. That same miniseries also featured Krysten Ritter's Jessica Jones, who had her own Netflix show that featured yet another "South of Heaven" actor, Jeremy Bobb.

That's not all the MCU connections, either. Shea Whigham played Roger Dooley in 2015's "Agent Carter" Season 1, while Jaime Zevallos, who plays Julio in "South of Heaven," previously portrayed Father Francis Xavier Delgado in Freeform's "Cloak & Dagger." As such, Jason Sudeikis' crime thriller is secretly one of the most significant unofficial Marvel team-up movies ever made.

Sadly, that didn't translate to one of Sudeikis' best films. "South of Heaven" bears a 48% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, with Amy Nicholson of the New York Times calling it a "Texas melodrama that's as convincing as a taxidermied jackalope." Craig D. Lindsey of the AV Club saw two very different films in "South of Heaven," one "straight-faced and suspenseful" and another "almost randomly nihilistic." Meanwhile, the Minneapolis Star Tribune's Chris Hewitt found Sudeikis' "subdued performance" to be "hugely likable" and Owen Gleiberman of Variety seemed to agree. "The movie gives Jason Sudeikis a chance to act without the safety net of comedy, and he proves that he's got the right stuff," he wrote, even if he also felt Sudeikis should have showcased his dramatic talent in a different movie — one that "offers the safety net of believability."

#3479. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3478. GTA 6 Officially Launches, Spoiler Warning Issued for Players Still Waiting

The global rollout of Grand Theft Auto 6 has begun

After many long years of waiting and a handful of delays, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 will finally be released on Thursday, Nov. 19. For some players, it's out right now.

GTA 6 has a rolling midnight launch schedule, meaning it's available to play at 12 a.m. your local time on Nov. 19. Due to the power of time zones and a round Earth, midnight local time on Nov. 19 arrives in some territories while it's still Nov. 18 in others. New Zealanders will get first access as GTA 6 gradually unlocks around the world.

The internet is beholden to no time zone. Until it's midnight Nov. 19 in your time zone, you'll have to be aware that spoilers will naturally flood social media and other sites. Depending on where they live, players in New Zealand and elsewhere will have multiple hours to play GTA 6 while the timer on their PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X is still counting down. For example, midnight in New Zealand on Nov. 19 is 6 a.m. EST on Nov. 18 on the east coast of the United States. U.S.-based players will have to be careful to avoid spoilers for essentially the whole day on Wednesday.

As GTA 6 will take players a long, long time to finish, I wouldn't expect any ending spoilers to flood the internet before Nov. 19 hits your time zone. However, GTA 6 could have plenty of surprises in its early game you still might want to avoid. Need I remind you of The Last of Us Part 2's monumental opening hours?

Maybe you can't wait to play GTA 6 when it launches in your time zone and want to get your hands on it early. I get it. There is always the "New Zealand" trick you can try out, and our guide explains how to do exactly that. It's a bit more intensive for PS5 players, which make up the majority of GTA 6's massive amount of preorders.

Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on Thursday, Nov. 19. Its launch follows a fun marketing blitz that included showcasing digital dog poop on South America (formerly South Park) and taking over Miami IRL, including a crossover with the Miami Heat.

#3477. This '80s R-Rated Superhero Movie Is Unlike Anything Marvel Or DC Has Made

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

We've been living in a world of mass entertainment dominated by superheroes and comic book characters for more than 25 years now, dating back to Marvel's earlier blockbuster hits like "X-Men" and "Spider-Man." Even small screen stuff like "The Walking Dead" has comic book roots. But decades before any of that, an indie film pioneer made a superhero movie unlike any other.

Lloyd Kaufman is independent film, in many ways, as the founder of Troma Entertainment. His media empire was built on the backs of low-budget schlock like "Surf Nazis Must Die" and "Pterodactyl Woman from Beverly Hills," among many others. But Kaufman's defining hit came in 1984 in the form of "The Toxic Avenger," an ultra violent, campy, R-rated superhero affair. It remains a distinct piece of punk rock cinema more than 40 years removed, unmatched in its insanity by anything Marvel or DC has done on screen.

The movie takes place in the fictional town of Tromaville, known as the toxic waste capital of America. A bullied young janitor in a popular gym falls into a vat of toxic waste and turns into a super strong but disfigured man. He begins cleaning up the streets from evildoers in an often funny yet violent fashion.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a long history on screen and is now a cult legend, but that legend began in '84, at a time when superheroes were far from bankable fare in the mainstream. Co-directed by Michael Herz and Kaufman himself, the resulting movie can't be accused of being high art, but it's one heck of a wild swing, and a testament to what the indie filmmaking spirit can accomplish.

At the time, Hollywood had only had the occasional superhero movie hit it big. "Superman: The Movie" in 1978 being the biggest one, while Batman didn't become a box office hero until 1989. Even that movie just led to the "Batman" franchise taking off rather than a broader trend of superheroes becoming big business. The '90s saw many try but few succeed, with stuff like "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" more the exception rather than the rule.

All of this to say, when Lloyd Kaufman decided to make a dark superhero comedy — an R-rated and super violent one no less — it wasn't exactly a recipe for success. At least not on paper. But decades before "Deadpool" broke the Marvel mold by going R-rated and injecting comedy into the genre, "The Toxic Avenger" dared to venture into that territory.

What's more, Kaufman and Co. did it on a shoestring budget of well under $1 million. "Deadpool" gets a lot of credit for being low-budget, but it still cost north of $50 million. What Kaufman pulled off with latex, old school special effects, and can-do indie spirit is nothing shy of impressive. Even those who are put off by the nature of this sort of exploitation film should be impressed by what was accomplished here with so little.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a demented sense of humor, and it doesn't give us a typical hero either. Toxie isn't a square-jawed, muscle-bound vigilante. He's a mutant who decides to clean up the streets with straight-up violence. The film has more in common with revenge driven horror/thrillers than it does any mainstream superhero movie. All the same, it became a cult hit and started a wildly unlikely franchise.

"No theater would play it," Lloyd Kaufman said of "The Toxic Avenger" to Parallax View in 2010. "We couldn't get one theater to play it anywhere and then we took it to Cannes and not one deal. Nothing! And then a few months later we got one movie theater in Greenwich Village, New York, and there was a line around the theater."

That single theater paved the way for more to follow. This was also at the dawn of the VHS home video craze, which is where the movie really thrived — so much so that Kaufman eventually produced a series of sequels. That includes 1989's "The Toxic Avenger Part II" and "The Toxic Avenger Part III: The Last Temptation of Toxie," also released in '89. Much later, "Citizen Toxie: The Toxic Avenger IV" would arrive in 2000. A gore-soaked remake of "The Toxic Avenger" starring Peter Dinklage was also released in 2025.

Kaufman's crown jewel is an elbow grease style, gory, raunchy, rubber-suit take on superheroes that doesn't resemble anything we've seen in the 2000s, really. Sure, "Clayface" brought body horror to the DC Universe, but it's completely without a sense of humor. It's also slick and relatively expensive (for a horror movie).

It was cutting edge then and it's impressively distinctive even now. More than that, "The Toxic Avenger" helped make the empire that is Troma. It's easy to write it all off as schlock, but Troma has been a haven for indie film for decades, with filmmakers like James Gunn ("Guardians of the Galaxy") cutting their teeth there. Without this movie, who knows if the empire as we know it even exists?

You can grab "The Toxic Avenger" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3474. How To Watch The Social Reckoning At Home

"The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market. It will become available to buy or rent on digital starting November 24, 2026, prior to its physical media release on January 12, 2027.

In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist. Almost two decades after he won an Academy Award for writing the screenplay for "The Social Network," a 2010 dramatization of the founding of Facebook directed by David Fincher, Aaron Sorkin decided to make a sequel that focuses on what Facebook has become in the 2020s. Jesse Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nod for playing Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," declined to return to the role and was replaced by "Succession" veteran, Emmy and Tony winner, and Sorkin's "The Trial of the Chicago 7" collaborator Jeremy Strong. With Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen starring alongside Strong, the project seemed almost too big to fail before it premiered in theaters on October 9, 2026.

Fail it did, though. Though it reportedly only lost a couple million for Sony (per Deadline), the film absolutely underperformed at the box office, and its rating on Rotten Tomatoes is a middling-to-bleak 54%. So what happened here? Well, from my perspective, "The Social Reckoning" is just a bad movie ... and /Film's chief film critic Chris Evangelista agrees with me. What went wrong as Sorkin tried to make a legacy sequel to one of the best films of the 21st century? Quite a lot actually!

I'll circle back to the "Social Network" of it all shortly, but the bottom line here is that "The Social Reckoning" just ... stinks to high heaven. From the embarrassing prologue featuring Portia Doubleday as a caricature named Kayleigh (I'm not kidding) to the fact that Aaron Sorkin keeps forcing Oscar winner Mikey Madison into outfits that would make her title character from "Anora" blush (in the name of corporate espionage), I found "The Social Network" to be a uniformly dreadful watch from start to finish. Not only is the script clunky as all hell — unfortunately, an ongoing problem with many of Sorkin's recent screenplays — but the story is attempting to make some sort of larger point that doesn't just fall flat but thuds directly to the floor. We already know social media makes everyone angry and insane, and we also know that social media has contributed to right-wing radicalization. Sorkin making a movie that beats us over the head with these two ideas and also ends in a full recreation of the January 6, 2021 insurrection is just as bad as it sounds in theory.

It's also incredible to me that Sorkin managed to cast a lot of great actors and coach them into giving some of the worst performances of their careers. Madison is an enigmatic and compelling performer, and Sorkin transforms her into the robotic Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, a deeply unlikable person who doesn't seem to understand human behavior. Jeremy Allen White's journalist Jeff Horwitz is nothing but an exposition machine, and Jeremy Strong's Mark Zuckerberg has no interiority and sounds like Kermit the Frog. The only person who's good in this movie is Bill Burr. Think about that for a second.

"The Social Network" might be one of my very favorite movies of all time, but I can tell you, from a completely unbiased perspective, that "The Social Reckoning" is a wholly undeserving sequel to that 2010 masterpiece. It's clear now, with plenty of hindsight and movies like this, that "The Social Network" was good because of director David Fincher and despite Sorkin. To be fair to Sorkin, he basically admitted that to The Hollywood Reporter after "The Social Reckoning" got soundly panned.

"I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony," Sorkin told the outlet on their "Awards Chatter" podcast. Not only did Sorkin also admit that he's "very worried that the parts of directing that [he's] not good at are those parts that you can't learn," he also said, "I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I'd managed to absorb [from other directors] ... I have no visual sensibility, it turns out."

I have to agree with him. Despite the same cinematographer — Jeff Cronenweth — working on both "Network" and "Reckoning," the sequel is visually bland, unimaginatively shot, and even recycles a couple reaction and establishing shots throughout its run time. Basically, "The Social Reckoning" is a poorly made film that I cannot in good conscience recommend; in fact, I'd recommend you just watch "The Social Network" instead. But if you're still interested, you can check out "The Social Reckoning" at home once it's available.

One of the most uncomfortable scenes in You Can See Everything is when co-director Nathan Fielder and surprise star Amanda Seyfried pay a visit to Elizabeth Holmes’ family’s house in Texas after she has been incarcerated on fraud convictions. Billy Evans, Holmes’ partner, and Seyfried get into a contentious discussion over dinner about Evans’ attitude toward Holmes. Evans, who has started talking about the box office hit more and more both in interviews and in a Reddit AMA, recently spoke about the visit, and it turns out he didn’t see what was coming at all. In fact, he thought he was extending a peace offering to Seyfried after her portrayal of Holmes in The Dropout.

Seyfried had already been working with Fielder for some time, and over the course of the second half of the movie, it’s clear she was getting more and more frustrated with Evans as she learned more about him. In fact, she was so upset by Evans’ behavior in the footage she had watched with Fielder that was filmed before Holmes reported to prison in 2023, that she expressed a desire to break the couple up. Evans recently told his side of the story to The Hollywood Reporter, saying of the dinner:

It made more sense to me after seeing the film, and hearing her say, ‘I want to break them up.’ I didn’t understand her intentions [when she came over]. I thought we were extending an olive branch and saying, ‘Look, we’re not angry with you. We’re happy to engage. We don’t blame you for your portrayal of Liz [in The Dropout]. You’re an actress, you didn’t write the script, you didn’t develop the story, you didn’t do the research or lack thereof.’

Seyfried’s intentions were never to ask for forgiveness for playing Holmes at this point. At this point, Amanda Seyfried isn't just the actress who portrayed Holmes. She is also an advocate for her. That’s even more apparent when she plays her again later in the documentary, in the recreations of Fielder’s meetings with the former CEO in the Texas prison. Seyfried had, at that point, developed sympathy for Holmes, which is weirdly exactly what Evans was hoping the film would do, though probably not at his expense. Not like this.

It’s impossible to rank all the wildest moments in You Can See Everything. The more I’ve thought about it over the weeks since I saw it, the more each scene stands out from the others. One day I think Evans taking the bowl of eggs out of Holmes' hand is the craziest; other times it's when Holmes seemingly doesn’t understand “Who’s on First?” That’s not even getting into the disputed scene that features Evans in the shower. However, the dinner confrontation is when I was squirming the most in my seat.

Seyfried pulls no punches in telling Evans what she thinks, and in turn, Evans doesn’t hold back his contempt, either. It’s a scene I can’t wait to watch again when I’m finally able to see the movie on streaming, presumably with my HBO Max subscription, soon.
