CBS News entered a new chapter in October 2025 when David Ellison hired Bari Weiss to serve as its editor-in-chief. Since then, Weiss has initiated a number of changes throughout the storied media organization, with some of those alterations being praised and others being panned. Early on, it was reported that Ellison had considerable faith in Weiss and, per a recent report, she entered the company like a “hero” of sorts. However, that same report includes claims about how the situation has allegedly shifted for her.

In some circles, Weiss was viewed as a breath of fresh air for CBS News, while other pundits viewed her as something of a wildcard. That latter assertion was mostly due to the fact that she had no formal experience working within the realm of broadcast journalism. Nevertheless, given her success with her online platform, The Free Press (which was acquired by the now-defunct Paramount Skydance), she had reason to be confident. However, per a source for RadarOnline, Weiss is facing ratings-related pressure:

Bari arrived like a conquering hero, promising to fix everything. But you can't save a network if nobody is watching. People are asking, 'What exactly are we paying for?'

The past few months have seen some of CBS News’ programming – like CBS Evening News and 60 Minutes – experience drops in their ratings. Said declines in viewership have notably come on the heels of staffing changes made the shows. For instance, Weiss named Tony Dokoupil as the lead anchor of the evening news program earlier this year, while she and executive producer Nick Bilton fired several high-profile staffers from 60 this past summer.

As noted by Radar, 60 Minutes’ October 11th broadcast notched on 6.06million viewers and, within that sum were 767,000 adults within the aged 25-54 demographic. That number marked a 10 million decrease from the previous week. All the while, CBS Mornings has come in behind morning news shows from rival networks. Following Dokoupil’s debut on CBS Evening News this past March, that show dropped below 4 million viewers, signifying a 15% decrease from the previous year. A network insider added this about the stats:

These numbers make executives nervous. You can survive bad press and angry employees. But when viewers disappear, everybody wants somebody to blame.

How Bari Weiss Responded After Being Asked If She’d Like To Run CNN

In terms of that remark about “bad press and angry employees,” that seemingly refers to the reports and rumors that have been swirling around Bari Weiss’ tenure. Former CBS staffers have criticized her, with some even making claims of “journalistic interference” amid her time on the job. Veteran newsman Dan Rather also didn’t mince words about Weiss and other execs, as he accused them of “destroying” the network. Meanwhile, company sources have shared varied takes on working with Weiss, as some call the experience productive and others making claims of difficulties on that front.

Weiss herself is aware of the concerns, and she recently addressed the 60 Minutes responses head on, asserting that the show is doing “tremendously well.” The E-I-C also shed light on her biggest goal for CBS News moving forward. Per Weiss, her desire is to build the company into an institution that the general public can rely on in “an era of collapsing trust.” She also wants to “marry the energy and vibrancy and vitality of the independent creator world” with “the rigor and standards of” a legacy news brand.

Nevertheless, another insider alleges that Bari Weiss is “making enemies inside the building while losing viewers outside it,” which is apparently a “deadly combination.” These allegations should, of course, all be taken with a grain of salt, as CBS News nor parent company Skydance have given any indication that Weiss’ job is in jeopardy. For now, we can only wait and see how she continues to navigate her position.

#3447. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3446. Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device

This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

On iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

#3445. 43 Years Later, A Christmas Story's Most Famous Line Remains The Best Christmas Movie Quote

Feeling that chill in the air, the rising number of Oscars-hopeful movie releases in theaters, and the unmistakable threat promise of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas is You" playing in every department store you enter for the foreseeable future? Yep, you know what that means: The holiday season is officially upon us and we're positively giddy with Yuletide cheer. Of course, we're even more excited about finally having an excuse to pop on our favorite films and celebrate the festivities properly.

For those of us who practically grew up on one particular classic, that involves ringing in the holidays with "A Christmas Story," arguably the most quintessential Christmas movie of them all. There are approximately a hundred different reasons why this of all movies captures the essence of the season the most — or, more accurately, the childlike wonder and innocence we all used to have come November of every single year. The seemingly endless wait for school to end and the fun to begin. The breathless anticipation every time our parents left the house for some clandestine gift shopping. The snowball fights and snow days and warm evenings by the fire, for those of us fortunate enough to live in more wintry climates.

"A Christmas Story" takes all those evocative feelings and wraps them inside a snow globe of nostalgia ... with a little commentary on crass commercialism, nuclear family dynamics, and some good ol' fashioned childhood bullying thrown in for good measure. Forty three years later, it's a pop-culture staple that endures. And one particular quote about a certain Red Ryder BB gun goes a long way towards explaining why.

"You'll shoot your eye out." — Ralph's mother.

Ah, the life-and-death stakes of being a child during the holidays. Every single item on our list is a must-have present or the world will end forever. Each day is fraught with the most impossible homework assignments we need to finish before we can have fun with friends. And every impulsive misstep or moment of misbehavior comes with the possibility of turning Santa Claus himself against us. For Ralphie (Peter Billingsley), the precocious 9-year-old boy living in 1940s Indiana retelling the events of "A Christmas Story" to us as an adult (narrated by Jean Shepherd), it all comes down to those five crushing words that destroy all his holiday hopes in one fell swoop.

"You'll shoot your eye out," of course, refers to his mother's (Melinda Dillon) appalled reaction to the #1 item on his Christmas list: an Official Red Ryder Carbine-Action 200-Shot Range Model Air Rifle with a compass in the stock and a sundial, to put it plainly. It's his white whale, the forbidden fruit that torments and dazzles poor Ralphie for the entirety of the film's runtime. And when he finally works up the nerve to ask his mom for her blessing, well, she sensibly points out exactly what could go wrong with such a violent "toy."

It's a perfect encapsulation of the beating heart of "A Christmas Story" and why multiple generations have gravitated towards this movie. It brings us right back to that indescribable feeling of being eight or nine or 10, with an entire world of possibility ahead ... if only the adults would let us free. After countless re-watches, well, the hilarious (and predictable) punchline proves kids don't always know best, after all.

#3444. GTA 6 Really Is Better On PS5 Than Xbox

If you’re planning to get Grand Theft Auto 6 at launch, you’ll be able to buy it on two consoles: PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. But while both are capable pieces of hardware, it sure seems like developer Rockstar Games has a preference between the two. Advertisements for the game have declared that it “plays best on PS5.” Sony has even gotten custom GTA 6 DualSense controllers in celebration of the launch. To some, it could look like GTA 6 is a PS5 exclusive, even though it very much is not.

Now that I’ve finally played GTA 6 for myself, it’s very clear why Sony’s console is the center of attention. It’s not so much about raw power, though the PS5 Pro is likely the best way for the techiest gamers to play, until we get a PC port; it has more to do with the DualSense. GTA 6 feels like it was built with the controller and its unique features in mind, making it a stronger sales pitch for the PS5 than most of Sony’s actual exclusives. It’s just a shame it’s coming so late in the console’s life cycle.

In terms of how GTA 6 runs on PS5, there are no real surprises there. I largely played on PS5 Pro, which was able to give me a relatively smooth 30 frames per second performance. I did experience some framerate dips during high-level police chases, but it otherwise impresses considering the sheer scale of the world and its high level of detail throughout. I’ve yet to test it on Xbox Series X, but there are no red flags here that suggest it might struggle on Microsoft’s console. (The Xbox Series S is a wildcard.)

What was instantly more noticeable during my playthrough was how GTA 6 goes all-in on the DualSense, to the point where it feels like Rockstar built the game specifically around the controller. You can see that in the little details. For instance, Jason and Lucia have cell phones that they can bring up at any time to send texts, make calls, and check apps. The sounds from that phone come through the DualSense’s built-in speaker. If someone calls you, you’ll hear the ring from the controller instead of the TV. That makes it feel like you, the player, are literally holding that phone in your hands — a small but effective bit of immersion.

In that same vein, Rockstar also goes all in on haptic feedback to great effect. When you’re swimming, for example, you can feel each individual stroke Jason or Lucia takes. Again, much of the game feels like it was designed with that level of detail in mind. When cloning a car key, you’ll need to move the right joystick around in a circle and find the strongest vibration point. As you can imagine, haptic feedback only makes that minigame that much more tactile.

Even the DualSense’s adaptive triggers get put to good use. Step on the gas in a car, and you’ll get a hit of resistance that simulates the feeling of stepping on a gas pedal. Crack open a shipping container with a saw, and you’ll need to very carefully increase pressure on the right trigger to make the cut. Stop to meditate, and you’ll feel the triggers rattle under your fingers as you press them to breathe in and out. Every little minigame interaction plays with the triggers or feedback in some way.

The more I played, the more GTA 6 reminded me of early-generation PS5 tech showpieces; it has the same toy-like quality that Returnal and Astro’s Playroom had in the early PS5 years. While there have been plenty of third-party games that have integrated the DualSense in their own ways, GTA 6 has the most fully realized implementation of its features outside of Sony’s first-party games. That’s why it almost feels like an exclusive; six years into the PS5’s life, we finally have the game that really sells how the tech.

None of that is necessary to enjoy GTA 6, mind you. The extra feedback is a great perk if you own a PS5 already, but you’re not going to miss anything because your in-game phone rings from your TV speakers instead of your controller. The Xbox Series X will likely get the job done, and you might even prefer it if you don’t love the occasional strain that comes with adaptive triggers. But when Sony says that GTA 6 plays best on PS5, it’s not exactly a bluff. It does, but "play” is the key word there. It’s not that it looks or runs the best on PS5. It’s just the best platform for those who love toying around with their games.

#3442. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.

#3441. Amazon's Jeff Bezos Clarifies Involvement In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

As exciting as it is that Robert Pattinson has been cast as James Bond, the irony of his 007 movie being overseen by a man who is about as close to a real-life Bond villain as you're likely to get is inescapable. What does Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos know about movies? Well, that remains unclear. But since Amazon bought Bond for an eye-watering sum back in 2025, he is the man who cuts the checks at the end of the day. That means he was always going to have a say in who plays Bond and it seems he was, indeed, intimately involved.

Bezos appeared at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event where he confirmed that he was "heavily involved" in Pattinson's casting (via Twitter/X). "We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on [the Friday before the official announcement was made the following Monday]," he said. "There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists."

.@JeffBezos tells @lizrhoffman he was "heavily involved" in selecting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

"Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous ... but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond." pic.twitter.com/1ro4R8meYO

According to the Amazon founder, the process of whittling down the finalists (let's agree never to use the phrase "down-selected" again) involved carrying out "old-fashioned screen tests" which he described as "interesting." These tests apparently involved "full costumes and real sets and other actors," with Bezos going on to explain how each of the five candidates performed three scenes on-camera. "Then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that," he continued. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director ... we all gravitated toward Rob."

It's interesting to hear Jeff Bezos' recollection of how Robert Pattinson was cast as James Bond. Soon after Amazon made the official announcement, reports emerged that claimed Pattinson wasn't actually director Denis Villeneuve's first choice for Bond. Instead, it seems the director was set on casting "Wake Up Dead Man" and "Disclosure Day" star Josh O'Connor, before the actor chose to take himself out of the process. To hear Bezos tell it, however, all five Bond finalists screen tested and the clear favorite was Pattinson.

Those finalists reportedly comprised O'Connor, Pattinson, "Slow Horses" star Jack Lowden, Callum Turner of the "Fantastic Beasts" films, and the man who will seemingly forever come in second to Pattinson: Nicholas Hoult. Rather than Pattinson being a second choice, in Bezos' recollection he simply came out on top after the screen tests and the decision was about as close to unanimous as you can get.

With all that in mind, it remains unclear just how the final days of the casting process unfolded. Was O'Connor still in the running on that Friday Bezos and co. watched the screen tests? How late, exactly, did Pattinson enter the process, considering he reportedly had to escape his "The Batman: Part III" contract ahead of his Bond casting? What is clear at this point is that the Amazon founder was right there alongside producers and Villeneuve to oversee the final decision.

Interestingly enough, during his Semafor event comments Jeff Bezos also claimed that Robert Pattinson didn't start out as the favorite for "Bond 26." "Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous," he said. "Like, maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond."

Indeed, Pattinson's 007 casting breaks a 60-year tradition of casting relative unknowns as the legendary spy. As such, you can appreciate why the producers were hesitant at first. Ever since "Dr. No" launched cinema's most enduring franchise back in 1962, audiences have gotten used to seeing a fresh face in the role with each new recasting. But Pattinson's star power is actually one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet. The last few entries in the franchise haven't been the most impressive, and the "Primetime" star will surely help restore a sense of prestige to a saga that's felt quite stale for some time. That's to say nothing of his considerable acting talent, which will no doubt immediately convince the naysayers the moment they see any footage from the film.

That certainly seems to have been the case with Bezos and the gang, who evidently felt Pattinson was a cut above the other Bond hopefuls after seeing his screen test. It remains to be seen what sort of influence the Amazon founder will have over Denis Villeneuve's movie during production, but let's hope he's too distracted by world domination to interfere too much.

#3439. 10 Years Ago Today: Hailee Steinfeld Starred In One Of The Best Coming-Of-Age Movies Of All Time

Actor Hailee Steinfeld broke out in the Coen Brothers' 2010 Western film "True Grit" as the precocious Mattie Ross, who speaks like she's wise beyond her years but lacks the experience that brings true wisdom. We at /Film consider Steinfeld as Mattie the greatest performance in any Coens movie, which is no small feat.

Nominated for an Academy Award at only 14 years old, it would've been easy for Steinfeld's career to have peaked there. But she has kept challenging herself with music, voice acting, and plenty of new movies, and one of her best is absolutely writer/director Kelly Fremon Craig's coming-of-age film "The Edge of Seventeen."

After a premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, "The Edge of Seventeen" hit theaters on November 18, 2016. It takes its title from the Stevie Nicks song yet applies it more literally to this story about a 17-year-old girl. The acerbic, awkward, and unpopular Nadine Franklin (Steinfeld) has lost the two people in the world who understand her. One, her father, Tom (Eric Keenleyside), who died a few years prior of a heart attack. Now, her best friend, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has started dating Nadine's older brother Darian (Blake Jenner), whom Nadine loathes for having their mother Mona's (Kyra Sedgewick) favor and being so effortlessly beloved and successful.

"I've gotta spend the rest of my life with myself," Nadine says while drunk. We all realize that and then come to terms with it at some point. Nadine's story fits in the gap between the realization and the coming to terms. Speaking as someone who was the same age as Nadine was in 2016, and saw "The Edge of Seventeen" in his senior year of high school, few coming-of-age movies depict awkward adolescence in the 2010s more honestly.

Critics compared "The Edge of Seventeen" to a modern John Hughes movie, as did Hailee Steinfeld herself. In 2016, she explained to Entertainment Weekly that she hoped that the movie could reflect her generation's teen years back at them while still being timeless, in the same way "Sixteen Candles" and "The Breakfast Club" — films made for 1980s kids — still resonated with her (someone born in 1996).

But "The Edge of Seventeen" doesn't soften itself by looking to echoes of older movies instead of real life. The film begins with Nadine marching up to her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (Woody Harrelson) in his classroom, announcing she's planning to die by suicide and wants someone to know first. That opening makes you think you're in for a movie about an inspirational teacher who talks a depressed student back from the edge and shows them why life is worth living. Well, not quite.

We see, as Mr. Bruner immediately recognizes, this is Nadine being dramatic. "I don't want to take up a ton of your time" she says right off, which is her first lie. The movie then rewinds (with the help of some voiceover from Nadine, though that fades pretty quickly) before catching back up with this cold open. What led to her current situation? Nadine accidentally sent a text to her crush, Nick (Alexander Calvert), describing very explicitly how she wants to hook up with him.

That complements one of the best bits of writing in the film, one that definitely helped it speak to my younger self. Nadine has a lot of movie-typical teenage boy qualities: she doesn't fit in, dresses in baggy sweatshirts, has a hopeless crush she never talks to, makes sex jokes while mistaking vulgarity for wit, etc.

During the "Edge of Seventeen" press tour, Kelly Fremon Craig and producer James L. Brooks spoke with /Film. Craig cited some "life-altering" writing advice from Brooks, that she needed to ask herself, "What is this movie saying about life?" I would answer that "The Edge of Seventeen" is about how, when you're a teenager, your problems seem like the whole world and that part of growing up is realizing others — even people who irritate you everyday (as Nadine's mom and brother do to her) — are dealing with their own pain.

Upon its release, "The Edge of Seventeen" saw only modest financial success, grossing $19 million in theaters against its $9 million budget. A spin-off TV series ordered by YouTube Red ultimately didn't move forward, either. I would also argue the film's anticipated reputation as "definitive teen movie of the 2010s" was overshadowed by Greta Gerwig's "Lady Bird," which came out the following year and hits similar beats while finding both great financial success and critical acclaim. Not that "The Edge of Seventeen" has been lost to time or anything, though.

In that aforementioned /Film interview, Craig claimed, "If [Hailee Steinfeld] didn't exist, the movie wouldn't exist," because she brought a sui generis quality to Nadine as she once did to Mattie Ross. The two would work together again on the "Transformers" spin-off film "Bumblebee," where Steinfeld starred and Craig performed rewrites. "Bumblebee" often feels like "The Edge of Seventeen" but with Transformers included.

A couple of times in "The Edge of Seventeen," Nadine looks up to the sky and asks if God is even paying attention to her. Perhaps it's not surprising that when Craig directed another coming-of-age film, she adapted Judy Blume's classic novel "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret."

#3438. GTA 6 Sets New Record As Highest-Rated Video Game of All Time

The 13-year wait for Grand Theft Auto 6 pays off

After more than a decade of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here. Rockstar Games' new open-world crime adventure game is playable by the masses — at least in some parts of the world — and has been playable by critics for some time. GTA 6's review embargo lifted on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and more than a hundred reviews have been tabulated by Metacritic. The consensus is clear: GTA 6 is "monumental," "unbelievably fun," and "truly remarkable," critics say.

The overwhelmingly positive critical response has helped GTA 6 set a new record: It's now the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic, where it currently sits above the previous title-holder, the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. GTA 6 currently has a 99 Metascore (out of 100), the same score that Metacritic displays for Ocarina of Time. The latter score is based on just 22 critic reviews of the Nintendo 64 game. GTA 6's Metascore is based on more than 150.

Both the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X versions of Grand Theft Auto 6 have a 99 Metascore, signaling "universal acclaim," according to Metacritic. The achievement puts GTA 6 atop a very strong top 10 on Metacritic — and knocks another Rockstar Games release out of the site's top 10 list.

Rockstar's Red Dead Redemption 2 held the No. 10 position until today, with its 97 Metascore.

"It’s a bold choice, considering the series’ cold-blooded reputation, but it’s also what makes GTA 6 one of Rockstar’s finest games to date."

Grand Theft Auto 6 was nominated for eight awards, including Game of the Year, at this year's The Game Awards on Tuesday, making it an early frontrunner for multiple GOTY awards. Ahead of launch, the game has reportedly sold more than 17 million copies, according to Sensor Tower, earning $1.65 billion in revenue for Rockstar Games and publisher Take-Two Interactive.

#3437. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3436. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Best Storyline Redeems A Controversial Peter Jackson Idea

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen. Indeed, this season is for the baddies, with the Dark Lord's menacing Nazgnagôl making their grand entrance and a thrilling civil war brewing in Númenor.

But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). From the moment he shows up, it feels like he's been a part of the show from the start, fitting in perfectly as a strong, funny, flirty elf who has excellent chemistry with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). Celeborn is the ultimate wife guy, and his relationship with Galadriel is the best romance we've seen in a Middle-earth adventure to date.

Nevertheless, there's trouble in Valinor for these two, as Celeborn has competition for Galadriel's heart. No, not Robert Aramayo's Elrond (despite them sharing a kiss in Season 2 to distract the orcs holding Galadriel captive), but Sauron, the Dark Lord on his dark throne in the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

That's right: "The Rings of Power" Season 3 has finally turned "The Lord of the Rings" into a romantasy story, placing a love triangle at the heart of the saga of the One Ring. And while J.R.R. Tolkien purists may scoff at this, the show's love triangle is so good that it redeems the controversial romances from Peter Jackson's otherwise beloved "Lord of the Rings" films.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films are the most widely celebrated fantasy movies of all time and changed the genre forever. As such, it's easy nowadays to forget that Jackson's trilogy stirred up its fair share of controversy upon its initial release. After all, as faithful as they were to J.R.R. Tolkien's original books overall, those films also made some big alterations. That includes erasing the Scouring of The Shire from "The Return of the King" and removing characters like Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, in addition to introducing a prominent love triangle.

In Jackson's movies, to jog your memory, a respectable amount of time is spent on Éowyn (Miranda Otto) falling in love with Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), with even King Théoden (Bernard Hill) buying into their match and congratulating Éowyn on finding a good and honest man. Meanwhile, Aragorn keeps thinking about Arwen (Liv Tyler), who is about to leave Middle-earth for Valinor. In fact, the original plan was for Arwen to be at Helm's Deep alongside Éowyn and Aragorn in "The Two Towers," which presumably would've fueled their love triangle even further.

Things get even worse in Jackson's "The Hobbit" films. There, he and co-writers Philippa Boyens and Fran Walsh introduce Tauriel (Evangeline Lilly), an elf who develops romantic feelings for the dwarf Kili (Aidan Turner). In that case, it's Legolas (Orlando Bloom) who rounds out the love triangle, as he's still racist towards dwarves at the time.

Neither of these Middle-earth love triangles really work (especially not the latter), so it's hard not to be skeptical of "The Rings of Power" introducing yet another one. And yet, this ends up being the most compelling aspect of Season 3.

There are two things that make the love triangle in "The Rings of Power" work. The first is that the show is very clearly in on the joke, with Sauron often behaving like a teenager when it comes to his borderline hilarious fixation on Galadriel. That he even goes to the trouble of disguising himself as Galadriel and kissing Celeborn to get information out of him shows Sauron is not beyond being a little bi-curious.

Then there's the fact that the series has been building to this since Season 1, starting with Galadriel slowly falling for Sauron in disguise as Halbrand and being seduced by his promises of power. By the time Season 3 rolls along, she still has complicated feelings for him, as evidenced by her dreams and visions of Sauron waking up in bed next to her. Thus, when Celeborn re-enters her life, and Galadriel sees both men in front of her, there's a tiny bit of hesitation on her part.

And yet, Season 3 never suggests that Galadriel would actually leave her husband for the Dark Lord. Instead, it juxtaposes Sauron's jealousy with Celeborn's confidence. Specifically, in Episodes 5 and 6, Sauron gets visibly flustered when Celeborn talks about how much Galadriel loves him. In the end, it works just as well as the incredible romances in J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, proving that Middle-earth is not devoid of effective romantic storytelling.

Heck, the scene in Episode 6where Celeborn talks about making the elven smith that Sauron has been looking for tell him the secrets of the rings, just so he can hear about every minute the smith spent with Galadriel, is arguably the most romantic TV scene of 2026. Stream Season 3 on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3434. Beats 360 vs Studio Pro: Here’s which Beats headphones you should buy

In September, Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That said, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

One of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. Currently, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

Despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

The biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

Beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

One of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

Of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:

Out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

As for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

Lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can quickly replace them on the Beats 360.

While it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

That said, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.

#3433. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3432. Meta's VR Glasses Could Be The Future Of Home Viewing (But They Probably Won't)

In stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies. A big part of why that's changed lies in the industry's embrace of unique Premium Large Formats, with numerous releases this year having been shown in formats like IMAX, 4DX, Screen X, Dolby Cinema, and so on. Along the way, screening on celluloid (70mm in particular) have become a draw unto themselves, and some cities are home to even more specialized formats, among them Las Vegas' immersive Sphere and the Cosm experience. And while the biggest draw to movie theaters will always be good films, it's clear that audiences also enjoy an experience they can't get elsewhere.

As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing. While most consumers have been content with things like big screen 4K TV's or even their handheld devices for watching at home or on the go, the latest attempt to leap forward from these is just around the corner, in the form of Meta's VR Glasses. It's important to note that these are not the latest version of the smart glasses that have existed on the market since 2021, as they're explicitly not designed to be used while engaged in other activity. Instead, they're a cutting edge virtual/augmented reality system intended to bring together multiple work and entertainment options while idle.

I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing. That said, there are some restrictions to them which, unless changed, mean they won't be replacing our existing personal devices anytime soon.

Although virtual reality, or VR, has existed in some form for decades, it's mostly been utilized as a gimmick more than a viable first choice for media. Fortunately, the folks behind Meta VR Glasses seem to understand this. I got to see a clip from the recent concert doc "Billie Eilish — Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (Live in 3D)" on the glasses, and the experience was like I was watching it on a movie theater screen. That is to say that the aspect ratio was exactly the same as its theatrical exhibition, and the 3D display was pitch perfect. Turning my head in any direction didn't move the "screen," but kept it fixed in front of me, as if it was a physical object in the space, which is a very smart design.

While the James Cameron documentary acted as a demo of how watching most films and shows on the glasses would go, the Meta employees next showed me what they're calling "Enhanced Cinema." Using a clip from "Avengers: Infinity War" in which Thor (Chris Hemsworth) constructs Stormbreaker, the presentation was almost exactly akin to the Cosm experience. This meant that the film was playing on a similar fixed "display" in front of me, while all around me (literally 360 degrees — I checked!) was the environment of the forge on Nidavellir. It's an effect that's totally immersive but not distracting, nor does it betray the original intent of the film itself. After being told that Meta has an exclusive license with the IMAX corporation to present movies filmed for that format on the glasses, I have no doubt that the device could brilliantly replicate those screens for home viewing, and that's incredibly exciting.

While the Meta VR Glasses are not intended to replace a smartphone or similar device, they do seem to do a lot of what those devices do, only bigger and better. From working on VR video games and multiple computer monitors at once to allowing you to watch sports games as they broadcast while seeing the view from courtside, the glasses seem almost too good to be true as a personal media device.

This is where the catches come in. For one thing, watching something with other people at the same time can only occur depending on the content. For another, though they're engineered to be used while stationary, the temptation for people to wear them in public while walking (or, god forbid, driving) exists, and it's quite troubling. Then there's the fact that the glasses seem designed to only work with whatever services and content Meta allows. This means that us physical media fans are SOL, and as with any all-digital service, the content available on the glasses could be subject to change (or disappear) at any time. That's a lot to ask for a device priced at $1,299.99 USD, which is about the same as a new iPhone.

Right now, Meta's killer app beyond the tech itself are its exclusive licenses, such as with IMAX and James Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment. The only way it'll compete with devices already on the market is if it can consistently deliver the quality experiences I got to have with it while being as user friendly as possible. If the glasses prove they can be used at home and on the go as smoothly as an iPhone can now, then they could be a game changer. Until then, they're just a gimmick, albeit a really nice one.

#3431. World of Warcraft Forever Officially Hits Player Peak it Hasn't Seen in 15 Years

The last time this many people were playing WoW, GTA 5 wasn't even out

It was already clear that World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard's reimagining of the early days of the MMO, was a smash hit. During early access, before the game's full release, it brought back plenty of lapsed players and garnered praise. Now, with the dust having settled slightly two weeks after release, it is becoming clear that Forever is returning World of Warcraft to a level of popularity it hasn't seen in years.

To celebrate Forever's continued success, the official World of Warcraft X account shared a handful of fun statistics ranging from how many characters and guilds have been created to how many times players have died. But it's a statistic shared by Holly Longdale, the game's executive producer and vice president, that really puts things into perspective. According to Longdale, World of Warcraft has more weekly players than at any point in the past 15 years thanks to Forever.

That means the last time this many people were playing World of Warcraft, Cataclysm was the game's most recent expansion. That last popularity spike was also closer to the actual release of the MMO in 2004 than it is to Forever's release this year. Even World of Warcraft Classic, Blizzard's playable trip down memory lane, failed to ignite this much interest after launching in 2019.​​​​​​​

While Longdale's reveal is perhaps the most noteworthy​​​​​​​, there are some cool tidbits in the statistics Blizzard posted about Forever's first two weeks. Over 15 million characters have been created, and they've died nearly 200 million times in total​​​​​​​. That would average out to just over 13 deaths per character. Nearly 30 million deaths were due to PvP kills, though the deadliest boss in the game is Shadowfang Keep's​​​​​​​ Archmage Arugal.

Forever is still fresh, though, and only time will tell if Blizzard can keep the game's momentum going as the weeks go on. The developer has consistently updated and tweaked​​​​​​​ the game to better address fan feedback and pain points. What would also be interesting to know is whether​​​​​​​ Forever has brought enough lapsed players back into the fold for them to return to the MMO's main retail version as well​​​​​​​. When the game's next expansion, The Last Titan, releases next year, perhaps​​​​​​​ the game will see a markedly​​​​​​​ larger player count​​​​​​​ as well.

#3429. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3428. 10 Years Ago Today: The Harry Potter Universe Expanded With A Star-Studded Spin-Off

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Harry Potter" is perhaps the defining franchise of the 2000s, but all good things must come to an end. That end originally came in 2011 with "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2" which had the biggest opening ever up to that point in cinema history. But creator J.K. Rowling and Warner Bros. weren't content to let the Wizarding World end there. Ten years ago, they expanded the universe with a star-studded spin-off.

Set decades before Harry Potter was even born, 2016's "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them," which opened 10 years ago today, brought the action to America and focused on entirely new characters within the Wizarding World. Specifically Newt Scamander, played by Oscar-winner Eddie Redmayne. Redmayne had an unexpected inspiration for his performance, namely film icon Buster Keaton. The movie itself was loosely based on an in-universe textbook mentioned in the main series, with Rowling eventually releasing a version of the book, though it didn't contain a narrative.

The resulting prequel/spin-off takes place in 1926 centered on magizoologist Newt Scamander as he arrives in New York during a worldwide tour to research and rescue magical creatures. A mysterious magical being begins causing chaos in NYC, which threatens to expose the wizarding world to the muggles of Earth.

Redmayne was far from the only big star to secure a role in the spin-off. The stacked cast also includes but is not limited to Katherine Waterston, Dan Fogler, Alison Sudol, Samantha Morton, Ezra Miller, and Colin Farrell. "Fantastic Beats" also cast Johnny Depp as Grindelwald in a surprise appearance. Arguably the most important casting decision the movie made, with the benefit of hindsight.

J.K. Rowling wrote the script for "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" personally, which wasn't the case with the other "Harry Potter" movies. David Yates, who helmed the final four "Harry Potter" movies, was recruited to tackle the spin-off as well, providing a sturdy hand.

The majority of the core cast were on the upswing. This movie was expected to be a big break for all of them. In many ways, it was. "Fantastic Beasts" was dubbed a worthy extension of the Wizarding World in many reviews, with audiences tending to agree. Even if it wasn't effusive praise, it was good enough.

The movie was released in November 2016 and did quite well for itself, pulling in $816 million at the global box office. That was more than enough to convince Warner Bros. to double down, with four "Fantastic Beasts" sequels announced before the first one even hit theaters. Everyone involved fully expected this to be the long-term future for the "Harry Potter" franchise. What's perhaps most surprising about that, especially in light of the first movie's success, is the fact that the words Harry Potter don't appear anywhere in the title. All the same, audiences found it.

The train had left the station and everyone involved had every reason to believe, on paper, that people would show up for the sequels en masse. After all, the first installment scored well enough with critics and was the eighth-biggest movie of 2016 overall. Unfortunately, the future had different plans.

Warner Bros. and director David Yates wasted no time, with the second "Fantastic Beasts" installment dated for November 2018. Much of the cast returned, with new additions entering the fold. But in no small part due to forces beyond the studio's control, "The Crimes of Grindelwald" doomed "Fantastic Beasts."

The sequel pulled in more than $650 million at the box office, but made a lot less domestically and had to rely on international audiences to bail it out. Then there's the Depp of it all. Controversy started swirling around the actor due to his public feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard, involving accusations of domestic abuse. Depp later dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise following a court case verdict. Mads Mikkelsen took over as Grindelwald in "The Secrets of Dumbledore," but the writing was on the wall.

The third installment made hardly more than $400 million globally, failing to break even theatrically. "The Secrets of Dumbledore" proved that the magic was gone, despite the appeal of Jude Law as a younger Albus Dumbledore in a lead role. The cast continued to be star-studded all along the way but, at a certain point, appealing casts only go so far. Especially in the 2020s when audiences are more content than ever to stay at home and stream something from the couch.

Controversy and middling results with diminishing returns eventually derailed "Fantastic Beasts." Ten years ago though, the spin-off arrived with a great deal of promise and a lot of potential. That potential just never proved out.

You can grab "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3427. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3425. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.
