#3423. The 8 Best Fantasy Book Authors of All Time, Ranked

Fantasy has been present in stories for just about as long as human storytelling has been a thing, but it didn't become an actual marketing label for the publishing industry until around the 19th century. Since then, we have gotten thousands of authors who can be called full-on fantasy authors, and there is many an element that makes up a great one. Without boundless imagination, deep technical craft, a purposeful eye for world-building, and the ability to write grounded characters, no fantasy author can be truly great.

But even though there have been hundreds upon hundreds of great fantasy writers over the years, there are eight in particular who can be considered the very best to ever grace the genre. These are authors who aren't just phenomenal from a technical or artistic standpoint, they are also of vital historical importance to the genre, still influencing countless fantasy authors the world over to this day. Their work is as foundational as it is essential, and their names belong on the bookshelf of all fantasy fans.

After graduating with a Bachelor's degree in Philosophy from the University of Manitoba, Canadian author Guy Gavriel Kay began writing poetry before turning to prose. Soon enough, he became one of the greatest—and most underrated—fantasy authors of his generation, penning many forgotten books that have aged like fine wine. His work has been particularly important in revolutionizing the mixture between fantasy and settings strongly resembling real historical places and periods, even though Kay himself rejects the label of historical fantasy.

Kay was hired by Christopher Tolkien to help assemble and edit J. R. R. Tolkien's chaotic mass of posthumous manuscripts into the legendary The Silmarillion.

Before he published a single novel of his own, Kay was hired by Christopher Tolkien to help assemble and edit J. R. R. Tolkien's chaotic mass of posthumous manuscripts into the legendary The Silmarillion, and that alone should already be proof enough of his quality. After that, he became a true pioneer of inserting historical elements into the high fantasy genre, delivering masterpieces of the caliber of Tigana and The Lions of Al-Rassan.

Robin Hobb is the pen name of Margaret Astrid Lindholm Ogden, who's undoubtedly best known for her iconic Realm of the Elderlings megaseries. It wasn't until she turned 30 that she published her first book under the name of Megan Lindholm, proving that it's never too late to join the pantheon of history's greatest fantasy authors. She began writing as Robin Hobb 12 years later, and her debut under that legendary pen name was Assassin's Apprentice, the first book in the Farseer trilogy from the Realm of the Elderings series.

Exploring themes like otherness, gender, and queerness across her incredible work, Hobb has crafted some of the fantasy books with the best world-building and the best character writing in history. Shifting the genre's focus from earth-shattering spectacle to deep psychological intimacy and philosophical complexity, she proved just how character- and theme-driven the genre could be when written by a gifted enough author.

If there's any one author worthy of being called the most prolific and widely celebrated fantasy writer currently working, it's almost undeniably Brandon Sanderson. His debut novel, Elantris, was published in 2005, by the time Sanderson had already written about a dozen unpublished books. He has been nothing but a writing machine since then, best known for his iconic Cosmere universe. Composed of multiple subseries and standalones, it's one of the best ongoing fantasy book series.

From the Mistborn series to the Stormlight Archive, Sanderson has written several of the most ambitious high fantasy books of all time, all the while building the biggest multi-decade meta-narrative that fantasy literature has thus far seen. Off the page, he has also trained and influenced countless authors over the years, and coined the distinction between hard magic and soft magic systems, being the undisputed master of the former.

British author, literary scholar, and Anglican lay theologian C. S. Lewis also wrote some incredible science fiction, but he's obviously better known for his fantasy work, particularly The Chronicles of Narnia, one of those fantasy series where every book's a masterpiece. He began writing fiction as a child, inventing stories with his brother and fellow author, Warren Lewis; and soon enough became one of the most important English writers of his generation.

Alongside his good friend Tolkien, Lewis still stands as one of the major pillars of modern fantasy. His work not only revolutionized and popularized portal fantasy, it also made fantasy as a whole more widely accessible, more culturally ubiquitous, and more deeply rooted in Western mythology and philosophy than ever before. Without authors like him, who's to say whether fantasy would have ever been fully legitimized as a genre worthy of being taken seriously?

Another instance of a fantasy literature legend who's best known for one particular series, but whose contributions to the genre extend far beyond that, Robert Jordan is the must-read author of some of the most perfectly-written fantasy books in history. He decided that he wanted to write books while recovering from his time as a Vietnam War veteran, and began writing while working as a nuclear engineer for the US Navy.

High fantasy had been very heavily inspired by Tolkien (or directly aiming to imitate him) for decades before Jordan came about.

The most prominent work of such an iconic career is The Stormlight Archive, far and away one of the greatest and most influential fantasy book series since the '90s. High fantasy had been very heavily inspired by Tolkien (or directly aiming to imitate him) for decades before Jordan came about, and it was authors like him who proved that the genre could start doing things differently. Darker, more mature, and more complex than most other fantasy novels from his time, Jordan's work broke the mold and has continued aging like fine wine.

Dramatic fantasy is of vital importance, and it's always a delight to read an author who actually takes the genre seriously and builds something deeply compelling out of it. However, comedic fantasy is arguably every bit as important, and as far as that subgenre goes, you don't get any authors more foundational than Sir Terry Pratchett, fantasy's most beloved satirist. He's best known for his Discworld series, composed of a whopping 41 fantasy comedies.

What makes Pratchett's work so brilliant is that even though his satirical fantasy works are undeniably hilarious, they're also surprisingly profound. On top of providing one of the best soft magic systems in history, Discworld proved that even comedic fantasy could be legitimately serious in its own way. Thematically complex and richly human, Pratchett's work interrogates human nature, institutions, and morality in all sorts of enrapturing ways. His books are brilliantly meta and quite diverse, making Discworld a must-read series for anyone who thinks that fantasy can't be hilarious and profound at the same time.

In the entire history of speculative fiction, few authors have ever been quite as important as Ursula K. Le Guin. Indeed, the American master could also very reasonably be counted among the eight most important and essential sci-fi authors of all time, but there are many who prefer her work in fantasy. Le Guin wrote her first fantasy story at age nine and submitted her first sci-fi story to a magazine at age 11, and from there, there was nowhere for her to go but up.

The daughter of an anthropologist and with a deep academic interest in mythology, Le Guin wrote masterpieces like Lavinia and the Earthsea Cycle, many of them among those books that are a masterclass in high fantasy writing. By introducing elements of Taoist philosophy, psychological realism, and non-Eurocentric anthropological and cultural depth to her work, Le Guin completely rejected many of the tropes and traditions that had ruled fantasy literature for years. She genuinely revolutionized fantasy, pioneering many new tropes of her own in the process.

You'd be hard-pressed to find anyone unwilling to call J. R. R. Tolkien the single greatest and most influential fantasy author of modern times, and that's for good reason. Never has the history of speculative fiction seen anybody quite like Tolkien, and it likely never will again. Sparked by the Professor's love for philology, ancient mythologies, and original myth-making, the world was treated to an authorial career that completely revolutionized fantasy. Indeed, many would divide the genre's modern history between the pre-Tolkien and the post-Tolkien eras.

Yes, Tolkien wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, his most celebrated works and perhaps the most influential fantasy novels of the 20th century. However, his contributions to the genre extend far beyond. He wrote several masterworks outside Middle-earth, he contributed to the academic study of fantasy, and he completely laid down the blueprint for modern high, epic, and heroic fantasies. Author of some of the most memorable characters, the most fascinating lore, and the best battles in the history of fantasy books, Tolkien was the greatest of all fantasy writers. It will take someone so special that he's truly out of this world to ever dethrone Tolkien.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

#3422. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3421. MacBook Neo 2: Here’s everything we know so far

Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

Apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

#3420. GTA 6: How To Easily Find Story Missions

GTA 6 is a stunningly deep open-world game with a lot to do, but naturally, the story mode is what a lot of players will gravitate toward. While many of the transitions to these missions are going to be natural, in classic GTA fashion, there are a handful of missions that aren't so obvious, and require a degree of waiting or a proactive approach.

Here's how to always stay on top of what missions you need to advance the story, and how to move things along if they need a little nudge. Given the direct control you have over both Jason and Lucia as protagonists, it's important to know all the tricks so you don't get stuck.

Press the touchpad on PS5 to open the map, which brings up a variety of missions and points of interest. Think of your map as a master list of everything to do, with icons for drop points (to stash/sell illicit objects), side quests, shops, banks to rob, and, of course, story missions.

These are indicated by a "book" icon near the top left of the screen, listing all story missions you can take part in. For the most part, this list will include at least one mission, all of which are required to progress "Jason and Lucia's Story," the campaign of GTA 6.

Note that occasionally, Lucia or Jason will be forced to go on solo missions. Think Lucia meeting up with her mom for a mother-daughter day, or Jason doing an odd job for an old friend that Lucia isn't interested in attending.

When these missions arise, make sure you say goodbye to your partner before entering the mission area. Sometimes the mission won't progress unless the required character's significant other is completely out of the zone, so if you're having trouble starting a story mission, that might be why.

We recommend knocking these story missions out as soon as possible, as they can be finicky and block progress on other missions.

When story missions aren't listed, here are the two things you can do to speed things up:

The game doesn't make it immediately apparent, but sometimes calling a key character is enough to advance the story. As you call each contact in the recents menu, they will disappear, indicating you have all the info you need from them, and a story mission may populate as soon as the call ends. By going to bed afterward, you can accelerate this story mission prep process and move things along.

If you're looking to go through the story of GTA 6 at a brisker pace, we recommend doing both in tandem. Go to bed at your home location, sleep until the next day, then call as many people as you can. It might take a few days, but story missions will pop up over time.

#3417. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3415. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3414. GTA 6: Easiest Ways To Earn Money

As in many open-world games, cash rules everything in GTA 6. You need it to properly prep for some of the tougher encounters in the game, and there are so many ways to earn money that it can be overwhelming. It is an open-world, expansive adventure, after all, but there are plenty of ways to simplify making money.

In addition to robbing places with Jason and Lucia together, you can string multiple robberies into one long crime session, or opt for more legitimate ways to earn money. No matter which option you choose, here are the easiest ways to earn cash in GTA 6.

It sounds obvious, but mainlining story missions is an easy way to earn cash and advance the campaign. Early on, Jason will get constant payments from jobs in his mailbox, so check it nearly every morning before driving off the property.

Some story missions can offer incredibly luxurious rewards, like gear, clothes, weapons, and of course, tons of cash. Some mid-to-late game missions offer tens of thousands of dollars in rewards, quickly boosting your bank account without doing much beyond playing the story.

Once you get to Chapter 2 with Lucia and meet Moses, you'll have the power to bring him cars, and either "register" them (so you own them above board), or sell them.

All you need to do is get in the car, then drive it to Moses (marked clearly on the map in the northwest portion of the game world), drive it into his garage, interact with him (L2/LT) and manually sell or register the car.

Selling nicer cars to Moses is a very easy way to get a ton of cash early in the game, and beyond.

Very early in GTA 6, you can knock off convenience stores and pawn shops, most of which have either one armored guard (who can easily be taken out as you enter) or no protection at all.

Walk into the store, take out the armed NPCs, and then point a gun at an employee. Hold L2 (LT) to bring up a prompt (typically confirmed with Square on PlayStation, X on Xbox), asking them to take money out of the cash register or let you know where valuables are kept.

Depending on where you rob, there might be an additional opportunity for extra cash:

Once you have the illegal goods (which are typically substances or marked bills), you'll need to deliver them to a specific NPC (marked in green on the world map) to "clean" them. This includes marked bills from banks, or illegal substances seized from enemy operations. Just bring the items (housed in a duffel bag) to the NPC, speak to them, and hand them over with a button prompt.

If you die or get caught by the police in GTA 6, you'll lose your goods in the duffel bag, so keep that in mind. If you're doing a huge job and have tons of cash and illegal goods in a duffel bag, you'll want to turn it in to a helpful NPC sooner rather than later.

#3413. Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

At long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America currently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the big screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

That’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

So far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

And they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

Skydance has set its film leadership team.

Their task will be to stabilize Warner Bros.‘ film output while rejuvenating or extending franchises like “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Conjuring.” Skydance executives have been horrified by the extent of the losses racked up by Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, with sources estimating them in the hundreds of millions of dollars. As part of this restructuring, Jeff Goldstein, who oversaw Warner Bros. distribution for many years, will retire, and Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, which he led. Richard Brener, a survivor of several mergers, will remain as president and chief content officer of New Line, where he guided hits like “Weapons.”

In a memo to staff, Goldberg and Greenstein praised Granger as “a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output.” They noted that at Netflix, Goldberg “oversaw a slate that included ‘Don’t Look Up,’ starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming ‘Bad Day,’ with Cameron Diaz, and ‘The Take’ starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Goldberg was also an executive at Fox, working on films such as “The Greatest Showman” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.”

Ehrman is a WB veteran who has worked on hits such as “A Minecraft Movie” and “Sinners.” Ireland joined Warner Bros. after years at Paramount. He left the studio after it was sold to Skydance in 2025.

“This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote. “We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership.”

#3409. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3408. GTA 6: How To Get Any Safe Code

GTA 6 is full of surprises. While there are tons of ways to make money, some of them are faster than others. But those methods are generally riskier, creating an interesting push-and-pull in how fast you earn cash in the game.

While other GTA games have had these elements front and center, GTA 6 expands the robbery mechanic quite a bit, allowing players to use disguises and hit a ton of places in rapid succession, quicker than ever before. There are a lot of factors to consider, but here's how to get any safe code, whether it's a small pawn shop or a big bank.

For the most part, there are two core methods for gaining access to the safe code, beyond improbably guessing the combination:

Before you do any of that, turn off the security feed and make sure you're isolated from what's going on outside. Taking Jason or Lucia with you can help you control the crowd, and avoid the police showing up earlier as you're searching for (or demanding) the safe code.

Generally, smaller places (like pawn shops) will have the code written down, and one employee present. These codes might be on a giant board close to the register, in a back room, or in an office.

The easiest way to try and force the code out of an employee. You can hold them up directly by aiming a weapon at them, holding L2 (LT on Xbox), and repeatedly pressing the Square (X on Xbox) button. You'll interrogate them for a code, and even if they don't give it to you, you can still try the same method on someone else. This method may also force NPCs to take cash out of the register and place it on the counter, making your robbery go a little faster.

Often, in the hectic event of robbing something (especially if it's a massive bank), it's easy to miss the notification that you acquired a safe code verbally. Because of this, make sure you look for the safe before leaving a bank for any reason, in case you picked up the safe code by accident. It'll take less than 30 seconds to load up your duffle bag with cash from the safe.

For the most part, any business will have an on-site safe, but that's not always the case. Look for locations to rob with a specific icon that shows how much cash the store has on hand and whether there are any illicit items in the backroom (like illegal substances).

That said, banks are one of the biggest-yield targets in GTA 6, so if you're going to hit one of those, make sure you go for the big rewards:

Robbing a place in GTA 6 with a low yield can get you caught in a nasty, escalating police chase, which can waste time and net you zero rewards if you end up dying or getting caught.

#3407. 'The Rings of Power' Stars Address Season 3's Most Complicated Triangle

Editor's note: The below interview contains spoilers for The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 5 & 6.

It's almost hard to believe, but The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 is officially past the halfway point. With Sauron's (Charlie Vickers) influence spreading across Middle-earth, the Dark Lord ultimately has his sights set on the goal of crafting something more powerful than he's ever attempted before — the One Ring to Rule Them All. To accomplish the task, he needs knowledge he doesn't yet have access to, so maybe the Elf he's currently holding captive can supply him with the info he wants.

Yet it isn't Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) whom Sauron has in his clutches, but her long-lost husband, Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who willingly surrenders himself to the Dark Lord in Episode 5. Initially, Celeborn seems more than capable of enduring the unique brand of torture that Sauron has for him in Episode 6 — before the situation takes a personal and even more twisted turn.

Before The Rings of Power's latest two-episode drop, Collider spoke with Bower and Vickers about the ever-complicated dynamic between Galadriel, Celeborn, and Sauron. Over the course of the interview, which you can watch above or read below, the co-stars dive into the premiere's fan-favorite return, Sauron's looming impact on Galadriel and Celeborn's relationship, and the evolving nature of Sauron's torture of Celeborn in Episode 6.

COLLIDER: Charlie, I want to start with you because I think the first episode really has a fun cameo that I don't know how many people are expecting. What was it like to reunite with Charles [Edwards] and get to explore the continuing haunting that Sauron is having with Celebrimbor?

CHARLIE VICKERS: It was so special. Charles is one of my favorite people in the whole world. We had such a blast, I cannot tell you, filming in the second season. When we found out that he was coming back for a few moments, it was so exciting. And he plays it so beautifully.

The thing that I think he captures perfectly is that it's not Celebrimbor — he wouldn't taunt like that. He is basically playing Sauron with, like, a figment of Sauron's imagination. So, yeah, it was such a joy to film.

It was one of those things where I just get to stand there and listen to him. I can feel him walking up behind me the whole time. And, yeah, it was really, really, really special. And I hope fans are excited to see the dynamic again in a slightly twisted way so immediately in the season.

Jamie, in Episode 5, your characters cross paths, and Celeborn gives himself up to Sauron to protect Galadriel — essentially, to divert attention away from where she's sleeping unawares of anything going on. But Sauron has really been this presence hanging over their relationship, because Galadriel doesn't want to talk about him and doesn't want to bring him into that relationship. I was curious about how you wanted to play the moment where you see Celeborn realize that Sauron is the person that she's been talking about the entire time.

JAMIE CAMPBELL BOWER: It's an interesting thing because, originally, I was like, "It has to be quite immediate." And then as we were exploring it further, I was like, "Okay, so maybe it's sort of piece by piece by piece, he starts to understand that it is this person." Because I think what I have to see is I have to see her pain, first of all, and understand the damage that it's caused. It's not until that prison scene, realistically for me, that I felt like all of those pieces drop together.

That line in [Episode] 5 where he says, “She'll come to you, but she'll come for me,” it's like that was the first thing where I'm like, “The fuck you talking about? What are you saying?” after having held space for the pain that she's gone through. So, it was really important. It was really, really important.

And within that, it was about choice and about understanding how he would feel, and the poisoning of that space. And she has said, as you rightly pointed out, “I don't want him here.” He's poisoning that space for her, and he ultimately poisons that space for Celeborn in Episode 7, too.

After ‘Stranger Things,’ Bower is letting his guard down as Celeborn in ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 — and finding freedom in the process.

Carrying into the next episode, the two of you get to really dig into the emotional minefield of this ever-complicated dynamic. Charlie, you have the great line, “Torture is but the beginning of what you and I are about to share,” which is going to be up in the pantheon of villain lines. What really excited the two of you most about using what starts as a physical torture and then slowly becomes more emotional and mental from Sauron’s side to explore these two and their relationship to each other and their relationship to Galadriel as well?

VICKERS: I think that's such a good observation, because it does start out as a simple thing of torture. But what makes it really interesting is it, from both sides, progresses into something that feels more personal. You always wonder about what Sauron's true intentions or feelings are with Galadriel, but I think Celeborn starts to needle away at that, and access that, and kind of gives Sauron a taste of his own medicine.

And then I always love sort of playing around with how affected Sauron is by that and tossing up the idea of: Is he actually affected? Is he pretending to be affected in order to break the walls down between them? Because in the end, Sauron actually needs them to become emotionally available to each other, to put it simply, in order for him to truly manipulate Celeborn. So, it is also his intention to get to the point where they truly know each other. I think I even have a line along those lines. Like, “Now we can begin.” Step by step, as these scenes progress, he gets closer to being able to do his kind of mind prison prism thing.

BOWER: For me, on that end, the choice to kind of not look at him at those beginning moments was the choice that I made because I was like, “If I let him see me, then he's going to find a way in.” And interestingly enough, from my perspective, with regards to the spit moment, where Sauron does say, “Now we can begin,” that is the moment where Celeborn meets Sauron in that low place. It's like, low blow, you know? “Now you're just as fucked up as I am. Welcome to the party,” basically.

The final two episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 premiere next Wednesday on Prime Video.

#3404. ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

“Madden” is technically a David O. Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact. Amazon MGM Studios, in their infinite wisdom, has decided to emphasize star Nicolas Cage’s performance as the larger-than-life NFL coach and sports broadcaster in its scant promotional material. While the trailer includes an obligatory “From the director of ‘Silver Linings Playbook’ and ‘American Hustle’” title card, the poster features Cage and Christian Bale, who plays Oakland Raiders coach Al Davis, flashing their Super Bowl rings, and no mention of Russell. Even the PR flack at the sparsely-attended press screening introduced the film by saying, “Please enjoy Nicolas Cage’s ‘Madden’!” Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

To be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy. Russell may be a problematic figure, but it wasn’t so long ago when starring in one of his films almost guaranteed an actor awards attention. During a brief five-year period in the 2010s, his work garnered Oscar wins for Christian Bale and Jennifer Lawrence, and nominations for Amy Adams, Bradley Cooper, and Robert De Niro. Putting aside the uneven quality of his work, Russell certainly afforded actors the opportunity to “make choices” in lavish studio productions, which often amounted to adopting broad accents and wearing flashy costumes, and receive acclaim for their efforts. It’s probably why people keep working with him in spite of the numerous incidents of on-set mistreatment (on top of a sexual assault allegation) that have continued to this day.

Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go big or go home remains sacrosanct. In “Madden,” Cage wore 30 pounds of prosthetics on top of the 25 pounds he gained for the role. He certainly resembles the man, at least if you ignore Cage’s actual face. Ditto Bale, who adopts Davis’s Noo-Yawk accent and bold fashion sense. But it’s all in service of a film so milquetoast that it will make you beg for the sheer personality exhibited in “Amsterdam,” which at least had the decency to have a narrative and occasionally spark tension and generally be about something.

Here’s what happens in Russell’s eleventh feature: head coach John Madden leads the Oakland Raiders to finally beat their longstanding rivals Pittsburgh Steelers in the 1976 AFC Championship, after which they win the Super Bowl. Following his diagnosis of a bleeding ulcer in his stomach, Madden permanently retires from his coaching career to be with his family. Realizing he’s a stranger in his own home after spending too much time away, he quickly transitions into sports broadcasting where he becomes a television mainstay. To secure his legacy and pass on his legendary playbook, he eventually lends his likeness to EA Sports for the “Madden” video game franchise, which becomes one of the most profitable on the market. He then lives happily ever after.

If that sounds like a film with little-to-no conflict, you would be correct. Part of the problem is that Madden, while being an American institution and a legendary NFL coach, isn’t really suited to be the subject of a biopic, largely because the details of his life are fairly free of drama or intrigue. He’s the kind of figure who should be the lead of a Saturday-morning cartoon where he helps kids solve mysteries using the power of his football mind. Rather than impose a zany plot onto his life or make up outlandish shit for entertainment purposes, which he’s known to do, Russell dutifully relates the major events in his life.

The bare-bones emotional foundation of “Madden” takes the form of the two loves in the eponymous character’s life. The first is with his wife Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), who longs for John to recommit to fatherhood and their marriage, at least until it becomes clear that he needs football to be a functioning human being. Hahn’s established joie de vivre ensures Viriginia is slightly more interesting than an archetypal long-suffering wife character, but, alas, her general lack of chemistry with Cage dampens their tender scenes together, and their intermittent marital troubles are too fleeting and half-hearted to make any dramatic purchase.

The second, and arguably most pivotal, is with Davis, whose slightly-problematic bromance with Madden serves as the film’s primary source of drama. Russell’s film briefly flirts with an interesting thread by portraying Davis as a devil on Madden’s shoulder, someone who seemingly wants him to continue coaching forever, his health and family life be damned. He constantly tries to pressure Madden into returning to the league long after he retires in the vein of an old buddy who wants you to stay out for “just one more beer.” Despite his size, Madden frequently shrinks in Davis’s presence, who knows just what to say to get him to do what he wants.

But while Russell gestures towards connecting Davis’s “maverick” professional style, which made him uniquely qualified for the world of sports ownership but nevertheless created controversy within the league, and his friendship with Madden, he ultimately chickens out from characterizing him as a truly malign influence. (“Madden” just isn’t set up to be a film with a villain or an antagonist of any kind.) Instead, Russell depicts John and Virginia Madden and Al and Carol (Sienna Miller) Davis as tightknit couple friends, admittedly a type of relationship that rarely receives the big-screen treatment, whose ups and downs are manageable because, well, they really just love each other.

It’s worth noting that “Madden” is technically a comedy. It certainly presents as one, featuring well-proven settings for laughter in sports comedies like the sidelines, the locker room, and the announcing booth. Intermittent jokes pop up in these spaces, though I’m genuinely hard-pressed to remember anything specific because much of it suffocates under Cage’s affectionately-caricatured performance. Russell trusts that the sight of the actor in a full-body fat suit is enough for audiences. Granted, Cage seems to palpably enjoy embodying Madden’s flamboyant energy and imposing figure, even if his inconsistent voice acting, complete with slurred speech and vowel-swallowing, occasionally threatens to tip into outright cruelty. (“Madden” features the real article speaking at the film’s end and it’s downright absurd how much Cage exaggerates his diction.)

If there’s one semi-sophisticated bit in the film, it’s that Madden’s one-track mind sees the world entirely through football strategy. He literally can’t write “XOXO” to his future wife in their yearbook without turning it into a play design. But Russell doesn’t really develop the idea any further and instead defaults to broad humor that tends to blend together and subsequently die on the vine. These often materialize as sight gags, like Bale’s increasingly ridiculous haircuts, or John Mulaney, who plays Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, costumed to resemble Steve Jobs. Sometimes it amounts to Shane Gillis delivering Shane Gillis-style lines, sometimes with a perm or donning a wizard’s outfit, or former running back Marshawn Lynch dressed like a nerd.

On paper, Russell is actually a neat fit for a film like “Madden.” He made his bones directing abrasive ensemble screwball comedies. He’s directed period biopics, including one that’s also a sports drama, and one of his most acclaimed films involves football fandom. Sadly, “Madden” features few Russellisms beyond tacky ’70s and ’80s fashion and some mild domestic discord. He’s replaced his typically messy, chaotic atmosphere for an overly genial one.

Anyone who has some familiarity with screen passes or end-arounds likely learned it downwind from Madden, who used whiteboards to make complicated play schemes accessible to the viewing public. His impact extends well into the realm of pop culture, like the Miller Lite commercial where he breaks through the wall, the custom-manufactured bus in which he drove around the country due to his well-documented fear of flying, and his famous turducken. “Madden” covers all of that material without offering any insight other than the security of the man’s legacy. The Russell who made “I Heart Huckabees” has long faded away, but it’s still a shame that he’s been reduced to directing one of the oddest and blandest examples of brand management in recent memory.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “Madden” in select theaters and on Prime Video on Wednesday, November 18.

#3403. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3401. GTA 6: How To Unlock Selling Cars

There are multiple ways to earn money in GTA 6, and not all of them are as efficient. While robbing smaller stores can be less risky than robbing a major bank, the yield is also low, and you still need to clean/fence that merchandise afterward.

In that sense, stealing and selling cars can be even easier to do, but you need to go about it the right way. Plus, you can't just sell cars at the start of the game. You'll need to work up Jason and Lucia's contacts, and eventually find someone who will take stolen vehicles for cash later in the game.

After entering Chapter 2, you'll take full control of Lucia, as you're whisked away to a hotel in the northwest corner of the map. This zone is fairly relaxed, with minimal organized gang activity and lots of woods to lose the cops in.

After completing the first few story missions with Lucia, you'll meet a mutual friend named Moses, who operates out of a garage and junkyard. Moses will walk you through the tutorial for stealing cars and returning them.

You won't be able to steal a car right outside of Moses' shop and turn it in for cash.

Moses will also provide you with the Slim Jim item, which makes stealing cars a lot easier. To use the Slim Jim, you'll press Triangle (Y on Xbox) instead of Square (X on Xbox) to smash the window. From there, you'll need to do another analog-stick-shifting minigame to fully pop the lock, then enter the vehicle without incident.

You can use the Slim Jim for the rest of GTA 6 with both characters. There's no need to equip it or anything; it'll automatically be part of Jason and Lucia's loadout. Keep it in mind if you're trying to steal a car, as it makes less noise and many car alarms don't even go off.

To get paid for stealing cars, drive a car back to Moses, bring it into his shop (the garage door will open), then speak to Moses directly. Make sure you use the L2 method (LT on Xbox) to focus on Moses, and bring up more dialogue options. This will let you sell the car to him directly, so you can complete the transaction.

Note that more expensive cars provide bigger yields, and you can search cars for their worth using the Waink app (the shortcut is holding up on the d-pad). Try to go for bigger sales and avoid picking up junky cars, as it'll only take more time to make a ton of cash.

Also, keep in mind that the Slim Jim is pretty much your main tool for stealing cars until later in the game, when you unlock the key cloner. Once you have that, you can steal higher-end cars with advanced security systems for even bigger profits.

As you progress through the game, Moses isn't the only person who will buy cars off of you. More vendors await in later portions of GTA 6, so you won't need to drive all the way to Moses to make a delivery.

#3400. The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there.

A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the new box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case.

9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

It is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets.

Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor.

One group of users hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the new Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

Carter now reveals that The X-Files Season 11 intentionally left its characters' fate ambiguously open to provide a takeoff point for future stories. Eight years later, Carter has not moved on from the world he created and has now confirmed that his plan to revisit the original is active and alive.

During a recent interview promoting his latest project, Queens for a Day, which reunites several The X-Files alums, Carter expressed readiness to return to The X-Files to continue Mulder and Scully's arc. Carter has also revealed that he wouldn't want his continuation to interfere with Coogler's upcoming reboot out of respect for what he's building. I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3397. Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

Ever since George Lazenby first replaced Sean Connery as James Bond in 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” fans have argued over who makes the best 007 — and those arguments are likely to resume once Robert Pattinson takes the screen as the latest Bond in director Denis Villeneuve’s new iteration. Although Craig has his partisans, Connery tends to be the consensus choice for the best Bond, though I’ve argued here for the merits of 1970s and ’80s Roger Moore. All the Bonds have their virtues, but Connery benefited from being there first — for anyone who discovered the series in its initial heyday, Connery simply is James Bond. Related Stories ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’? ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Yet Connery actually wasn’t the first actor to play Bond. That honor goes to journeyman MGM contract player Barry Nelson, who played Bond in a “Casino Royale” adaptation eight years before Connery made the character famous in “Dr. No.” Connery may have been the first 007 to grace the big screen, but Nelson established Bond on the small screen in an episode of the CBS anthology series “Climax!” opposite Peter Lorre in the Le Chiffre role that would later be inhabited by Orson Welles (in the goofy 1967 “Casino Royale”) and Mads Mikkelsen (in the 2006 adaptation that introduced Craig to the series).

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is a fascinating artifact that includes elements that would go on to characterize future James Bond movies, while also going in a few other very different directions. The key difference is in the scale, stripped down by necessity for television production. The hour-long “Climax!” episode is all interiors, taking place entirely in the hotel and casino of the title. It’s more a James Bond play than a movie, with Bond and Le Chiffre facing off in a series of verbal — and ultimately physical — jousts in confined spaces, and it’s surprisingly effective.

It’s also a very strange beginning for a franchise that would come to be known for its globetrotting locales and elaborate action set pieces. Not that this “Casino Royale” was officially part of the James Bond franchise as we know it. In fact, although there have been three adaptations of Ian Fleming’s first James Bond novel, only the third incarnation with Daniel Craig was from EON Productions, the company that controlled the character from “Dr. No” through the Craig era before selling the rights to Amazon.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” came about when producer Gregory Ratoff optioned the rights to Fleming’s novel in May of that year. The novel wasn’t yet a hit, and Fleming was sorely in need of cash, which led him to make one of the worst deals in movie-rights history when he sold the book outright to Ratoff for $6,000 after the TV episode aired. This left “Casino Royale” out of the deal when EON secured the screen rights to James Bond as a character, so Bond producers Albert Broccoli and Harry Saltzman could only sit back and grit their teeth when Ratoff turned “Casino Royale” into a comedy in 1967 and cast Peter Sellers, David Niven, Woody Allen and others as rotating Bonds.

EON ultimately made a deal to bring “Casino Royale” under their umbrella and used the novel to reboot the franchise with Craig, but in 1954 it served as the source for a much more modest affair. The biggest similarities between the 1954 “Climax!” episode and the Daniel Craig movie come in the time spent on extended gambling sequences, and the centering of a brutal torture scene. Given censorship restrictions of the time, Nelson’s torture in a bathtub is considerably less graphic than the mallet to the testicles inflicted on Craig, but it’s rough enough stuff for a 1950s TV production.

Certain aspects of Nelson’s characterization, like Bond’s mix of sexual swagger and icy indifference, would later be adopted by most future 007s, to varying degrees. The biggest difference between Nelson and future Bonds is a simple one: He’s American. Although Broccoli and Saltzman flirted with the idea of an American Bond throughout the series’ history (going so far as to cast James Brolin in “Octopussy” before Moore decided to return at the last minute), to date they’ve never actually pulled the trigger on casting outside the UK.

Nelson is probably best known to modern audiences as the affable hotel manager Stuart Ullman in Stanley Kubrick’s “The Shining,” but in the 1950s he was a sturdy character actor and occasional leading man who bounced around television after an initial sojourn as a studio contract player. As a young man, he appeared in several important MGM films, including “Shadow of the Thin Man,” “Bataan,” and “A Guy Named Joe” (the source material for Steven Spielberg’s “Always”). Later on, he popped up in “Airport” and had a successful Broadway career. He was nominated for a Tony acting opposite Liza Minnelli in Martin Scorsese’s 1977 production “The Act.”

In 1954, though, he was in the middle of a prolific and productive era as a TV stalwart, both as a series regular (on “The Hunter” and “My Favorite Husband”) and a frequent guest star. He doesn’t exhibit a ton of range as American “Combined Intelligence” agent “Jimmy” Bond, but that too is in keeping with the overall conception of the character, at least until Craig tried to bring a little more emotional depth to the role.

In Americanizing Bond, the “Climax!” edition of “Casino Royale” ends up making a number of related changes that are small but make the film feel just a bit off for fans of the EON productions. American Felix Leiter (later played by Jeffrey Wright) becomes Brit Clarence Leiter, for example. Although there’s none of the Bond gadgetry that would become famous later, there are hints of what’s to come in the form of props like a villain’s cane that hides a gun, and the opening credits for the “Climax!” series itself feature a gun barrel pointed at the viewer that predicts the iconic graphics of later Bond title sequences.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is noteworthy for another reason: its composer, Jerry Goldsmith, who would ultimately score hundreds of major films, including “Planet of the Apes,” “Chinatown,” “Basic Instinct,” and most of Joe Dante’s work. Yet in some ways what’s fascinating about “Casino Royale” is how unremarkable it is — it’s a decent, solid piece of entertainment from an era when proliferating anthology shows provided similar programs every week.

If Fleming had his way, it would have only been the start for 007 on television; he wrote several outlines for episodes of a James Bond series before CBS canceled the project. Luckily, he repurposed most of what he wrote as short stories for his 1960 book “For Your Eyes Only,” and television’s loss was cinema’s gain. By 1962, James Bond belonged to the movies — and to Sean Connery.
