#3396. Apple engineers ‘actively working’ on Face ID for iPhone Duo 2’s outer display: report

Next fall, Apple will introduce its second-generation iPhone Duo. It’s unclear what it’ll offer in terms of meaningful upgrades outside of the usual chip upgrades and camera improvements, but Apple engineers are reportedly attempting to bake Face ID into the device. That said, the feature might not make the cutoff.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has two priorities for iPhone Duo: Face ID and the Action Button. The latter might just end up being a new software addition to Camera Control that allows you to remap the hold action from Siri in Camera to an app of your choice.

As for Face ID, Apple engineers are ‘actively working’ on integrating the technology on the device, specifically on the outer display:

Other goals for the next couple of generations include adding a telephoto camera and making the device thinner and lighter overall. But Face ID is the top priority. I’m told that Apple has already developed prototypes of the iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, and engineers are still actively working to integrate the facial-recognition system into the outer display of the second-generation model.

That said, the feature might not make it. According to Gurman, the timelines are tight here and it isn’t quite ready – so he isn’t reporting with certainty on whether or not this feature will make it. If it doesn’t debut with the iPhone Duo 2, it’ll likely be in the cards for iPhone Duo 3 in 2028.

Later down the road, the company wants to introduce an improved camera system for the iPhone Duo, including a telephoto camera. It also wants to make the device even thinner and lighter. The Duo definitely needs to be lighter, but making it even thinner would be an interesting feat.

While Face ID on the iPhone Duo would certainly be much appreciated, I’m not quite convinced that it’ll be super meaningful on only the outer display.

Being 8 years late to the foldable party, kinda makes you wonder why they weren't "actively working" on it during that time. They got it into the Air afterall.

If they magically make it happen for the Duo 2 then it looks like they held it back purposefully for yearly incremental improvement reasons as opposed to it not being possible.

I’m fine with Touch ID, but whenever it is bothersome, it’s usually on the inner display, where it can be hard to reach the button depending on how you’re holding the device. If I could only have Face ID on one display, I think I’d rather have it on the inner display.

Orientation can make a huge difference for how you reach Touch ID on the inner display, whereas you’re generally only going to hold the outer display one of two ways: upright in your left hand, or upright in your right hand.

#3395. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

#3394. X-Men Unveils Cyclops' Darkest Moment, Worse Than Anything Magneto Ever Did

X-Men just took Cyclops to his darkest place ever. The franchise has gone full horror as "the clock strikes midnight" in the newest offshoot of the Marvel Universe, and the genre switch has quickly proven to be about more than just gore. X-Men is now a full-blown psychological horror story, and it is Scott Summers who takes center stage, and the brunt of the suffering, in the latest chapter.

What are the first things that come to mind when fans think about Cyclops? Natural leader. Mentally tough. Stalwart hero. What would it take to break him? To bring him to his knees? That's the question Midnight X-Men #2 answers, and the shocking thing about the issue isn't necessarily what happens to Scott, but how easy it turns out to be.

As the saying goes, "love conquers all." Usually, that's supposed to be a good thing. Well, author Jonathan Hickman has managed to give the axiom a dark new meaning in Midnight X-Men, as Cyclops' undying love for his wife, Jean Grey, is weaponized against him in the most horrifying possible way.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for X-Men Midnight #2!

Midnight X-Men #1 introduced readers to a new Marvel timeline, in which vampires and mutants had combined to become a terrifying third thing: "empyres." Legions of these empyres, led by Storm, exist in an uneasy truce with the rest of mutantkind after years of conflict. The series second issue goes back in time to explain how so many mutants were turned before the "ceasefire" was established. It all goes back to one person: Scott Summers.

No shame on Cyclops for the first trap he leads his team into, which ends up with most of the original X-Men, including Jean Grey, turned by Storm. His real tragic mistake is letting himself be fooled into thinking he could rescue Jean, leading him to bring another X-squad to the vampirized mutants on a silver platter. If all that doesn't sound bad enough, that's when the story takes its truly horrific turn.

Utterly defeated, Cyclops begs to be turned, so he can join his team. And he's rejected. Instead, he becomes Jean's thrall. Her Renfield. His job? Keep assembling teams to bring to the empyres to be converted or killed. Use mutantkind's trust and faith in him in the ultimate act of betrayal. It is a hardcore twist on Cyclops' usual portrayal, and it sets him up for a gripping character arc as Midnight X-Men continues.

Cyclops narrates Midnight X-Men #2 from the vantage point of years later. At a point in the future well after Jean Grey's vampiric-psychic hold on him has been broken. He knows the truth of what he did, and he carries around the crushing guilt of it. That is going to have major implications for the story of Midnight X-Men. It could be laying the groundwork for a redemption arc, or it could be set up to turn Cyclops into a villain. Either way, it has made him a tragic figure to a degree few X-stories have ever done before.

[Midnight X-Men #2] uses lore and backstory to serve a heartbreaking character portrait, rather than using characters as "instruments of a greater plot."

For now, though, readers are left with Cyclops' haunting monologue as he reflects on his sins, the terrible price he paid for his failure as a leader and a hero. "Love is total annihilation of the self," Scott Summers concludes. "I have loved...and it destroyed me."

It is one of those moments where a story transcends IP, and lore, and canon, and becomes about something universal. It uses lore and backstory to serve a heartbreaking character portrait, rather than using characters as "instruments of a greater plot," as Chris Claremont once put it. That puts this new horror genre spin on the X-Men and Cyclops' lore off to a strong start only two issues in.

X-Men Midnight #2 is available now from Marvel Comics.

#3393. How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

James Gray never hid that Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway were playing fictional versions of his real-life parents in his 2022 drama “Armageddon Time,” based on the writer/director’s experience as a sixth grader growing up in Queens in the 1980s.

“Jeremy is doing my father to such a degree that it is disturbing.  He sounds exactly like him, looks exactly like him; it’s bizarre. Annie, too, is uncanny about [playing my mother],” said Gray while a guest on this week’s episode of IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “So I had had such a great time with them shooting ‘Armageddon Time,’ I said, ‘Well, why don’t we do this again?’” Related Stories Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Gray knew his next film (what would become “Paper Tiger”) would be set in 1986 and once again focus on a Jewish family of four, with two sons, in Queens. In the project’s early stages, Hathaway and Strong were up for reprising their roles, but it soon became clear Gray would have to wait 18 months — after both “The Odyssey” (Hathaway) and “The Social Reckoning” (Strong) finished filming — to start production.

“You can’t wait a year and a half,” said Gray. “And then I started thinking, ‘Well, maybe this is a blessing in disguise.’ That the [film] could start to take on a new style, and so then I started to pursue it in a different way. So in the beginning, in its origin stages, it was [a sequel of sorts], but like any movie, it’s like a wild horse that’s going to get away from you.”

While Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller’s characters in “Paper Tiger” are inspired by Gray’s parents, they are not as deeply grounded as Hathaway and Strong were in “Armageddon Time” as facsimiles of Gray’s parents in how they talked, looked, dressed, and behaved. Through this lens, Gray began to see the film as less of a straight memoir, freeing him to embrace elements of the crime genre in his storytelling.

Explained Gray, “What I tried to do was to make a film more in — for lack of a better way of really explaining — a bit more Hitchcockian in certain places. Almost — again, ‘pulpy’ is not quite the right word — a little bit more, how do I put this — more of an engagement directly with a tense idea of narrative, that it would be a driving, tense story.”

What also changed is the sympathetic lens through which Gray now saw his father. In “Paper Tiger,” Irwin (Teller) puts his family in danger when he unwittingly gets entangled (pursuing environmental consulting work for businesses along the polluted Gowanus Canal) with the Russian mob. While Irwin is guilty of pride and naivety, it is (especially compared to Gray’s previous films) a positive portrayal of a hard-working and earnest father pursuing the American dream.

In this sense, the shift from Strong to Teller was fortuitous. Strong had painted an unforgiving portrait of a miserable, strict father — tortured by generational trauma and unbending with his sons striving for upward mobility — whereas Gray saw something in Teller he could lean into for a different portrayal of his father.

“Miles has a kind of — I can’t believe I’m going to say this, he might even resist this— a softness to him, which would probably offend him, but I think that’s a great thing,” said Gray. “He doesn’t have a softness in his persona. He doesn’t have it in physical terms. It’s actually a tenderness inside. You have to embrace [that] beauty in him and hope it works for the film.”

When it came to recasting Hathaway, Gray was more practical, saying he needed three characteristics: another bankable star, who was also Jewish, and a real New Yorker. He believed the way the city seeps itself into a person’s bones is not something that even the best actors can learn to portray. Those three unnotiables made Scarlett Johansson the clear number one choice.

“I had met [Scarlett] years before on a project that never wound up happening, and quite liked her. She’s a total New Yorker through and through. Then when I found out that Annie [Hathaway] was going off to do Chris [Nolan’s] movie [‘The Odyssey’] for a thousand years, she was the first choice because you’re talking about one of the biggest stars in the world, and she’s also a Jewish woman from New York,  checks the boxes,” said Gray. “When I sent [the script] to her, I sent her a note, ‘There’s probably no chance in hell you’re going to do this, but I love you, can you read this?’ And then she texted me back very, very quickly and was like, ‘Let’s go.’”

While Hathaway’s portrayal of Gray’s mother was more open and loving than Strong’s version of his father — and therefore didn’t require as sharp a contrast in how the role was recast — Gray believed Johansson’s approach better fit the needs of “Paper Tiger.”

“It’s a more operatic idea of character than Annie’s was in ‘Armageddon Time,’” said Gray. “It’s much more a kind of high emotion. And of course, because the situation is much more tragic, and she embraced it completely.”

“Paper Tiger” opened last weekend in New York and Los Angeles, and expands on November 20.

#3392. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3391. ‘GTA 6’ Is Officially the Highest-Rated Game of All Time

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Of all the games Rockstar Games had to beat this week, the one that gave it the most trouble came out on the Nintendo 64. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held a 99 on Metacritic for years. Even Nintendo’s own remake fell three points short earlier this month, and its 96 was good enough to make it the best-reviewed game of 2026. Link got to enjoy that distinction for about two weeks.

Rockstar has come close before. Grand Theft Auto 4 earned a 98 for Niko Bellic’s trip to Liberty City. Grand Theft Auto 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 both sit at 97, so that’s where the bar was when critics finally got to talk about Grand Theft Auto 6 on Wednesday morning, 13 years after Michael, Franklin, and Trevor first got together in Los Santos. It took more than a hundred reviews and a pair of car thieves to move it.

The PS5 version of GTA 6 debuted at No. 1 on Metacritic’s Best Games of All Time list with a 99, matching the score of the original Ocarina of Time. Metacritic placed Rockstar’s game first despite the shared score, likely due to the higher number of reviews available. The score can still move as more reviews come in, but as of now, it seems unlikely to drop significantly.

Jason and Lucia meet trying to steal the same car, which might be the most Grand Theft Auto way two people have ever fallen in love. ScreenRant’s Chris Carter gave the game a 10/10, writing that it “takes a page from Red Dead Redemption 2’s book.” That comparison makes more sense once you know what critics took away from the final missions. Over at The Guardian, Keza MacDonald described getting up and pacing in front of her TV because she was worried about what would happen to Jason and Lucia, which is a long way to come with a couple whose first shared interest is somebody else’s car.

Polygon’s Giovanni Colantonio found much of the fun in “a reactive place governed by intricate rules that beg to be bent and busted.” Take the question of what happens after you’ve successfully stolen a luxury car, for example. As NME’s Mark Beaumont discovered, cloning the key will get you into the driver’s seat, but the tracker still works, and it keeps telling the police where you are. Suddenly, there’s a pretty good argument for picking a cheaper car, which is the kind of decision Vice City used to leave to people who actually paid for them.

Game Rant’s Anthony Taormina also awarded GTA 6 a 10/10, calling Leonida “a world that is a joy to simply exist in.” For anyone who spent more time in GTA 5 driving around Los Santos with the radio on than they ever spent planning a heist, that might be the most persuasive line in any of the reviews.

Grand Theft Auto 6 launches November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

#3390. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

From a purely awards-hunting perspective, there’s a great argument to be made that Netflix could have pushed back its late November release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” until next year. Historically, the perception of the embattled studio is that its had issues being distracted by too big an awards slate to pin down its Best Picture frontrunner. Remember in 2023 when it seemed like the streamer did not realize until the Oscar shortlists (in mid-December!) that “All Quiet on the Western Front” was its best bet at Best Picture? The Edward Berger film went on to win four Oscars, including Best International Feature. Related Stories How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

This year, Netflix is running their best awards campaign yet with “La Bola Negra,” which the studio acquired out of Cannes, where its helmers, Los Javis, won the jury prize for Best Director. Come the fall festivals, it became the first Netflix film to win the People’s Choice Award at TIFF. Since then, it has fronted Netflix’s experiment in expanding the theatrical distribution of its awards slate, doing admirable business in key markets. The consensus among prognosticators is that the film is not only a lock to receive a Best Picture nomination, but is also sure to win the Oscar for Best International Feature on behalf of Spain.

If Netflix wanted to secure a second Best Picture nomination, with “Cliff Booth” out of the picture, the team could put all its energy into Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love.” Not only is the near-three hour film, which won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice, another Best International Feature contender (on behalf of South Korea), but it is one of this season’s most critically lauded films. If enough critics’ groups get behind it in the coming weeks, a la “The Secret Agent” last year, then a second Best Picture nomination for Netflix at the 2027 Oscars becomes highly plausible.

Somewhere along the way, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” became something of a puzzle for Netflix. The streamer had no choice but to follow through with putting it out around Thanksgiving, because it was already set to replace the IMAX screens that had initially been secured for Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” film. So how does a company not run an awards campaign for the sequel to a recent Best Picture nominee, directed by a three-time Oscar nominee, written by a two-time Oscar winner, and starring Brad Pitt in the role he just won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for?

What reads as a home run on paper is more of a double or triple in execution. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is made by people who know what they are doing, and that expands past director David Fincher, screenwriter Quentin Tarantino, and star Pitt.

Cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt, editor Kirk Baxter, production designer Donald Graham Burt, set decorator Jan Pascale, and composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross have all won at least one Academy Award. Costume designer Trish Summerville was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Mank.” Even if there is a low bar for getting the Academy excited about a late-’70s period piece set in Hollywood, “Cliff Booth” easily clears it.

But we are in a spectacle-heavy year, with “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” in the awards conversation, and “Dune: Part Three” and “Werwulf” on the horizon. Even “Digger” is a formidable contender in the craft races. So if the feeling is that “Cliff Booth” is more of a hangout movie than a cinematic event, then the focus of its awards campaign should be on categories that are more willing to embrace that, like Best Production Design or Best Costume Design. (Not so much Best Sound, which “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did actually receive nominations for.)

In terms of the acting performances, again, Pitt is great as Cliff Booth, but there is no rush to nominate him for a performance he already won for. And there are plenty of other Best Actor contenders, like Matt Damon and John Malkovich (who have never won) and John Turturro and Andrew Scott (who have never even been nominated for an Oscar before).

The top performance of the film is with Cliff’s love interest, played by Emmy winner Elizabeth Debicki, who actually does have a shot at her first Oscar nomination, given the love for her performance in “Wicker” as well, and the lack of current consensus in the Best Supporting Actress race.

Everyone else in the film, from Scott Caan to Yahya Abdul-Mateen II to Carla Gugino, is very additive to the project but does not necessarily cross the threshold into Oscar-contender territory. In that way, it is similar to Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” another awards hopeful from this season.

Ultimately, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is entertaining enough to garner support from certain branches of the Academy, but falls too late in the year, in too few theaters, to truly become the last-minute surprise blockbuster that would get as many as 10 Oscar nominations, something its predecessor “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did handily.

#3389. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3388. Tommy Replaced Himself In Landman But It Won’t Work

Tommy Norris (Billy Bob Thornton) started his own oil company, but replacing himself as President ultimately won't work in Landman season 3. Taylor Sheridan and Christian Wallace's hit Paramount+ boomtown oil drama closed out season 2 with Tommy taking his future into his own hands, founding the oddly named CTT Oil Exploration & Cattle company.

Landman's series premiere quickly established Tommy Norris as the most knowledgeable and competent landman in West Texas. When he worked for M-TEX Oil, Tommy spent nearly every waking hour of every day driving hundreds of miles across the Patch and beyond, troubleshooting every conceivable crisis that can befall an oil company. This even resulted in Norris getting kidnapped and tortured by a Mexican drug cartel.

Tommy was promoted to M-TEX's President when his best friend and M-TEX's chairman, Monty Miller (Jon Hamm) died. However, Monty's widow, Cami (Demi Moore), found a business partner she liked better in Danny Morrell (Andy Garcia), who is also a drug kingpin named Gallino. Cami ultimately fired Tommy, which led Norris to start his own oil outfit to control his own future. That need for control will become an issue in Landman season 3.

When Tommy formed CTT Oil Exploration & Cattle in Landman season 2's finale, he recruited almost all of his friends and family members, giving them positions in its corporate structure. Tellingly, Tommy didn't name himself President; instead, he took the Vice President role and gave the President's job to his son, Cooper Norris (Jacob Lofland).

Landman season 3 is filming now, and social media footage from production shows a slow burn storyline kicks into full gear in the new season.

Tommy decided to become Vice President because it gives him the freedom to continue as a landman. Even when he was M-TEX's President, Norris refused to go corporate and spend his time behind a desk. Giving Cooper that role means Tommy can do what he does best: drive all over the Patch, cut deals, solve problems, and run and gun. However, it won't be quite so easy.

Cooper likely won't want to be desk-bound either, but Tommy's son really has no business being President of an oil company, even a startup, and Tommy is smart enough to know that. Cooper has proven instincts in the field, but he's not a CEO. This means Tommy will not only clean up any messes Cooper creates, but he's likely to eventually lose patience and take on the President's role himself.

Or worse, anything Cooper doesn't know how to do (which is plenty), Tommy will pass off to Nate (Colm Feore), his treasurer, or, most likely, Rebecca Falcone (Kayla Wallace), the COO and Chief Counsel. This will infuriate Rebecca, who has lingering issues with Cooper from Landman season 1, and she surely doesn't think he is fit to be President either.

No matter what, Tommy will run CTT himself and everyone will treat him as the guy really in charge, which he is. Cooper will be a de facto President, and that's another powder keg in Landman season 3.

Cooper as CTT's President is a liability for Tommy in another way: Norris has too many enemies who can strike at him through his son. From Mexican drug lords to his frenemy Gallino to oil magnate William Crockett (Michael Kelly) joining Landman season 3, and maybe even Cami Miller, there are plenty of people who won't want Tommy's new oil company to succeed.

​​​​​​​Earnest and inexperienced Cooper will have an even bigger target on his back as CTT's President.

When Tommy found out Cooper struck a business deal with Gallino, not knowing who "Danny Morrell" was, he immediately tried to shield his son. Earnest and inexperienced Cooper will have an even bigger target on his back as CTT's President, and Ariana Medina (Paulina Chavez), CTT's new secretary, is also vulnerable because she dates Cooper.

The corporate structure Tommy built for CTT Oil Exploration & Cattle is wonderful in terms of including friends and members of the Norris family, but it's a house of cards bound to collapse. The problem starts at the top with Cooper as President, and Tommy knows that. Norris' problem is he should be President, but he would rather be a landman.

The truth is, no one in Landman can replace Tommy, but there's also only one of him. Cooper should have been the new landman and Tommy should be President. In CTT Oil Exploration & Cattle's current structure, Tommy will be stretched too thin trying to do everything himself and solve problems Cooper would be better off tackling as he learns to be a landman.

#3387. Here’s one small change that could improve iPhone Duo’s unoptimized apps

iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

That said, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an issue.

Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

One of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

So, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to quickly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

#3386. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3385. A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team

Maybe it’s just because we can’t get enough headlines and discussion about “Backrooms” and “You Can See Everything,” but despite the banner year A24 has had at the box office, its TV division has quietly had nearly as strong of a year.

The indie label has produced more shows in 2026 than in any year in its history, including sleeper commercial and critical hits across the board, and even managed to land shows on virtually every streamer in town.

Led by Sam French, the U.S. head of TV at A24, the studio this year has cranked out the third season of “Euphoria” on HBO Max, the second season of “Beef” and the third season of “Survival of the Thickest” both on Netflix, “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” on Apple TV, the “Friday the 13th” prequel series “Crystal Lake” on Peacock, and most recently the British sitcom “It Gets Worse” on Paramount+ led by the UK Heads Piers Wenger and Rose Garnett. Its unscripted division, led by Johnny Hausfater, has also ramped up aggressively, with shows like “Neighbors,” “Born to Bowl,” and “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” all on HBO Max. Related Stories Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?

Not unlike its film slate, its series have been a blend of auteur-driven prestige and genre shows with a twist. The David E. Kelley series “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” is a tongue-in-cheek, real-world satire on motherhood and the modern economy about a young single mom played by Elle Fanning who needs to turn to OnlyFans for extra cash. On the other side of the coin, “Crystal Lake” follows masked killer Jason Voorhees’ mom and stands out from other modern horror TV shows by, as our critic wrote, not trying to secretly be a family drama or a slapstick comedy or some other genre or metaphor, but it just amplifies the grisly kills in the best way it can.

The recurring theme between these shows isn’t genre but the stamp of quality that A24 lends.

While something like “Beef” saw a steep drop in viewership of a reported 60 percent between its first and second seasons, “Euphoria” in its return was up 17 percent in its finale ratings compared to Season 2. “Crystal Lake” was also a big hit on Peacock, its top show on the streamer last month, logging 1.3 billion minutes watched over its first 11 days, making it the fourth-highest scripted original series ever on Peacock. A24 now has roughly 30 to 40 shows in various stages of development, pre-production, or active production, with its executive team expanding from about 15 from just 3 people in its early days.

It’s been able to ramp up firstly because of its partnership with numerous TV buyers across the major streamers, but also because of working with largely first-time creators and showrunners. While “Crystal Lake” is a notable exception, A24 generally is operating on its TV side the same way it does with its film, leading with the artist and the project they want to pursue rather than the IP.

That has produced some very personal and idiosyncratic projects over the years like “Ramy” and “The Curse,” the latter of which was the kernel of getting Nathan Fielder to working with A24 again on “You Can See Everything.”

The breadth of content A24 has amassed on its TV side and continually making shows that have the same barrier-pushing flavor and stamp of quality that has become known with A24’s brand is what will help make it as essential a part of the company’s overall business and valuation as its film and distribution business. But we’re seeing even its TV division branching out and embracing IP and tentpoles in the same way its film side has.

Coming up for A24 are a Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor drama “The Spot” on Hulu and “The Apology” with Gwyneth Paltrow on Netflix, which already got a two-season order and was an example of a show that grew out of Paltrow being convinced to try TV after already working with A24 on the film side for “Marty Supreme.” The studio is also is working with Ben Stiller on a New York Knicks documentary series for HBO and a competition cooking show based on the video game “Overcooked” for Netflix. A24 could’ve made a Knicks series with anyone, but teaming with a superfan like Stiller was another example of putting the creator above the concept.

Yet, both a strength and weakness of its TV model is that it does not have a distribution mechanism the way it does on the film side. It’s not bogged down with an unprofitable streamer, a dwindling linear cable channel, or a broadcast network, but that makes it reliant on the many partners it has built up across the industry.

Warner Bros. merging with Paramount arguably reduces the buyers in the market, even if there are still two streamers at Skydance. Netflix just had a massive shakeup of its leadership team that could easily have a different attitude toward A24’s series. And the overall industry trends around the end of Peak TV mean it’s always a volatile business for independents in the TV space.

But no one saw “Backrooms” or “You Can See Everything” coming either, and A24 has as good a chance as any to have lightning strike twice with the next “Euphoria” or “Beef.”

#3384. The New James Bond’s Viral A24 Thriller Is Officially an Apple TV Hit

Just when you thought this year couldn't get any better for Robert Pattinson, he has been officially announced as the new James Bond. Following in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig, Pattinson will help lead cinema's greatest spy series into a bold new era under Amazon, after its billion-dollar acquisition of the franchise. Pattinson will re-team with Dune: Part Three director Denis Villeneuve on the next movie, with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight penning the script.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement as the first days of a new era begin. This new role for the man who is also Matt Reeves' The Batman feels like a reward for his faultless year of film, which includes stand-out performances in Christopher Nolan's epic adaptation of The Odyssey, A24's The Drama alongside Zendaya, and the aforementioned Dune: Part Three, which is heading to theaters on December 18.

But not only has Pattinson become the next Bond, but he might even become an Academy Award winner next year for his hugely impressive lead performance in Lance Oppenheim's Primetime, another A24 movie from this year. Based on the television series To Catch a Predator, with Pattinson portraying Chris Hansen, Primetime took a hugely controversial subject and managed to mold it into one of the best-reviewed films of the year, thanks in no small part to the lead performance of our new 007. Collider's Taylor Gates called Pattinson's performance his best in her review, "not just of this year, but of his entire career."

No doubt boosted by the new Bond announcement, Primetime has now jumped up the streaming charts, officially ranking as the sixth-most-watched movie on the Apple TV Store in the U.S. The current top spot on the platform is held by David Ayer and Brad Pitt's new survival thriller, Heart of the Beast, which scored just shy of $200 million at the box office before moving to PVOD. Primetime made $57.8 million during its theatrical run against a $15 million budget.

#3383. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3382. Guarding Stars Review: A Charming Holiday Movie That Follows All The Rules

Guarding Stars is far from groundbreaking as far as Christmas romcoms go, but Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki make it worthy of a watch.

Somewhat cheesy Christmas romcoms have been a holiday season staple for decades now, and unlike many other genres, part of the popularity of these films is their predictability. Generally, people aren't checking out the latest Hallmark or Netflix holiday movie looking for plot twists or significant departures from the standard fare. In fact, as much as the tropes of this genre – like a city girl making her way to a small town, finding love and the joy of Christmas, and deciding to abandon her corporate job – have become comedy fodder online, that is exactly why they work.

The bar was therefore relatively low for Netflix's latest holiday movie, Guarding Stars, which was just released on the streaming platform. Yet, two elements of this movie raised the stakes slightly. For one, Guarding Stars is an adaptation of a novel, titled The Bodyguard, and that always adds a slightly different level of expectation. Fans of the book have their own ideas about how the characters should act, look, and sound.

Additionally, the leads of Guarding Stars are both major names: Gossip Girl's Leighton Meester plays the protagonist, Hannah, and Jared Padalecki, of Gilmore Girls and Supernatural fame, plays her love interest, Jack. Ultimately, both of these aspects helped. The source material gives the movie more originality than is typical of the genre, and Padalecki and Meester are both very charming in their roles. However, this movie is far from revolutionary, and audiences will (more or less) only be getting exactly what they came for.

Unsurprisingly, given their respective backgrounds, both Padalecki and Meester nail their characters in Guarding Stars. They are easily the standouts of the movie, and honestly why this holiday entry has a solid chance to stand at least a little apart from the crowd. While Meester is funny and relatable, it's often Padalecki who steals the show. This is somewhat unexpected, not because he doesn't have the acting chops, but rather because he's never really played a lead in a romcom like this.

Guarding Stars hits all the points that romcom fans will appreciate.

Yes, when he was younger, he was Dean on Gilmore Girls, a role for which he was almost exclusively a love interest – but that show was certainly different from a Netflix Christmas movie. Hilariously, the closest approximation audiences have really seen from Padalecki is his hipster Sam Winchester persona in one episode of Supernatural. That's only really true in the beginning, when Jack comes across as a cool, slightly jerk-ish celebrity (although it's very clear that Padalecki is having fun with that character type, which makes it all the more enjoyable to watch).

Guarding Stars also hits all the points that romcom fans will appreciate, from the basic plot involving a fake dating dynamic (a tried and true romance novel scenario) to the "only one bed" romcom trope. And, to Netflix's credit, while the movie plays it more than safe by touching on those plot points, there are ways in which Guarding Stars is better than the typical streaming Christmas movie. For one, Meester and Padalecki have legitimate chemistry; for another, there are some genuinely funny, sweet moments that, at the very least, make the film fun to watch.

Nevertheless, Guarding Stars' shortcomings are numerous and obvious. The greatest offense of the film is its primary villain (although, in fairness, there is actually a story decision toward the end that ameliorates this problem to a degree), who is, at multiple moments, cartoonishly evil. The motivations the villain has are also flimsy at best, and this entire arc feels like a throwaway concept to give the movie an edge while really wanting to focus on the relationship between Jack and Hannah.

What should be the most harrowing moment of the plot is also undercut by the fact that the stunt itself looks like a clip one would see from behind-the-scenes footage before editors get their hands on it and make it look significantly more convincing in the final cut. Even so, Guarding Stars does what it set out to do. Yes, it's a typical holiday movie, and it mostly follows the story beats one would expect, but it is also fun and even cute in its goofiness. Fans of the book will no doubt like it, and those looking for a new feel-good holiday film will find it here.

Guarding Stars is now streaming on Netflix.

#3381. IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods

On Tuesday, November 17, the International Documentary Association (IDA) announced the nominees for its 42nd annual IDA Documentary Awards, including everything from the highly publicized blockbuster “You Can See Everything” to under-the-radar Best Documentary Feature contenders like “Concrete Land.”

“I couldn’t be more excited to celebrate these meaningful and creative documentaries. It’s a challenging time for documentary makers, but also a really inspiring moment for IDA and for the field,” IDA Board President Ina Fichman said in a statement. “This year we see nominees whose deeply personal stories share narratives of resistance and exile, and we see artful, innovative filmmaking that is capturing new and robust audiences. I hope many will join us on December 4 as we honor our incredible community.” Related Stories A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

The 2026 IDA Documentary Awards will also present the following special honors: the Career Achievement Award for the late Chilean filmmaker Patricio Guzmán; the Truth to Power Award for Amy Goodman and Juan González of Democracy Now!; the Emerging Filmmaker Award for Maia Lekow and Christopher King; and the Amicus Award for Cannes Docs, the documentary program of the Marché du Film led by Pierre-Alexis Chevit.

This year, IDA received a record 650 entries in all categories from 95 countries, an increase over last year both in the total number of entries and the countries represented. 32 countries are represented among the final lineup of nominees.

IDA members from around the world will vote for the winners in the Best Feature Documentary and Best Short Documentary categories from November 17 to November 29, 2026. All other category winners are selected by juries representing the international documentary community.

The Awards will take place December 4, 2026, at The Ebell of Los Angeles, hosted for the second year in a row by documentary field leader Tabitha Jackson.

Nominees in each category are listed in alphabetical order by film title.

#3380. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3378. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.
