#3377. How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World

Though the days when every film gets a massive DVD release are gone, and all kinds of logistics shape how companies like GKIDS plan home releases, the core requirement remains the same. Someone on the GKIDS team has to be a fan.

Director of Home Entertainment Alison Kozberg is a fan of all the titles the company is releasing this winter, from the incredibly personal and warm “Linda Linda Linda” to the more wrenching (though you would expect nothing less from Hideaki Anno) “Love & Pop.” But crafting a personal fan experience dictates the presentation and bonus features behind each release, and that can look wildly different for each title GKIDS puts out. Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

“ Every project is really different. Every project has different access. Some films have creators that are living; some films don’t. Some films have a rich archive; others don’t. So you’re always navigating different conditions of production,” Kozberg told IndieWire. “[We think about] what is emotionally resonant for us. And we really have conversations about that. What do we feel about this film? What artwork and images impact us? What is particularly interesting? Like, when thinking about bonus features, you also think about what captures your imagination.”

When it came to putting out a box set for the Netflix series “Arcane,” for instance, the team was guided by the incredibly rich tradition of cosplay and fanworks in the “League of Legends” community online. They imagined fun art that would be right at home in an artists’ alley at a convention expo hall, and that guided everything from the art on the discs to the set of dice that came in the box set. But with this year’s collector’s edition of “Angel’s Egg,” the incredible collaboration between director Mamoru Oshii (“Ghost in the Shell”) and legendary artist Yoshitaka Amano, the home entertainment team wanted to cultivate a completely different experience.

“We were really, really, really passionate about being able to bring ‘Angel’s Egg’ to people in North America, both theatrically and on disc,” Kozberg said. “We really, really wanted to create a forum to extend access to the creators, but also to create access to Amano’s artwork, which we know fans are so passionate about, and which is so exquisite. So when putting the package together, we tried to be really thoughtful, and really restrained, and really platform these beautiful illustrations.”

It was also important for the set to do what great home releases have been doing since we all went hunting for behind-the-scenes content hidden as Easter Eggs inside DVD menus. It was important to teach curious audiences about how filmmaking works and the context that makes a particular story such a miracle to have gotten made. The interviews and essay booklet were designed to build the historical context for a film as dense and thematically rich as “Angel’s Egg” and to give fans a platform to extend their conversations about it.

“We’re always thinking about ways to additionally kind of facilitate and support other people’s creative inspiration,” Kozberg said. “And  there is a real genuine joy to having objects connected to films you love in your life. I look at the ‘Angel’s Egg’ art cards. I think it feels really special and joyful to be able to have those displayed in your home, to think about ‘Angel’s Egg’ in the day-to-day, to see the artwork.”

While GKIDS releases a mix of live-action and animated titles, the overall theme of their work is facilitating fandom. “We talk a lot about kind of like seeing people’s fandom and reflecting it back to them. So [our goal] is understanding what about a film is emotionally resonant, and then creating opportunities to reflect and engage with that emotion,” Kozberg said.

#3376. Apple provides a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health

This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots …

Apple launched its Research app back in 2019 with the goal of allowing customers to help universities and medical institutions with health studies. You typically agree to share certain anonymized information from the Apple Health app in order to provide data that can advance medical research. You may also be asked to complete questionnaires.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is one of these, but it works in a somewhat different way. You’ll still be invited to share some of your health data, but will also be able to ask an AI system questions about your health.

When you ask health questions of a typical AI chatbot, you don’t know how reliable those answers may be or what will happen to your data. Apple study offers three assurances:

Apple says that answers will be generated by the same platform used by healthcare professionals.

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature.

The answers provided to you will include links to peer-reviewed clinical citations.

CNET reports on Apple’s assurance that none of your chats will be retained.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours. A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

Access to the study is currently limited to users in the US by downloading the app. If you try it, please do share your thoughts in the comments.

#3375. 'Riverdale’ Star Casey Cott's New Thriller Takes a Deadly Turn in First Official Trailer

How far would you go to fit in? Would you play a game to the death if it meant winning over your boyfriend’s friends? That’s the question at the heart of Games We Play, a new psychological thriller starring Riverdale’s Casey Cott and FBI’s Margot Pitts. Pitts, who makes her feature debut with the film, co-wrote the script with Molly Scharlin Ben-Hamoo, while Rachael Dahl makes her feature directorial debut. Dylan McTee (Wrong Turn) and Adam Faison (Hellraiser) round out the cast, and Collider is excited to exclusively debut the film’s brand-new trailer.

“Tapping into the increasingly resonant themes of social pressure, groupthink and the universal desire to belong, Games We Play follows Imogen (Pitts), who joins her boyfriend Jack (Cott) and his two childhood best friends, Gage (McTee) and Freddie (Faison), for a weekend getaway. When she finds herself the unmistakable outsider, Imogen becomes desperate to win their approval. But as she is forced to participate in a tournament of high-stakes games, the experience takes a sinister turn, pushing her to compromise her identity and instincts while questioning both her sanity and her safety. What begins as a pursuit of acceptance spirals into a chilling psychological game where the stakes are far more dangerous than fitting in.”

Vertical, which holds North American rights, will release Games We Play in select theaters and on VOD on December 4. Blue Fox Entertainment has acquired the film’s international rights and is introducing it to buyers at the American Film Market.

The trailer finds Imogen playing along with Jack’s friends, joining a round of Sardines and surrendering her phone for their tournament in an effort to become part of the group. Things soon take a darker turn as Gage’s interest in Imogen becomes a little too intense, and rather than questioning his friends’ behavior, Jack starts questioning her. The result looks twisted and genuinely unsettling, turning the kinds of games that felt harmless as kids into something far more menacing.

Games We Play appears to borrow the same scare tactic that made Ready or Not work so well: take a game everyone knows how to play and raise the stakes until it becomes a fight for survival. Because the rules are so familiar, it’s easy for viewers to put themselves in Imogen’s shoes. She goes along with everything for her boyfriend’s sake, and who hasn’t wanted to win over a new group of friends? It’s a relatable impulse, just not one worth following once the games start turning deadly.

“Games We Play is a timely examination of the universal struggle for social survival, where the desire to belong can become just as dangerous as the fight to stay alive,” said Scharlin Ben-Hamoo, who also serves as an executive producer alongside Pitts.

“Rachael Dahl has crafted a compelling psychological thriller that taps into the pressures we all recognize, while taking them to a terrifying extreme. We are excited to partner with Vertical Entertainment and Blue Fox Entertainment to bring this story to audiences around the world.”

Produced by Taryn Gates and Raza Rizvi (Lemonade Blessing), Games We Play arrives in select theaters and on VOD on December 4. Check out the exclusive trailer above.

#3374. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3373. Video podcasts coming soon to Apple TV and other devices

Apple will soon be adding a video podcasts section to Apple TV, which will also be available in the Apple TV app on other devices like smart TVs. That means it will come to more than a billion devices in total.

Access to the video podcasts will be free, with no requirement for an Apple TV subscription. Testing begins today, with the full rollout promised “soon” …

Apple shared the news with The New York Times.

On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users […] Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app.

The company says the move will benefit creators and listeners alike.

“We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.”

While podcasts began as audio only, it’s become increasingly common in recent years for them to be released as video also. This expands the reach to video platforms like YouTube, Hulu, and Netflix. Creators have welcomed Apple’s latest move, even if some are a little sad about what it says about the medium.

“It’s so helpful that people can go on their phones, they see a clip on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter and open the Apple app and now watch it on video,” he said. “People are already on their iPhones and they’re used to watching videos on their phones so it was the next logical step” […]

“Everything is TV now, which is a little bit heartbreaking for a lifelong audio person to say,” Ms. Martin of NPR said.

No date has yet been announced for the public rollout.

#3372. CBS Refuses To Solve Tracker’s Biggest Colter Problem

Warning! SPOILERS about Tracker season 4, episode 6 ahead.A Colter problem that Tracker has highlighted since the very beginning had a chance to be tackled, but wasn’t in season 4, episode 6. After a mini-hiatus following Russell’s return in Tracker season 4, episode 5, Colter had a new job lined up by another loved one asking for his help, this time coming in the form of Reenie’s request to find her mentor’s daughter. The case brought Colter to discover developments far darker than he initially anticipated when he thought that Erica had simply disappeared because she didn’t want anything to do with Gale anymore.

Colter’s visit to Denver, Colorado, nevertheless caused other consequences that were only partially related to finding Erica Mcgill. Being in town to help reunite Gale and Erica made it possible for Colter to finally visit Reenie and Randy’s new offices and meet Mel in person, after only having heard about her from Randy. Solving the case even brought Colter to socialize with Reenie, Randy, and Mel after work, giving Colter a chance to spend some time with his team in the place where the bulk of the work to support him is done.

However, Colter finally spending time with Reenie, Randy, and Mel recreationally also ended up highlighting his usual impulse to run away after some time with his loved ones. He seemingly got better with it in some instances, like making plans with Russell, but Colter leaving without saying goodbye in Tracker season 4, episode 6, goes exactly against solving Colter’s aloofness problem.

It would be unfair not to note that Colter made great strides in keeping up with his friends and helpers. After all, in Tracker season 1, episode 7, Colter ditched Reenie and Bobby well before they could celebrate their saving Sun in any way. Instead, Colter paid two visits to Reenie’s office, and he also unwound with them after closing the case.

Colter’s decision to leave without saying goodbye nonetheless proves that the instinct to be by himself has not left him in all these years. That is a key aspect of Colter’s personality, and Tracker wouldn’t exist in the form that it does if Colter spent a lot of time with others, especially characters who know him well. Still, respecting his desire for independence doesn’t have to mean avoiding saying goodbye to his friends as he did in Tracker season 4, episode 6.

Colter quickly ditching his team after spending fulfilling moments with them seems to follow a one-step-forward, two-steps-back kind of progress. It’s a step in the right direction, as it means Tracker season 4 has finally begun to tackle Colter’s persistent need to keep his distance from those closest to him. It’s nevertheless frustrating to see him employ his usual tricks to avoid connecting with his loved ones for too long.

In its four installments until now, Tracker has shown Colter always going the extra mile for his clients, never in relation to how much a job paid, but always with a wish to bring them some closure, thus hinting at the very likely reality that Colter would do almost anything to solve a case. Looking over Mel’s mom’s murder, which Tracker already indicated as a replacement for the Shaw family mystery, can finally force Colter to spend more time with his team.

Colter not shying away from the possibility of dating Jenna already proved his openness to maintaining relationships in Tracker season 4. Updating Mel on her mother’s case could force more visits to Denver from Colter, which in turn can make checking in physically with his team and friends a repeat occurrence. By making it part of his routine and being connected to a case, spending time with Reenie, Randy, and Mel could feel less daunting for Colter.

A development in Tracker season 4, episode 3 introduces a variable that the CBS TV show rarely relied on before, potentially changing it in a big way.

Colter’s promise to help Mel find some answers about what was behind her mom’s murder can thus work as both a solution to Colter’s biggest problem in Tracker and become a case central enough to successfully supplant the Shaw family mystery narratively.

#3371. What Happens If We Break Letterboxd?

Earlier this month, the Trylon in Minneapolis gave people six chances over three days to see “Kanał,” Andrzej Wajda’s 1957 film about Polish resistance fighters retreating into the sewers of Warsaw. After opening night, programmer John Moret saw enthusiastic reviews on Letterboxd.

The next evening, he remembers, ticket sales picked up.

Moret could imagine the calculation for somebody still on the fence. “Oh, these people I trust went to go see this movie, and they loved it. And it’s just playing for two more days.”

On November 5, the New York Times reported that its parent company was in exclusive talks to buy Letterboxd for roughly $330 million. Under the deal being discussed, the film-logging site would likely keep operating on its own and use the Times Company’s advertising technology. Related Stories How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods

For theaters like the Trylon, what matters is whether people who went on opening night can still reach those who might go tomorrow. In 2026, that handoff is working remarkably well.

Five days before “Kanał” opened, Ken Russell’s “The Devils” sold out at the Trylon on election night. Moret also co-founded the national Programmers’ Jam with Bret Berg, theatrical sales director at the American Genre Film Archive, and Dan Halsted of Portland’s Hollywood Theatre. When the Jam met in Los Angeles in May, Berg told IndieWire that programmers had access to more restorations than ever before. They also had more places to show them and a new audience coming through the doors.

When we spoke again this month, Berg said Letterboxd drives “the FOMO of needing to be conversant in a movie of the moment.” For a few days in Minneapolis, that movie was “Kanał.”

Berg can see why a press company might be a good home for Letterboxd. He also remembers what the last sale made plain to him. Something people had spent years helping build was “just an asset to be bought and sold.” In the r/Letterboxd thread about the talks, one commenter saw an upside to a newspaper owning a site that rates movies. They worried about paywalled features and ads, but liked the prospect of a ratings system free of “studios putting their fingers on the scale.”

You come home from a movie and write what you thought. Your friends get a tip, the theater gets a little local press, and Letterboxd gets something to put an ad next to. Years later, someone who’s never been to Minneapolis can land on the same page and read what it was like to see that movie with a crowd.

Moret keeps his own movie diary in a paper notebook. He stopped posting what he watched for a while because people kept asking if it meant he was going to program it. Sometimes a guy just wants to watch a movie. He still checks Letterboxd after a screening. “I can see that night exactly how they responded,” he said. He’s seen patrons meet Trylon volunteers and follow them afterward. He’s also heard from people who knew one another by their Letterboxd handles before they started going to movies together.

Moret did have an ulterior motive for December’s Dede Allen series. He wanted to show “Mike’s Murder,” James Bridges’ 1984 mystery starring Debra Winger as a bank teller trying to find out who killed her tennis instructor. A Letterboxd user could make a pretty good list out of movies you didn’t know shared an editor like Allen. Moret gets to put them on a calendar. If you like what Allen does with a bank full of hostages in “Dog Day Afternoon” on December 11, you can come back for “Mike’s Murder” on December 18. Both play in 35mm.

Berg reads the reviews from one town with the next town in mind. A joke review with thousands of likes might tell him very little about who’d pay to see a movie. Five people leaving a one-off screening at a DIY microcinema and feeling compelled to write about it might tell him quite a lot. Their reviews can tell him what got a reaction in the room or whether people were excited to see a particular restoration. For someone deciding which films in the archive’s catalog deserve another look, that’s “some interesting free data.”

Even Berg comes across movies he’s never heard of in his own catalog. Three and a half stars on Letterboxd is enough to make him give one a closer look. Then, he wants to know what kind of time people had. “How many audience moments are there? That’s what I care about.”

For a horror movie, he might be counting jump scares. With Herzog, he’s thinking about how many iconic images there are. (I personally suggested that the nation craves the sight of a steamship being pushed up a mountain. “Oh, it’s true,” Berg said.)

Berg named Spectacle in Brooklyn and Whammy! in Los Angeles as places where he could count on hearing from a few people whether a movie made an impression. And he can look for the same things he would on a research viewing, with the added benefit of a crowd. Was everybody there to see a new restoration? How full was the room? Somebody who mentions how many other people turned up has given a distributor in another city information he couldn’t get by sitting down and watching the film himself.

Berg also thinks about who’s had the chance to write film books, or to be taken seriously as a critic on a national stage. He singled out trans critics among the writers who can find an audience on Letterboxd without first persuading an editor to commission a review. The person who finally gets you to watch a movie might write three sentences half a century after the original reviews ran. They might be the only person you follow who’s even heard of it.

If the people writing those reviews scattered across half a dozen sites, Berg could still go looking for them. It would take longer. If Letterboxd imploded altogether, he’d expect “a return to gut feeling.”

Berg has some experience with the decision to leave. He still uses Vimeo for his day job, but the price helped persuade him to move his own project, Museum of Home Video, to a cheaper service. Finding another place to put a video was manageable. The Letterboxd equivalent would mean finding another place to put a review, then finding the person whose reviews got you to sign up in the first place.

In that same Reddit thread, one person was already looking for the exit. “Any other apps people know about with similar list-building functionality?” they asked.

Andrew Masyk, the founder of rival tracking site Simkl, says its importer can bring over your watchlist, ratings, and the full text of your reviews. Custom lists can come over using a separate tool. The comments and follows stay behind. “People have to find each other again, and that’s the hardest part of moving,” he wrote.

Masyk has every business reason to make switching easy. Even so, he figures people who have spent years keeping a movie diary are inclined to stay put. “What moves people is the product changing under them: core features going behind a paywall, heavier ads, or getting your data out becoming harder.” His test for a buyer is whether it keeps the exit open. “So the export button matters more than who owns the company,” he wrote.

The export button can save a review. The friend who used to see it in their feed still has to find it. And that can get harder long before anyone leaves. If a buyer gave sponsored posts more room in the feed, you could still log every movie you see and miss the three sentences from a friend that would’ve gotten you to the Trylon.

If Letterboxd breaks, the Trylon loses one way to fill a seat, and a programmer in another town loses one way to tell whether “Kanał” might fill a few seats there, too. Hear about “Kanał” on Monday, and you can still go. Hear about it on Wednesday, and you’ve missed it.

#3368. Tilda Swinton, Mark Ruffalo, Jacques Audiard, and Others Join in Protest of Jafar Panahi’s Prison Sentence

The film community is marshaling to support Oscar-nominated, dissident Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, who was given a prison sentence of five years and one month by the Tehran Revolutionary Court back in October.

A letter initiated by the International Coalition for Filmmakers at Risk (and shared with Variety) so far features more than 200 signatories “deeply concerned by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, in absentia.” Panahi returned to Iran in the spring following the end of Neon’s awards run for his Cannes Film Festival Palme d’Or winner “It Was Just an Accident,” nominated for Best International Feature and Best Original Screenplay at the 2026 Academy Awards. Related Stories What Happens If We Break Letterboxd? How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World

Actors and filmmakers who’ve signed the letter include Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Jacques Audiard, Kleber Mendonça Filho, Catherine Breillat, Bertrand Bonello, Alice Braga, Arthur Harari, Asif Kapadia, Lucrecia Martel, Rob Epstein, Rodrigo Teixeira, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Geeta Gandbhir, and many more. Festival leaders who signed the letter include Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle, New York Film Festival artistic director Dennis Lim, Venice’s Alberto Barbera, Telluride head Julie Huntsinger, and others — many of whom have hosted Panahi’s films across the last four decades.

Previously, Panahi was sentenced to one year in prison and a two-year ban on leaving Iran in December, in absentia. The new October 2026 sentence carries additional penalties, as the letter notes, including confiscation of his assets, freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban, and a two-year social media ban.

Panahi has a long history of legal entanglements with the Iranian government, which his films have criticized, including numerous imprisonments, a temporary house arrest, and being barred from participating in filmmaking activities. These punitive actions have frequently forced Panahi to make his films in secret or structure them around his filmmaking process or legal status — such as in the 2022 Venice prize winner “No Bears.”

Panahi’s bank accounts were frozen around the October sentencing, according to Panahi’s attorney Mostafa Nili. Panahi could not be reached in October for the sentencing, according to reports, despite being present in Iran as recently as September.

“In March 2026, the 66-year-old Mr. Panahi courageously decided to return to Iran, aware of the risks but having always spoken of his deep love for his country, and for his desire to stay and work there. In October 2026 he learned of the new court verdict against him after his bank accounts were frozen, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said in a statement to the Iranian press. The new charges against him remain unclear, but appear consistent with repeated efforts to intimidate him into ceasing his filmmaking. The case will now go to regional court, and the sentence can be appealed. This requires resources, but all of Mr. Panahi’s accounts have been blocked,” the letter states.

“We stand in solidarity with Mr. Panahi and all Iranians facing persecution for their work at the hands of their own government. We call on the Tehran Revolutionary Court to rescind all actions to penalize and imprison Mr. Panahi and to abide by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to which the Iranian government is a signatory.”

See the letter in full here. The Cannes Film Festival issued a similar letter in protest earlier this week.

#3367. Robert Pattinson’s Biggest Box Office Hit Officially Comes Home With 90 Minutes of Extras

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Matt Damon has had a rough time getting home in Christopher Nolan’s movies. In Interstellar, somebody finally comes to collect him, and he immediately makes everybody regret it. The Odyssey gives him a much better reason to want the trip to end. As Odysseus, he has a wife and son waiting in Ithaca, with the aftermath of the Trojan War and a succession of gods and monsters between them. Nolan shot the journey around the world, making the sea itself one of the problems his cast and crew had to contend with.

Audiences followed him to the tune of $1.8 billion worldwide. According to NBCUniversal, that makes The Odyssey the biggest movie of Nolan’s career and the highest-grossing release in Universal Pictures’ history. The first movie shot entirely in IMAX has spent months giving people a reason to find the biggest screen within driving distance. Now the people who have already made that trip can finally spend some time looking at how Nolan pulled it off.

The Odyssey is available to watch at home as of November 17. The movie is available to buy or rent through digital retailers including Prime Video, the Apple TV app, and Fandango at Home, with 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray, and DVD editions arriving the same day. Damon leads a cast that includes Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, Zendaya, Samantha Morton, and Charlize Theron.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

The home release includes more than 90 minutes of special features, with a collection of 12 production featurettes personally overseen by Nolan. The Trojan Horse gets a feature of its own, which feels fair for a prop that has to fool an entire city while the audience already knows what’s inside. Other pieces follow the construction of Troy in Morocco, the ships used for the voyage, and the stunt work with Damon and Holland.

The physical editions also include the IMAX prologue, along with a conversation in which Reece Feldman asks Nolan to explain what happens to the movie after it leaves the set. Ludwig Göransson takes viewers through the score in a separate featurette, including the instruments and vocals used to build it. Together, the extras give the production’s enormous scale some individual faces. Somebody had to make those ships seaworthy, dress those armies, and get the cameras into position before Odysseus could have the worst trip of his life.

The Odyssey is available now on digital and physical formats.

#3366. One 1960s Star Trek Episode Made Spock Nasty For No Reason

The Star Trek universe is full of nasty little things that can make a person act out of character. Pass through the galactic barrier and develop a god complex. Touch some red stuff, and your crew mates are suddenly waving swords around shirtless. It's just another day in Starfleet. Sometimes, however, the only explanation for a character acting strangely is inconsistent writing, as is the case with Spock in Star Trek: The Original Series season 3's "That Which Survives."

Spock is, of course, very well known for his dedication to logic and empirical proof. He rejects emotional judgments in favor of scientific deductions, and regularly finds himself confused by the subjective whims of human colleagues. Crucially, though, Spock is not cruel or mocking when expressing his Vulcan perspective. Leonard Nimoy's character may not fully understand why humans act the way they do, but he at least acknowledges and respects the difference between species.

If McCoy suggests a course of action driven by the heart, Spock offers one driven by the head. If Kirk does something silly, Spock responds with "fascinating," and adds another mental entry to his ongoing study into the chaotic nature of humankind.

That's not what happens in "That Which Survives."

This particular episode sees Spock berate colleagues for using metaphors. He aggressively corrects them when they offer any degree of approximate measurement. Anyone who dares offer an opinion gets shot down with a verbal bullet of cold logic. And it happens in virtually every scene Spock's present for. Making other Enterprise officers feel small becomes his entire character.

While most Star Trek episodes play the 'Spock gets super-logical' card at some point, it's far more intense in "That Which Survives," almost like the Vulcan is expecting every other crew member to think the way he does, and he's surprised when they're incapable of doing so. Anyone would think this is Spock's first time working alongside so many Earthlings.

One might think that Spock's change in attitude is due to spending most of "That Which Survives" in charge of the Enterprise, with Captain Kirk stranded on an alien planet. But there are plenty of episodes where Spock "has the Conn," and in none of them does he transform into the boss from hell.

More to the point, Spock's attitude in the episode is... highly illogical.

As the Vulcan himself should know, expecting humans to think like his own people is a futile endeavor. All he's doing as stand-in captain is lowering morale on the bridge. Uhura and Lt. Rahda (Sulu's temporary replacement) appear to shrink in the face of Spock's withering criticism, while Scotty, in the middle of performing a delicate repair that could blow up the entire ship, is pressured by Spock's constant countdown and calls his superior officer a "cuckoo clock" through grimaced teeth.

Ultimately, going around the bridge and making the people you're expecting to save the day feel useless isn't very productive.

Spock may enjoy some lively disagreements with Dr. McCoy during his Enterprise career, but "That Which Survives" marks a rare occasion where Nimoy's character comes across as genuinely unlikable to other characters.

One explanation is the teleplay being written by John Meredyth Lucas. A producer on Star Trek's second season, Lucas is only credited as a writer on a handful of other episodes. Of those, the only one that features Spock heavily is "Patterns of Force," which couldn't be more different in its setup to "That Which Survives." Perhaps Lucas simply viewed Spock's command style differently compared to the rest of the show.

Rather than attributing Spock's odd attitude to the episode's writer, another possible explanation is that the inconsistency came about due to Star Trek's ongoing struggle with quality in season 3. Kirk's Enterprise found itself limping toward cancellation at this point, so expert characterization might simply be too much to ask for.

#3365. New camera sensor coming to the iPhone 20 Pro’s main camera, says leaker

The biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch.

A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear …

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

The second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

We’ve seen two previous reports suggesting that a larger sensor is on the way for future iPhones. One of these suggested that it would be coming in 2027 or 2028, although a later one suggested the latter date was more likely.

The reports were not without a catch, however, suggesting that the larger sensor would only be for the telephoto lens and would have a 200MP resolution. Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an issue with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

A brief report from leaker Ice Universe suggests that the iPhone 20 Pro will get a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera.

iPhone 20 Pro to feature a new sensor using 17nm logic process for its main camera next year.

(Under Apple’s current naming system, next year’s iPhone Pro would be the iPhone 19 Pro. However, it’s widely expected that Apple will jump to the iPhone 20 nomenclature in order to mark a significant design upgrade for the 20th anniversary of the device.)

There are no further details, so we don’t know whether the size of the sensor will be increased or remain the same.

#3364. Microsoft outage saw 80% of servers fail – here’s what happened

Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The company has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected …

The company said at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs announced the previous month.

Users were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Sorry but you have to be change the name now. Thems the rules pic.twitter.com/5UttZ8nt9f

It certainly points out that when you base your business on cloud services, you also take the risk that comes with that.

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He said it resulted from a combination of two issues. The company maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […]

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the update wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

While the company claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the update. #3362. Faizon Love Sued Over Alleged Comedy Show No-Show Amid Child Support Drama

Faizon Love is being sued for allegedly skipping out on a $12,500 comedy show ... and the promoter claims his child support troubles were already raising red flags before the gig.

According to new legal documents obtained by TMZ, event promoter Inga Harden says she booked Love for a July 17 benefit supporting local businesses in Florence, Alabama and claims she shelled out $6,250 upfront for the comedian to perform for at least an hour.

But, according to the complaint, weeks before the show, Love's child support drama in Florida had her worried he might not show up ... so Harden says her attorney reached out to Love's agent, Eric Young, to make sure everything was still on.

She claims Young called back and questioned why everyone was "panicking."

According to the suit, things got even messier 11 days before showtime ... when Harden claims an attorney representing a woman seeking child support from Love contacted her, demanding she withhold a portion of any money owed to him and warning she could face sanctions.

Ultimately, Harden claims Love never showed up ... and she says nobody from his team gave her a heads-up that he wasn't coming.

As we previously reported, Love was arrested in Florida in June on contempt of court charges tied to his case with Tiffany Lee, who claims he owes around $250K in child support.

Harden says she demanded her deposit back, but never got a refund. Instead, she received a mysterious $1 Cash App notification days later, followed by a text allegedly from Young asking her to verify her account. The suit doesn't say who exactly sent the dollar.

The promoter is suing Love, Young and Young's company for $6,436.50 in remaining deposit money and fees ... plus additional damages.

#3361. Severance Meets Harlan Coben In New Disney+ Series Adaptation

Severance meets Harlan Coben's mystery novels in a new Disney+ series adaptation.

Disney+ has announced a new adaptation of a published novel, which will bring together elements of cryptic mystery to create a memorable new series on the platform. Disney+ original series have ranged across the board for various audiences. From the forthcoming return of Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3, to a number of K-dramas exclusive to the platform, Disney provides audiences with a bit of everything across the board. Such is the case with its next big adaptation.

Deadline has confirmed British comedian Bob Mortimer's debut novel The Satsuna Complex is being adapted into a Disney+ original series. Mortimer, whose recent work includes the comedic reality TV show LOL: Last One Laughing, will serve as creator, writer, and executive producer on the series. Production company Quay Street will serve as producers, with boss Nicola Shindler serving as an executive producer. Mortimer and Shindler released statements about the forthcoming series, expressing excitement for its development and teasing what to expect.

Check out what Mortimer and Shindler had to say below:

Bob Mortimer: I am majorly chuffed and fully carbonated by the news that Gary and his friends and enemies are to be brought to life by Disney+ and Quay Street Productions.

Nicola Shindler: [The Satsuna Complex is] unmistakably Bob: brilliantly funny, wonderfully distinctive and full of heart, with a gripping mystery at its centre.

First published in the United Kingdom in 2022, The Satsuna Complex follows South London legal assistant Gary Thorn who, while out to a pub with his friend Brendan, meets a mysterious woman. He has a short but memorable conversation with her but doesn't catch her name, only seeing that she was reading a book titled The Satsuna Complex. The next morning, Brendan is found dead, leading Gary to investigate what happened to his friend, and how the mystery woman may be tied to everything.

The Satsuna Complex was inspired by the writings of Japanese author Haruki Murakami. It went on to win the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize in 2023 for best comic fiction. The book is described as funny, while also peeling back plenty of layers for its characters and mystery to make it a compelling read. Its translation onscreen is promising, as it means the book can showcase all its strengths from the page to streaming. Since the source material was so well-decorated, the TV show has a chance to experience the same fate.

As of writing, there hasn't been any confirmation about the series' cast, nor any other details about its production. The Satsuna Complex was greenlit for Hulu and Disney+ by Hulu's vice president of scripted content, Lee Mason, and the head of content at Disney+, Angela Jain. The news of the series' development comes one day after Disney confirmed projected spending on original content will increase by 9% next year, alongside intentions to triple its original output across both streaming platforms.

The Satsuna Complex is in a strong position to perform well for Disney. Mortimer's involvement coupled with the title having such a strong history means it's likely its translation into a mystery TV show will do right by the source material. Since the comedian himself is also overseeing production, it seems like the adaptation is guaranteed to maintain the author's original vision. With development still in early stages, it remains to be seen when the series' production will begin in full force.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3354. HomeView missing some podcast feeds? Here’s why

Apple’s new HomeView features the Podcasts app, but not all feeds appear to be supported for now. Instead, HomeView appears to have the same bug that tvOS 27 introduced to the Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

tvOS 27.0 added playback support for HLS-based video podcasts on Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

The same update introduced a bug that dropped support for syncing shows manually added via URL.

The new Apple HomeView appears to have this same bug. Video podcasts using HLS technology are supported, but shows added via URL do not work.

As of tvOS 27.3 beta 1, the bug is still present on Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and newer.

Because tvOS 27 doesn’t run on Apple TV 4K 1st-gen, URL-based subscriptions still work in the Podcasts app — just not HLS-based video feeds.

Anyway, if you’re missing certain feeds in the Podcasts app on HomeView, this is likely the reason.

#3353. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3352. Heidi Gardner's Late Boyfriend Ray Tintori Recorded Podcast Days Before Death

'SNL' star Heidi Gardner's late boyfriend Ray Tintori was working right up until days before his sudden death ... and now his best friend is making sure their final conversation together gets heard.

Jordan Fish, who co-hosted the podcast "To the White Sea" with the late filmmaker, revealed the two recorded an episode just days before Ray died at 43.

Fish shared an emotional tribute on social media Tuesday, calling Ray his "best friend and lifelong collaborator" and saying the loss was sudden and devastating ... revealing their final recording featured the cast of "Waiting," an Ethan Coen one-act play the longtime friends produced and directed at Spring Break.

Fish says he's now preparing the episode for release, telling listeners he's eager for them to hear the pair's "jovial and in-depth conversation" about their work together and the production.

Despite losing his longtime friend and creative partner, Fish says the podcast will continue, adding he believes Ray would want them to finish the script.

We broke the story … Ray -- who was dating former "Saturday Night Live" star Heidi Gardner -- died at age 43, after fire and EMS personnel went to his residence for a welfare check and discovered him. His cause and manner of death have not been released.

Ray had an impressive filmmaking résumé, directing music videos for MGMT, Arcade Fire and The Killers. His work included MGMT's "Electric Feel" and "Kids," Arcade Fire's "Chemistry" and The Killers' "Spaceman." He also appeared as a cameraman in Timothée Chalamet's "Marty Supreme."

Ray and Heidi made their relationship public in July 2025, when he shared a heartfelt birthday tribute to her, describing her as the coolest person he'd ever met and saying she held his heart perfectly.

Every week, I cast an eye over the latest arrivals on Prime Video, all in an effort to pick out the latest thrillers added to the streaming service library.

While November continues to be dominated by Christmas movies, I've still been able to find three worthwhile thrillers. Okay, so one is more of an action-horror, but it does have its share of thriller-style twists and turns. The other two are a psychological trip and an '80s classic starring Matthew "Ferris Bueller" Broderick. Each one is worthy of your streaming consideration.

So, let's jump into the three new to Prime Video thriller movies I recommend you watch this week.

Perhaps the most “traditional” thriller among my picks this week, “Blink Twice” might not reinvent the genre, but it’s an intense watch that slowly builds tension until a shocking twist. It marked the directorial debut of Zoë Kravitz, and stars Naomi Ackie, most recently seen in “Clayface,” alongside Channing Tatum. It’s an effective first filmmaking effort from Kravitz, even if it’s perhaps not quite as intelligently plotted as the strong first act suggests.

Frida (Naomi Ackie) is a cocktail waitress at a swanky party where she meets tech tycoon Slater King (Channing Tatum). Invited to his private island for a vacation of unparalleled luxury, Frida and her friend Jess (Alia Shawkat) initially think they’ve found paradise, and Frida might have even found love with the charming tech mogul. But as lazy sun-soaked days blur into nights of glamorous partying, Frida can’t shake an uneasy feeling that something is wrong.

Three years before starring in one of the most popular movies of the 1980s, Matthew Broderick made his breakthrough with his second major feature film role. He might have made his debut in “Max Dugan Returns” in the spring of 1983. However, it was the techno-thriller “Wargames” released in the summer that saw Broderick identified as a talent to watch, and, well, those labeling him a rising star at the time were certainly proved right.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Sure, it’s a little outdated in the 21st century, but "Wargames" is still a compelling mix of technology-driven thrills and teen drama. David Lightman (Broderick) is a gifted high schooler but with a lazy streak. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers to unknowingly access a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. Unaware that he’s playing with real weapons of war and thinking he’s playing a video game, he might have ignited World War III.

Rounding out my picks this week is “They Will Kill You,” a real genre-blender that mixes action, horror, comedy, and thriller elements into a movie that isn’t exactly tonally consistent, but does have quite a few slick moments. Most notably, there's a very fiery action sequence and a satisfying early reveal that flips the storyline on its head. It’s also a great showcase for Zazie Beetz, who is best known for her TV roles in “Atlanta,” “Easy” and “Invincible.”

Asia (Beetz) arrives at a posh New York City high-rise apartment building posing as a maid, but she’s really hoping to find her missing sister. Once in the complex, she discovers it’s not just home to the city's wealthy and elite, but houses a satanic cult. I’ll say no more for fear of spoiling the surprises within this action-horror, but let’s say things get very bloody, very fast. “They Will Kill You” is stylish, taking cues from Quentin Tarantino, even if it never matches the iconic director’s sharp writing and memorable characters.

#3350. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.
