#3349. Rod Wave Indicted on Drug Possession, Gun Charges

Rod Wave has been indicted on drug and gun charges ... after he was arrested last year for allegedly blowing through a stop sign.

The rapper has been charged in Georgia with possession of a Schedule II controlled substance, possession of a firearm during commission of a felony, and reckless driving.

According to a report from the local outlet Atlanta News First ... an officer alleges they saw Rod, whose real name is Rodarius Marcell Green, speed through a stop sign in a residential neighborhood.

The officer says they followed Rod to a parking lot ... and told him he was being arrested for reckless driving when he stepped out of the vehicle.

The officer claims they then found drugs and multiple guns in the car ... including oxycodone in a backpack. Per the report, Rod Wave allegedly admitted the backpack was his during the arrest.

This is just the latest legal issue for Rod ... who recently asked a judge to throw out evidence prosecutors want to use against him from an April arrest. In that case, Rod was booked on 14 charges, including aggravated assault involving the use of a firearm.

Despite the legal issues, Rod's spirits may be picked up slightly by other events in his life ... after all, his song "Sinners" -- from the movie "Sinners" -- has been nominated for a Grammy.

Rod Wave's attorneys Drew Findling, Marissa Goldberg and Zack Findling tell TMZ ... Rod "was unjustly profiled and unlawfully arrested in Atlanta. The arresting officer belongs to the Atlanta Police Department's controversial Crime Suppression Unit -- a group known for its aggressive tactics and emphasis on high arrest numbers rather than genuine public safety."

They add Wave was targeted because of the unit's "quota-driven approach" ... a practice they say completely undermines true justice as well as trust in the community. The lawyers say they looked forward to defending Rod and pointing out the "clear violations of [his] rights in court."

Jordan, who appeared on Gabby Windey and Rachel Recchia's Season 19 of "The Bachelorette" and Season 9 of "Bachelor in Paradise," just wrapped up a breakout 2026 season in the NHRA ... finishing third in the Funny Car championships during his rookie year behind the wheel of a 12,000 horsepower nitro machine.

But Jordan's road back wasn't a straight shot ... after competing in 11 Top Fuel events in 2019, he spent years away from the driver's seat, later returning as a FOX Sports NHRA reporter in 2024 and 2025.

Not too shabby for a guy whose career once took a detour through reality TV!

With John Force Racing preparing for its 50th anniversary season in 2027, Jordan has given the legendary team plenty to be excited about!

The deals cover quite a few different networking needs, from compact travel routers that let you connect multiple devices to hotel wifi to more powerful home routers designed for faster internet plans and households with lots of connected devices.

TP-Link’s Roam routers are compact enough to travel with and let you share a hotel or public internet connection across your devices through a private Wi-Fi network—and right now, Amazon has three models on sale: the Roam 6 AX1500 for $44.99 (was $59.99), the Roam 6 AX3000 for $55.98 (was $79.99), and the Roam 7 BE3600 for $87.99 (was $119.99). Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3334. I spent 4 weeks testing a $319 headband designed to beat insomnia but slept better the night I stopped using it — here's what happened

The Spatial Sleep Headband uses audio resonance therapy to improve your sleep but it's an uphill climb to get there. Vibrating your skull while filling your brain with unusual noises, the first few nights are rough going, but it does eventually pay off... slightly. The soothing noises became a pleasant bedtime addition but any sleep changes were minimal. At $319, it's a heavy investment in tech that takes a while to show results.

Clinical research suggests it can help insomnia

First few weeks are disruptive to your sleep

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When you can't sleep, you'll try anything to drift off. But I can almost guarantee you've never tried something like the Spatial Sleep Headband. This peculiar wearable uses acoustic resonance to send you snoozing. I put it to the test and yes, it's as weird as it sounds.

Type: Sleep headbandBest for: Insomnia, trouble falling asleepDimensions: 4" x 7.8" x 3.7"Weight: 2.5 ozWarranty: 90 days limitedPrice: $319 at SoundHealth

The Spatial Sleep Band sits on your forehead where it vibrates and plays sound. With regular use this combo should train your brain's neural response to build better sleep, no hard work required. Although I'll be honest, the Spatial Sleep Band isn't what I'd describe as easy.

I used the Spatial Sleep headband nightly for four weeks and I'll dive into my full experience below. In brief, it's an odd sensation and one that comes with a steep learning curve. And while eventually the Spatial Sleep Band does become a soothing addition to your bedtime routine, it's a struggle to get to that point.

As someone with only mild sleep issues, I've yet to see any real benefit from the Spatial Sleep Band. And the adjustment period was frustrating enough that I'd have given up if it wasn't my job to keep going. For those with more severe sleep problems, the annoyance of the Spatial Sleep Headband will likely feel like less of an intrusion, and the benefits more noticeable.

But it's an expensive gamble, with a Spatial Sleep Headband costing $319 (although that's slightly more affordable than similar sleep headbands like the Muse S Athena and the Elemind). You do get a 45-day return period as well, and by that point you should have a good idea if this product is for you. And it's subscription-free — that's rare for this kind of sleep tech.

The Spatial Sleep Headband costs $319 — an investment, for sure, but this is a fairly standard price tag for a high-tech sleep aid. There's no subscription required and a 45-day returns policy is included.

The overall design of the Spatial Sleep Headband is relatively simple. The slim band is made from a soft material and the Velcro strap is easy to adjust.

Its secret lies on the inside, where you'll find two purple nodules. These press against the forehead and deliver the acoustic vibration that makes the Spatial Headband work.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There's one more important part to the Spatial and that's the three lines on the front of the design. These are used to align the band with the center of your face, to ensure the sound is delivered to the right part of the forehead.

I used the Spatial Sleep Headband for four weeks as part of my usual routine, wearing it to bed (with an eye mask). Here's how I rate the performance...

Setting up the Spatial Sleep Headband is simple, for a piece of complex tech. First you have to charge it, then turn the headband on (there's a button on the front) and connect it to the app.

You'll be asked to scan your face — this helps Spatial create a sound just right for you. When you're ready to sleep, get the band in position and press start on the app.

The sound automatically plays for 45 minutes, at which point you should be asleep (fingers crossed). You can pause and restart the sound from the app, in case of late night wake ups.

The battery lasts for roughly 90 minutes, or two sessions, and I have used mine through two nights without charging. However, I recommend charging after every session, to avoid the sound cutting out. A USB-C cable is provided and charging takes roughly 30 minutes.

The app is mostly used to kick off the audio at night, but there's a fun memory game you can play as well.

I'm normally game for testing any kind of weird sleep tech but when I first strapped the Spatial Band to my head, I felt like I'd made a terrible mistake. Nodules pressed into my forehead and my bones rattled to a dissonant hum that sounded like pans clattering to the ground in the distance. I clenched my jaw and waited for it to end.

There was an important lesson here, echoed in the bright red dents on my forehead: do not over-tighten the band.

With a slightly looser band, night two went better. But the first week was rough. The sound and sensations of the Spatial Headband are far removed from my usual sleep comforts. I was hoping using it would help me drift off quickly but instead I lay awake, questioning the life choices that had led me to this moment.

Spatial does warn that it takes persistence before you see results and week two went better. The sound and I had gotten used to each other, meaning it no longer sat at the forefront of my mind. Now I enjoyed a pleasant background hum and only occasionally worried about my vibrating skull.

By week three I could see a glimmer of progress. The distant drone of the sleep headband had grown relaxing. One night, on the brink of sleep, I even found myself wondering what the pleasant noise was.

These benefits have yet to be reflected in my sleep score, however. On some nights it still takes me up upwards of 30 minutes to drift off fully. And I'm still experiencing brief wake ups in the night. (Including waking up to take the headband off — the nodules are uncomfortable when they press against your face.)

Last night, having reached the end of my four weeks testing period, I decided to ditch the headband and go back to my usual sleep patterns. I got an 88 sleep score from my Oura Ring, my highest in 12 nights.

As someone with only minor sleep problems, the Spatial Sleep Headband is a steep learning curve for a small advantage. But I don't want to write it off entirely. There are strong reviews from other users and Spatial has conducted some notable research. Spatial is designed to improve your natural sleep frequency, so for those who have a sleep routine that's completely off-beat, the Spatial sleep might help set the pace you need.

The Spatial Headband uses acoustic vibrations and sleep-friendly frequencies to improve the quality and quantity of your sleep. It requires regular use to see the results and after several weeks the strange hum of the Spatial should be the backdrop to a decent night's rest.

The problem is that those first weeks are challenging, to put it mildly. From the sound to the feel, the Spatial band is simply strange to use. It feels like a disruptive force and you might be tempted to give up before you feel the benefits. Or rather, if you feel the benefits — I stuck with mine and noticed only minor differences.

✅ You're experiencing long-term sleep deprivation: The Spatial Sleep Headband didn't work for me but it is backed by some serious research. Its impact might be more noticeable when overcoming bigger sleep problems.

✅ You've tried all kinds of sleep tech and nothing works: Acoustic resonance is unusual and not the kind of sleep enhancer you pick up on a whim. If you're struggling to improve your sleep, this might be worth a try.

✅ You're kept awake by disruptive noise: When the Spatial band is on, it drowns out most other sounds. That's good news if traffic or rowdy neighbors are contributing to your sleep problems.

❌ You want a quick solution: Spatial suggests it takes three to four weeks to feel the benefit of the Sleep Headband, and I found week one to be a steep learning curve. The Muse S Athena sleep headband was much easier to get used to.

❌ You share a bed with a light sleeper: Some sound does leak from the Spatial headband which might disturb co-sleepers.

❌ You want a small sleep boost, rather than a total overhaul: For minor sleep issues the Spatial Sleep Band is a pricey investment that takes time to get used to. Try low-cost options like sleepy tea and guided meditations before diving in with the Spatial.

The Muse S Athena uses your brainwaves to track your sleep and, when it senses you're about to be disturbed, plays a sleep-inducing sound to send you back under. I tested it and found the performance impressive but it is a premium buy, retailing for $479.99 at Muse and Amazon.

The Snoozeband isn't as high-tech as the other options listed here but this comfortable set of sleep headphones can help you drift off in noisy environments. It utilizes thin speakers in a soft headband to deliver sleep sounds without the discomfort of an earbud. From $49.99 at Snoozeband.

#3332. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Soundbars From Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3331. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

In another clip, you can't hear what she's saying, but you can see her on their front porch trying to talk to them through the window.

Erica wrote in the caption ... "So, this is what I'm dealing with," adding she's got private security in place, called the LAPD a few times, and has contacted mental health protocol.

The Mary Mary singer also said their daughter had FaceTimed her to say she'd seen a strange lady -- who'd come by their house before -- in their backyard.

She emphasizes the seriousness of the situation ... saying what's happening is "not a joke" and "not a game" -- adding her post comes after telling her church congregation that someone had allegedly slashed their tires.

Erica and Warryn have been together for more than two decades, tying the knot in 2001. The couple share three children together.

#3328. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3327. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.
